outlier.title: Flushed DRAM rows read DRAM latency, not SLC (DC CIVAC reaches the SLC)
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001, Jesse's results dated 2026-10-31), analysed 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-02
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Run 1 had flushed DRAM rows at 256 KiB, 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB. Flushed means every line was cleaned and invalidated with DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate-by-address instruction) before one timed pass. The 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB flushed rows read 52.716, 52.714, 52.713 and 52.711 ns per load (best of 3 reps) [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:12, :17, :22, :27]. The fresh 32 MiB chain (a random pointer chain walked once, never flushed) read 52.300 ns per load [latency-dram-large.csv:46]. The fresh 512 KiB to 2 MiB chains read 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load [latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :22], and the fresh 3 MiB chain 25.449 ns [latency-dram-large.csv:26]. The SLC (system level cache, in the CMN mesh) that caches DRAM is 3.75 MiB [membench-jibin-001 README.md:23]. A 1 to 3 MiB footprint fits that SLC. So the 1 to 3 MiB flushed rows were expected near the fresh-chain values of the same sizes (23.8 to 25.4 ns), not at the DRAM value. The 256 KiB flushed row read 35.689 ns with 0.78 to 0.90 L3 read refills per load, a separate defect (prefetch on a re-walked chain) [latency-dram-flushed.csv:4 to :7].
outlier.why_wrong: The flush was meant to clear only the core caches (L1, L2, DSU L3). The refill counters show that each timed load missed every core cache: 1.00 L1, L2 and L3 read refills per load on every flushed row from 1 MiB up [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:9 to :26]. The time per load equals the 32 MiB fresh chain within 0.42 ns. So DC CIVAC also removed the DRAM-backed lines from the SLC, and the timed pass read DRAM [membench-jibin-001 README.md:36; run1-report.html:471; RUN2-PLAN.md:74 to :76]. Such a row cannot stand for an SLC hit. OCM rows were unaffected (OCM lines are locked SLC ways; see the OCM-mode entry).

tests_added.name: Shrink the flushed DRAM rows to one 8 MiB row, run as a fresh chain plus flush (latency --cpu 2 --perf --fresh 3 --flush --sizes 8M), and keep it as the DRAM reference. Drop the 256 KiB and the 1 to 3 MiB flushed rows. Run 1's flushed rows had used --flush --reps 3 (fresh=0: a chain already walked twice in warm-up); run 2's row is fresh=3 [run_asimov.sh:24 to :32, :114 to :115; membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:1; membench-jibin-002 latency-dram-flushed.csv:1]. The SLC is taken from the fresh chains instead.

outlier.what_tests_showed: Run 2: the flushed 8 MiB row read 52.712 ns per load [membench-jibin-002 latency-dram-flushed.csv:6] and the fresh 32 MiB chain 52.233 ns [latency-dram-large.csv:46], a gap of 0.48 ns, inside the 1 ns criterion [RUN2-PLAN.md:502]. The flushed 8 MiB row has stayed the DRAM reference on every later run: 52.711 ns (control run 003), 52.738 (run 3, 004), 52.739 (boots A, B, D), 52.657 (boot C, 007 bootC/latency-dram-flushed.csv:7), 52.659 (boot E, 010 bootE/latency-dram-flushed.csv:7), 52.658 (boot F1, 011). The SLC is quoted from the 2 MiB fresh chain: 24.053 ns on boot C [007 bootC/latency-dram-large.csv:23] and 24.177 ns on boot E [010 bootE/latency-dram-large.csv:23]. The core page states it as 'from the SLC in 24.2 ns and from DRAM in 52.7 ns (every line flushed)' and its table 4.1 labels the 2 MiB fresh row 'SLC (mesh cache)' and the 8 MiB flushed row (52.659 / 52.738 / 52.657 ns on E / run 3 / C) 'DRAM' [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, short version and table 4.1]. The run 4 pages chart the same row as 'core, random chain, every line flushed, 8 MiB: 52.7 ns per load' [asimov-c1nano-run4.html; asimov-cme-run4.html].

outlier.title: Flushed OCM rows stay at 19 to 26 ns: way locking or CMN OCM mode?
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001, ran 2026-10-31); the question was written in run1-report.html on 2026-11-01 and answered by Jesse's agent on 2026-11-01 21:37 PST
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Every flushed OCM row in run 1 read 18.8 to 25.5 ns per load on the best rows (18.8 to 26.0 ns over all nine single reps) [results/membench-jibin-001/results/19700101T000000Z/latency-ocm-region0..4.csv and latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv]. The same DC CIVAC flush (clean and invalidate from the core caches) pushed DRAM-backed lines out of the SLC: the flushed DRAM rows of 1 to 8 MiB read 52.7 ns per load, the DRAM value [latency-dram-flushed.csv best rows 52.716, 52.714, 52.713, 52.711 ns; results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 36]. The 256 KiB flushed DRAM row read 35.7 ns best (44.7, 39.0, 35.7 ns across its three reps) because some of its lines were prefetched [README 001 line 34]. OCM (on-chip memory, 4 locked SLC ways of each home node, 256 KiB per region) kept its data through the flush. No memory sits behind OCM [README.md lines 40 to 46].
outlier.why_wrong: The question was how the OCM lock is set up. A plain locked range (hnf_slc_lock_ways and lock_base) and the CMN OCM mode behave differently on a flush. The Arm CMN S3 TRM says a CleanInvalid of an OCM-mode line does nothing in the SLC. It also says a locked line in a normal range can be pushed to memory by a non-allocating request [run1-report.html line 491, tags stripped]. Run 1 showed that the data stayed, so the question was about interpretation and not about safety [same line]. The claim that OCM mode needs a power-of-two number of home nodes is not in any primary file, plan, page or memory note in this folder (Insufficient data: the CMN S3 TRM text is not in refs/).

outlier.what_tests_showed: OCM is CMN OCM mode. The home node sends no requests to memory. A CleanInvalid or CleanShared terminates in the SLC and does not invalidate the line [memory note asimov-run1-facts.md, from Jesse's agent reply of 2026-11-01, checked against the SCP source and the TRM; README.md lines 40 to 46; RUN2-PLAN.md line 63]. Node ids 88, 160, 216, 288 and 344 hold OCM0 to OCM4 [README.md line 37; RUN2-PLAN.md line 64]. Run 2 confirmed both points on the chip. The per-region rows from CPU 2 with fresh chains plus a flush read 18.46 to 22.00 ns per load (best rows 19.770, 18.456, 21.355, 21.535, 22.001 ns), against 18.78 to 23.17 ns in run 1 [results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv; README 002 section Against round one]. In each of the 20 per-region rows the region's own home node received 111,468 to 123,460 requests, against 9,042 to 10,576 at each other node, so the node ids are right [README 002 section Mesh counts]. The flush-based OCM rows are safe by design. The four generated pages (asimov-c1nano-perf.html, asimov-cme-perf.html, asimov-c1nano-run4.html, asimov-cme-run4.html) do not mention the lock mode; they carry the node ids only.

outlier.title: OCM write and copy rows at 7.2 and 12.0 GB/s timed the flush, not the write
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31; Jesse's note in README.md line 35 that three OCM row kinds were timed without a flush first
outlier.what_looked_wrong: One core (CPU 2) wrote OCM1 (256 KiB, --flush-after, one pass) at 7.18 GB/s [membench-jibin-001 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7; command in log.txt:29]. The same core copied OCM1 to OCM2 (256 KiB, --flush-before --flush-after) at 11.96 GB/s [bandwidth-ocm-copy.csv:7; log.txt:30]. Four cores writing one region each read 29.2 GB/s, 7.2 to 7.4 GB/s per core [bandwidth-ocm-4core.csv:14]. The same core writes DRAM at 30.6 to 32.0 GB/s at every footprint from 16 KiB to 32 MiB [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11,26,41,56,71,86]. The write row took 36.5 to 36.6 us (262,144 bytes at 7.16 to 7.18 GB/s; the CSV's elapsed_s column prints 37 us at 1 us resolution) [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:4-6]. 256 KiB of stores at 32 GB/s take 8.2 us. The copy row took 43.8 us (524,288 bytes at 11.965 GB/s) [bandwidth-ocm-copy.csv:5].
outlier.why_wrong: With --flush-after the timed region held the 256 KiB of stores plus the DC CIVAC (clean and invalidate by address) of 4,096 lines [run1-report.html section 5a, citing bandwidth.c:248 to 254; RUN2-PLAN.md lines 77-81]. The stores take 8.2 us at the core's 32 GB/s store rate. The remaining 28.3 us is the flush, about 6.9 ns per line (est.). So 7.2 GB/s is the rate of stores into the core caches followed by a serial write-back to OCM, not a streaming OCM write rate. The copy row (43.8 us) is about 16 us of loads from OCM1 and about 28 us of the flush of OCM2 (est.) [run1-report.html section 5a]. The 4-core write row has the same defect. A 256 KiB write cannot be measured from one core anyway: it fits in L2 plus L3 (128 KiB + 256 KiB = 384 KiB), so the lines never leave the cluster during the timed pass [run1-report.html section 5a; RUN2-PLAN.md lines 121-127]. Jesse's README found three OCM row kinds timed without a flush first (run_asimov.sh lines 113, 126, 128 and 147: the all-five fresh-chain latency, the four-pass all-five read, and the write rows flushed after inside the timed region), against the README's rule that every timed OCM pass starts flushed [membench-jibin-001 README.md line 35].

tests_added.name: Streaming OCM write over all five regions, one core: bandwidth --threads 1 --cpus 2 --mem ocm --ocm-regions 0,1,2,3,4 --bytes 1280K --kernel write --flush-before --passes 8 --reps 3 [membench-jibin-002 log.txt:59]. The 1.25 MiB buffer is 3.3 times the 384 KiB of L2 plus L3, so lines reach OCM by eviction during the passes [RUN2-PLAN.md lines 121-127]. The write-then-flush row, the copy row and the 4-core OCM write row were dropped [RUN2-PLAN.md lines 228-232]. (run1-report.html section 5a proposed 4 passes; the plan and the run used 8.)

outlier.what_tests_showed: Run 2: one core writes OCM at 20.3 to 20.4 GB/s over the three reps, best 20.433 GB/s [membench-jibin-002 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:4-7], the first clean number. Jesse noted it sits below one core's 32.0 GB/s store rate to DRAM [membench-jibin-002 README.md line 86]. The control run (run 2's code on run 1's firmware) reads 20.338 GB/s [membench-jibin-003 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7]. Run 3: core 20.326 GB/s [membench-jibin-004 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7], CME 19.795 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7], while the CME writes DRAM at 62.0 to 63.9 GB/s at every footprint [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11,26,41,56,71,86,101,116] and the core writes DRAM at 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11-86]. Run 6 boot F1 (L3 on): the core's OCM write stays at 20.326 GB/s, unchanged to three decimals [membench-jibin-011 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7; asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.6], while the CME's OCM write rises to 30.659 GB/s by the bracket and 30.977 GB/s in span, 1.549 times run 3 [membench-jibin-011 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7; README.md line 317]. Boot F2 (prefetchers off): CME 30.994 GB/s bracket, 31.327 in span [membench-jibin-012 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7]. Why the core's OCM write sits at 20.3 GB/s, below its 32 GB/s DRAM store rate, is not explained in any primary file. The OCM and DRAM write rows differ in two ways that the files name only for the CME's OCM read rows: page size (OCM in 4 KiB pages, DRAM buffers in 2 MiB pages) and flush state (the OCM write row is flushed once before its 8 passes per rep, the DRAM write rows are never flushed) [membench-jibin-004 README.md line 84; CSV header lines]. No test separates these two.

outlier.title: 256 KiB OCM rows count fewer than 1.0 L3 refills and more than 1.0 L2 refills per load (prefetcher fills)
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001), ran 2026-10-31 [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 3]; counted again on run 2 (002, 2026-11-02), run 3 (004, 2026-11-03), run 4 boots A (005, 2026-11-04) and B (006, 2026-11-04/05)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Every 256 KiB flushed row in run 1 (the five OCM region rows and the DRAM 256 KiB row) counted 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load and 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills (event 0x17) per load [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv]. Rows of 1 MiB and more counted 1.00 of each (DRAM flushed 1 to 8 MiB: 1.0001 to 1.0012; OCM all-five flushed 1.25 MiB: 1.0004 to 1.0012). Run 2's fresh chains (a chain never walked before each timed pass) did not change it: the 40 timed passes of the 20 per-region rows counted 0.76 to 0.95 L3 and 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv]. In 19 of those 20 rows the faster pass is the one with fewer L3 read refills [002 README line 66]. Run 3's sparse chains (one member line per 4 KiB page) counted 1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills and 0.47 to 1.14 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 140 passes; 004 README line 111]. The run 1 DRAM 256 KiB row got faster as its L3 count fell: 44.698, 39.031 and 35.689 ns per load at 0.9043, 0.8459 and 0.7839 L3 read refills per load [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv reps 0 to 2].
outlier.why_wrong: A dependent chain asks for one line per load. So each cache level should show at most 1.00 refills per load. Fewer than 1.00 L3 read refills means 9 to 23 % of the lines were already inside the cluster when the load asked for them (1 minus 0.91, 1 minus 0.77). More than 1.00 L2 refills means the L2 filled lines the chain never asked for. The run 1 to run 3 counter set (0x03 L1 refills, 0x17 L2 refills, 0xA2 L3 read refills) counts fills by level, not by cause [common.h line 336]. So a hardware prefetcher was a hypothesis, not a measurement, until run 4. A second fact only run 4 boot B showed: the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data on runs 1 to 3 and boots A and B (snoop-filter-only mode), so 'L3 read refill' on these rows means a demand read that left the cluster, and the early-arriving lines sat in the L2 [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1].

outlier.what_tests_showed: Run 2: fresh chains did not help (0.76 to 0.95 L3, 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load) [002 README line 66]. Run 3: sparse rows were not cleaner (1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills per load); the dense all-five control read 25.340 ns per load against run 2's 25.506 ns, a 0.166 ns gap, with 1.00 refills per load at L1, L2 and L3 [004 README line 110]. The dense all-five chain is the OCM number the pages quote [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Short version]. Boot A: the three new events count (on the sequential 8 MiB chain 0x81BC reads 0.9999 and 0x0111 0.9999 per load beside 1.0000 L1 and L2 refills, at 6.917 ns per load) [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.1]. On every OCM row, L2 refills minus 0x81BD equal the L3 read refills: the row means differ by -0.022 to +0.000 per load [table 3.4]; single 64-load passes differ by -0.125 to +0.016 (one pass counts in steps of 1/64) [005 CSVs, 218 rows recomputed]. So the extra fills are made by a hardware prefetcher that targets the L2: 0x81BD per load, row means, dense per-region rows 0.236 to 0.459, sparse 1.112 to 2.223, vary 1.152 to 2.980, all-five sparse 1.051 to 1.066, all-five dense 0.000 [table 3.4]. The L1 prefetcher made none: 0x81BC and 0x0111 read 0.000 on every OCM row [table 3.4; 005 CSVs]. Also, 0xA2 does not count prefetch fills: on the sequential chain it reads 0.0001 per load while L2 refills read 1.0000 [table 3.1], which is why a prefetched line lowers the L3 count below 1.00. Boot B: every prefetch refill counter reads 0.0000 per load (rounded to four decimals) in all 559 counted rows; the one non-zero value is 1.907e-06 (one refill in 524,288 loads) on the first pass of the 32 MiB row of latency-dram-large.csv [006 README line 7]; on the OCM rows all are exactly 0 [006 CSVs]. Sparse rows count 1.002 to 1.007 L2 refills and 1.011 to 1.022 L3 read refills per load (row means) [section 11.5; 006 CSVs]. By the median of passes the dense OCM rows read +9 to +18 % slower than boot A, the vary rows +2 to +30 %, the sparse rows -10 to +6 % [section 11.2, table 11.3; 006 README line 49]. So the L2 prefetcher helps a dense chain and does nothing for a sparse one. Which prefetcher (stride or spatial) reacts to a one-line-per-page chain is not named: the per-prefetcher refill events 0x00D9 to 0x00DB, 0x010F and 0x0110 were not run [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, H2 paragraph].

outlier.title: OCM latency 18.8 to 23.2 ns per region against asimov-bench's 14.42 ns
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31; the run 3 README (004, 2026-11-03) and the F1 README (011, 2026-11-06) still call the gap unexplained
outlier.what_looked_wrong: In run 1, CPU 2's flushed chase (a chain of dependent loads, one per 64-byte line) of OCM1 read 18.782 ns per load at best, with 0.8157 L3 read refills per load [001 latency-ocm-region1.csv, rep 2]. The five regions read 18.782 to 23.165 ns [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]. In run 2, with fresh chains, CPU 2 read 18.456 to 21.355 ns from the three regions one crosspoint away (OCM0 to OCM2) and 21.535 to 22.001 ns from the two three crosspoints away (OCM3, OCM4) [002 latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv, best rows]. asimov-bench, the other team's benchmark, had measured 14.42 ns per load for a 64 KiB (16-page) chase of the same OCM1 region (0xE0100000) after DC CIVAC, on RTL 6da3026 [001 README, cross-check table]. Our fastest row sits 4.4 ns (30 %) above it.
outlier.why_wrong: Both numbers are chase averages that start flushed, on the same CMN and C1 logic (the RTL differs only elsewhere), so they should agree [001 README, cross-check]. Jesse's README gives two reasons the gap could be real but not a CMN difference. First, asimov-bench's chase reads below its own 20.0 ns waveform read of one SLC line, so it counts some lines already fetched before their load [001 README SLC row; 002 README cross-check]. Second, asimov-bench's 16-page set fits the core's 16-entry L1 data TLB (the translation cache), while each of our regions spans 64 pages [002 README cross-check; 004 README, Caches]. Our own per-region rows are also not one home-node read per load: they count 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills and 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills per load, so some lines reach the cluster before their load, most likely by hardware prefetch [001 README, Reading the numbers].

outlier.what_tests_showed: Run 2: the per-region bests order by mesh distance. They average 19.64 ns at 1 crosspoint (8 rows), 21.82 ns at 3 (10 rows) and 24.58 ns at 5 (2 rows), about 1.1 to 1.4 ns per crosspoint [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 20 best rows; 002 README, OCM and SLC latency by mesh distance]. The fresh chain did not remove the early fetches: 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills and 0.76 to 0.95 L3 read refills per load. Run 3: the sparse rows from CPU 2 at one crosspoint read 22.969, 21.359 and 22.297 ns (OCM0 to OCM2) [004 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv, best of 7]; over all four CPUs the one-crosspoint bests are 20.141 to 22.969 ns (mean 21.58). The dense all-five row from CPU 2 reads 25.340 ns with 1.0009 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv]; the README calls the gap to 14.42 ns 'still not explained' [004 README, line 135]. Boot B (prefetchers off): the route rows fit 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step within 0.09 ns rms (derived) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 6, Distance]. So a one-crosspoint OCM read with no prefetch is about 21.7 to 22.7 ns. Boots C and D (64 KiB translations): CPU 2's L1 data TLB refills fell from 0.66 to 0.77 per load (boot A) to 0.17 to 0.20 per load, but the sparse TLB-set rows read 23.297, 22.109, 21.469, 24.484 and 24.594 ns against boot A's 23.719, 24.062, 24.266, 25.312 and 24.531 ns [005 and 007 latency-ocm-region0..4-tlb-cpu2.csv]. The core OCM rows read 0.977 times boot A's by geometric mean, the sparse TLB-set rows 0.950 [007 README, line 52]. So the TLB explanation accounts for about 1 ns at most, not the 4 ns gap. Boot E and F1 (L3 on): the sparse rows from CPU 2 at one crosspoint read 20.297, 18.656 and 19.516 ns with only 0.31 to 0.52 L3 read refills per load in the best pass [011 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv], so part of each row is served inside the cluster. The dense OCM1 chain from CPU 2 on boot E reads 14.847 ns with 0.4365 L3 read refills per load [010 latency-ocm-region1-dense-cpu2.csv], which matches asimov-bench's 14.42 ns, but the page says such rows sit below the true OCM latency [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, OCM paragraph and table 4.2]. The F1 README still calls it 'the large gap round three's README notes' [011 README, line 142]. Hypothesis, not shown by these sources: asimov-bench's chase may have run on a core whose L3 held data (the stock SCP enables the full L3 for cluster 0 only [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Platform]), or may have counted lines fetched before their load. The measurement that would settle it: asimov-bench's chase re-run on this image from CPU 2 with the L3 read refill counter (0xA2) open, or our dense OCM1 chain from a cluster 0 core. The gap itself: 4.4 ns on run 1's OCM1 row (18.782 against 14.42), 4.2 ns on F1's (18.656), 6.9 to 8.5 ns on run 3's sparse one-crosspoint rows, 10.9 ns on the dense all-five row.

outlier.title: DRAM chase at 52 ns is too short for DRAM: the memory model has zero configured delay
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (001), run date 2026-10-31 [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 3]. Jesse's run 1 README compared the 52.3 ns with asimov-bench's 31.65 ns and 53.3 ns and called it close to the 53.3 ns figure, so it did not flag it as too low [README.md line 50]. The doubt is Bill's review. The replies to Bill are dated 2026-11-04 by file time [message-to-bill.md 18:55, message-to-bill-52ns.md 19:01]. The date of Bill's own message is not in the primary files. Jesse answered the memory-model question in the F1 README (question dated 2026-11-06) [results/membench-jibin-011/README.md line 245].
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The 32 MiB random chain, walked once, read 52.181 to 52.875 ns per load on every boot from run 1 to boot F1 (ten boots; 52.300 on 001, 52.233 on 002, 52.297 on 003, 52.185 on 004, 52.181 on 005, 52.248 on 006, 52.238 on 007, 52.249 on 008, 52.875 on 010, 52.212 on 011) [latency-dram-large.csv, row dram,33554432,best, of each run]. The flushed 8 MiB random chain read 52.657 to 52.739 ns on the same boots [latency-dram-flushed.csv, row dram,8388608,best]. The unflushed 8 MiB and 16 MiB chains read lower, 45.0 to 45.3 ns and 50.6 to 50.8 ns [latency-dram-large.csv rows 8388608 and 16777216]. The 2 MiB chain fits the SLC and measures the core-to-home-node round trip alone: 24.096 ns on run 3 (004) and 24.177 ns on boot E (010) [latency-dram-large.csv, row dram,2097152,best]. So the memory behind the home node adds only 28.5 to 28.9 ns (52.659 minus 24.177 = 28.482 ns on boot E; 52.658 minus 23.714 = 28.944 ns on F1; 52.738 minus 24.096 = 28.642 ns on run 3). The CRB (a Neoverse V3AE board at 2.8 GHz with DDR5-8000) reads 148 ns for a DDR5 random read [message-to-bill.md line 41; not in the crb-validation CSVs of this tree, whose largest flushed row reads 97.127 ns at 8 MiB]. asimov-bench read 31.65 ns on RTL 6da3026 (a 64 KiB, 16-page chase after DC CIVAC) and 53.3 ns on RTL bc5596aa (one line per page after DC CIVAC), both on host-model DRAM [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 50].
outlier.why_wrong: A random read on LPDDR5X costs about 50 ns (est.) inside the chip alone: precharge, activate and column access, before the controller and wires [message-to-bill-52ns.md lines 5-6]. A 29 ns memory leg is shorter than one row cycle [message-to-bill-52ns.md lines 7-8; message-to-bill.md line 10]. Bill's reading: too good to be true [message-to-bill-52ns.md line 1]. Two readings were possible: a prefetcher served some of the chain's loads early, or the memory is a fixed-delay model. The 50 ns LPDDR5X figure is the session's estimate and names no external source in the files.

outlier.what_tests_showed: Boot A: the flushed 8 MiB chain read 52.739 ns with 0.0000 prefetch refills per load in all three prefetch columns and 1.0001 to 1.0002 L3 read refills per load, so every load was a demand miss [results/membench-jibin-005/results/bootA/latency-dram-flushed.csv rows fresh1, fresh2]. The 32 MiB chain read 52.181 ns with 0.0000 prefetch refills and 1.0000 L3 read refills per load [latency-dram-large.csv, rows dram,33554432]. Boot A's address-order chain with prefetchers on read 6.917 ns with 0.9999 L1 prefetch refills per load [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005]. Boot B (prefetchers off): address order 52.762 ns, random 52.739 ns, a 0.023 ns difference [latency-dram-seq.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006; results/membench-jibin-006/README.md line 7]. Boot D repeated it: 52.763 ns [results/membench-jibin-008/README.md line 9]. So the memory serves address order no faster than random order: it has no row behaviour. Jesse (F1 README): the AP DRAM is four embedded Cadence AXI memory models, one per SMS lane (XMS lanes 32-35), with every delay control at zero (read latency 0, write-response latency 0, READY delays and burst gaps 0, no bandwidth or refresh scheduler) [results/membench-jibin-011/README.md line 247]. With controls at zero the model answers 3 lane-clock cycles after it accepts a read, 3 ns at the 1 GHz lane clock, checked only in the repo's Xcelium test, not on the Palladium build [line 249]. By a count of RTL stages (an inference), the SN node's read request to the first data beat back takes 20.0 to 20.5 ns on SMS ports 0-2 and 19.0 to 19.5 ns on port 3; the rest of the about 29 ns leg is inside the CMN (home-node miss handling, mesh hops to the four SMS SN nodes, the SBSX CHI-to-AXI conversion), and nothing in the tree configures that part [line 250]. Nothing on the path models banks, rows, page hits or refresh [line 251]. The core page's run 6 section reports this answer [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, 'The memory model's delay, answered' and the settled list]. The DRAM rows on the pages are labelled as the emulator's memory model, not silicon, and the pages carry no CRB DRAM row [message-to-bill-52ns.md line 18; no 'CRB' text in asimov-c1nano-perf.html]. One inconsistency: the core page's section 5 still says the model's delay 'was asked of Jesse and is unanswered [message-to-jesse-round4.md]' while its run 6 section says answered, and message-to-jesse-round4.md is not in the tree [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, stripped line 176 against line 85].

outlier.title: All-five OCM rows read 1.1 to 1.5 ns above an SLC hit
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The 1.25 MiB all-five OCM chain (one chain over all five 256 KiB regions) read 25.22 ns per load fresh and 25.51 ns flushed on run 1. The DRAM-backed 2 MiB fresh chain, which sits in the SLC, read 23.98 ns on the same run. So the OCM row sat 1.24 ns (fresh) and 1.53 ns (flushed) above an SLC hit. Run 2 repeated the pair from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8. On every CPU the all-five row sits 1.12 to 1.48 ns above that CPU's 2 MiB row (CPU 2: 25.51 against 24.38 ns). Run 3's dense controls show the same gap on CPUs 2, 4 and 8 (1.24, 1.51 and 1.46 ns) and a smaller one on CPU 6 (0.64 ns).
outlier.why_wrong: OCM is 4 locked ways of each home node's SLC array (the firmware locks 4 of 16 ways per home node as OCM). So an OCM read should cost about the same as an SLC hit, not more. Two differences between the rows could carry the remainder. The OCM rows run on 4 KiB pages (/dev/ocm maps a region in 4 KiB pages) and the DRAM rows on 2 MiB huge pages, so the OCM chain can miss the TLB where the DRAM chain does not (Jesse's run 1 README names this). A difference in mesh distance between the five OCM home nodes and the home node of the 2 MiB buffer is the other candidate (hypothesis; no file states the 2 MiB buffer's home node).

outlier.what_tests_showed: Run 2: both rows count 1.00 refills per load at L1, L2 and L3 (0.998 to 1.001), so each load is one home-node read. The rows order the CPUs by their mean distance to the five home nodes: CPUs 2 and 6 (1.8 crosspoints) fastest, CPU 4 (2.6) next, CPU 8 (3.4) about 2 ns behind CPU 2 (2.19 ns on the OCM row, 1.87 ns on the SLC row). Run 3: the dense controls repeat run 2 within 0.17 ns (-0.166 to +0.009 ns). The sparse all-five rows read 0.45 to 1.16 ns above the dense ones. Run 4: with the OCM in 64 KiB translations the dense all-five row from CPU 2 falls from 26.01 ns (boot A) to 24.96 ns (boot C), and from 25.58 ns (boot B) to 24.96 ns (boot D), while the 2 MiB row stays at 23.89 to 24.18 ns. So the gap on CPU 2 falls from 1.92 ns (A) to 0.91 ns (C) and from 1.67 ns (B) to 1.07 ns (D). The page size carries about 0.6 to 1.0 ns of the gap (est., from the boot pairs, not from a TLB counter on the all-five row). About 0.9 to 1.1 ns remains on boots C and D and is not attributed. Run 6 boot F1 (L3 on): the gap stays, 1.82 ns on CPU 2, 1.10 on CPU 4, 1.06 on CPU 6 and 1.50 on CPU 8. No all-five row was ever run under the TLB counter set (the TLB-set rows are per region only), so the TLB share is an estimate from the boot pairs.

outlier.what_looked_wrong: Fresh chains (walked once, never re-walked) of 512 KiB to 2 MiB read a flat 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load on CPU 2 [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-large.csv rows 6 to 22, best rows]. The 3 MiB chain read 25.449 ns [row 26]. That is 1.469 ns above the 2 MiB row (23.980 ns). The two repeats of the 2 MiB row differ by 0.139 ns, so the 3 MiB step is 10.6 times that spread. The 3 MiB chain fits the 3.75 MiB SLC, so it should not rise. At 4 MiB the chain read 29.760 ns [row 30]. That is only 20.4 % of the way from the SLC value (23.980 ns) to the DRAM value (52.300 ns at 32 MiB fresh, row 46), although 4 MiB is larger than the 3.75 MiB SLC. The 4 MiB row is the one core latency row that moved more than 1.5 % between runs: 29.760 ns (run 1), 28.704 (run 2), 28.399 (control 003), 28.270 (run 3 = 004), 29.838 (boot A), 28.161 (boot B), 29.216 (boot C), 28.234 (boot D), 28.321 (boot E), 29.379 (boot F1); every other repeated latency row agreed within 1.44 % between runs 1 and 3 [membench-jibin-003 README.md line 51].
outlier.why_wrong: The SLC (system level cache, 5 home nodes of 1 MiB in 16 ways, 4 ways per node locked as OCM, so 3.75 MiB caches DRAM) has a known size [membench-jibin-001 README.md line 23]. A simple model of an ideal 3.75 MiB cache (hit fraction = capacity / footprint, hits at the 2 MiB value 23.98 ns, misses at the 32 MiB value 52.30 ns) predicts 24.0 ns at 3 MiB and 25.8 ns at 4 MiB (est., model from the session transcript, recomputed from the run 1 rows; not in the README or the pages). The measured 25.449 and 29.760 ns are above both. Inverting the same model at each point gives implied capacities of 2.84, 3.18, 2.64, 2.04 and 0.88 MiB at 3, 4, 6, 8 and 16 MiB (est., model). None is 3.75 MiB and they do not agree with each other. So the sweep shows a transition spread from 2 MiB to 16 MiB, not a sharp step at 3.75 MiB [run1-report.html, SLC line: 'The transition sits between 2 and 16 MiB']. Possible causes named in the session: set conflicts across the five home nodes, and a replacement policy that is not ideal LRU (not measured). 4 MiB sits just above the SLC size, so a small change in how many lines the SLC keeps moves that row the most; the firmware between run 1 and run 2 changed the mesh setup (route overrides) [membench-jibin-002 README.md lines 88 and 92].

outlier.title: One-core read beyond L2 stops at 9.2 GB/s from both SLC and DRAM
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (001), 2026-10-31: 9.306 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.178 GB/s at 32 MiB [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]. Raised as a defect by Bill on 2026-11-04 09:26 PST (comment "Bill 6" on asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html) [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, the Bill 6 heading].
outlier.what_looked_wrong: One core reads 9.311 GB/s at 2 MiB (the SLC footprint) and 9.172 GB/s at 32 MiB (DRAM) in run 3 [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]. The same core reads 58.127 GB/s at 16 KiB (L1) in the same file. It reads 15.0 to 16.6 GB/s from one OCM region in run 1 (regions 0 to 4: 16.327, 16.623, 16.274, 15.295, 14.971 GB/s) [001 bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]. The CME on the same DSU reads 36.564 GB/s from DRAM at 32 MiB and 36.899 GB/s at 2 MiB [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]. Eight cores read 67.756 GB/s at 2 MiB, 8.47 to 9.04 GB/s per thread, so the limit is per core [004 bandwidth-all8.csv, 2 MiB rows]. The CRB (the Arm Neoverse V3AE reference server) reads 30 GB/s from DRAM with one core; that figure is quoted in the message to Bill and is not in the results folders [message-to-bill.md, the table in point 5]. Bill: "The read throughput from DRAM is too slow. I doubt that's reality. It's probably a software mechanism issue." [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, Bill 6].
outlier.why_wrong: The rate is the same at a 24.1 ns level and a 52.2 ns level (the 2 MiB chase reads 24.096 ns, the 32 MiB chase 52.185 ns) [004 latency-dram-large.csv, best rows], so the memory is not the limit. By Little's law the core holds about 3.5 lines in flight at 2 MiB (9.311 GB/s x 24.096 ns / 64 B = 3.51) and about 7.5 at 32 MiB (9.172 x 52.185 / 64 = 7.48; 7.56 with the flushed row's 52.738 ns) [derived from 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv and latency-dram-large.csv / latency-dram-flushed.csv]. Two candidate causes were named: the core's miss-handling capacity, or the software not getting enough loads in flight (Bill's suggestion) [message-to-bill.md, point 6]. Hypothesis H7: the plain ldp loop keeps too few lines in flight, so a streaming read is limited by how far the hardware prefetcher runs ahead, and a software prefetch hint or a second stream raises it [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10 "Ask 2, the one-core read"].

outlier.what_tests_showed:
Run 2: the 2 MiB read spread evenly over the five home nodes, 87,386 to 88,013 requests each (nodes 88, 160, 216, 288, 344: 87,786, 87,780, 87,386, 87,730, 88,013), about twice the plan's estimate of 40,000 [002 cmn-counts.csv, dram-read-2M-cpu2 rows; 002 README.md line 72]. Run 3 repeated it at 87,579 to 88,012 per node [004 cmn-counts.csv].

Boot B (prefetchers off): the plain loop reads 5.031 GB/s at 2 MiB and 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB. PRFM 4 lines ahead reads 12.146 and 6.334 GB/s (2.41 and 2.66 times the plain loop). PRFM 8 ahead reads 10.878 and 5.705, PRFM 16 ahead 9.475 and 4.919, two streams 5.033 and 2.370 (no change) [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]. So the number of lines in flight sets the rate, and the hardware prefetcher supplies most of them (H7 supported for the prefetcher-off case) [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 11.4]. Boot D repeats B within 0.5 %: plain 5.007 and 2.377, PRFM 4 ahead 12.145 and 6.336 GB/s [008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv].

Boot C (prefetchers on, L3 off): the plain loop reads 9.294 and 9.196 GB/s, run 3's rate. PRFM 4 ahead adds 3.8 % at 2 MiB (9.651 GB/s) and 1.5 % at 32 MiB (9.339 GB/s). Two streams reads 11.400 GB/s at 2 MiB (+22.7 %) and 8.681 at 32 MiB (-5.6 %). The plain loop counts 0.992 to 0.999 L1 hardware-prefetch refills per line, so the prefetcher fetched nearly every line [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. So the software hint adds little once the hardware prefetcher runs [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 12].

Boot E (prefetchers on, L3 on): the plain loop reads 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 at 32 MiB, 2.68 and 2.67 times boot C with the same refills per line (5.13 to 5.22 cycles per line against C's 13.78 to 13.93). Every variant is slower than the plain loop on E (PRFM 4 ahead 20.196 and 20.353, two streams 17.982 and 18.911 GB/s) [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. Run 6 boot F1 confirms it on run 3's own rows: 25.044 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.575 at 32 MiB (2.68 times run 3), while the home nodes received 85,518 to 85,777 requests each (0.975 times run 3) in a command 0.648 times as long [011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv; 011 cmn-counts.csv dram-read-2M-cpu2; 011 README.md]. This is the read-stream-rise entry.

With no prefetcher one DRAM latency carries about two lines: the boot B plain loop takes 53.84 cycles per line at 32 MiB, 26.88 ns at 2.003 GHz, and 52.185 / 26.88 = 1.94 lines [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, cycles_per_line; asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 2.3 "What is known"].

What is not measured: no file on disk counts requests in flight, so the limiting unit (core miss handling, cluster, or prefetcher reach) is not named [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 2.3 "The test"]. The run 7 plan proposes the home nodes' read-queue occupancy event (PMU_HNF_POCQ_OCCUPANCY_EVENT) around the same reads on an L3-on and an L3-off boot, and the one-core read sweep on the prefetchers-off boots with the L3 on and off [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 14].

outlier.title: Read streams run 2.7 times faster with the L3 on, at footprints the L3 cannot hold
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot E against boot C (010 against 007), both run 2026-11-05 UTC; confirmed by run 6 boot F1 (011, run 2026-11-06 UTC) against run 3 (004, run 2026-11-03)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: One core reads 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB on boot E against 9.196 GB/s on boot C (2.669 times). The two boots share one build, and the L3 mode is the one change. F1 against run 3 shows the same on every read stream of 48 KiB and above: one-core reads 1.561 times at 48 KiB up to 2.690 times at 2 MiB (24.575 to 27.299 GB/s against 9.172 to 17.483), four readers on four DSUs 33.957 to 98.072 GB/s at 16 MiB (2.888 times), eight readers 66.673 to 107.593 GB/s at 16 MiB (1.614 times), one-core copies 1.31 to 1.75 times, one-core OCM reads 1.206 to 1.358 times (14.817 to 16.619 GB/s up to 19.883 to 20.143), CME OCM reads 1.451 to 1.714 times (23.178 to 23.352 GB/s up to 33.638 to 39.846) with 0.46 to 0.47 times the requests on the region's home node (regions 1 to 4; 0.78 for region 0). No core write stream moved: one-core writes 1.000 to 1.003 times (31.996 to 31.997 GB/s at 32 MiB), four-DSU writes 1.000 (127.98 GB/s), the six writer-placement rows 1.000; the all-eight write read 1.064 at 2 MiB and 1.005 at 16 MiB. The CME's writes did move: its OCM write 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s (1.549 times) and its DRAM write 63.865 down to 42.639 GB/s at 2 MiB (0.67 times). No DRAM-sized chain moved: the 32 MiB random chain reads 52.185 ns on run 3 and 52.212 on F1; 52.238 on boot C and 52.875 on boot E.
outlier.why_wrong: A 32 MiB stream is 128 times the 256 KiB L3, so the L3 cannot hold it. The refill counters per 64-byte line are the same on both boots at 32 MiB: L1 refills 0.9998 and 0.9998, L2 refills 0.9997 and 0.9998, L1 prefetch refills 0.9994 and 0.9994; L3 read refills from the mesh 0.0004 on C and 0.00003 to 0.00005 on E. So each line still enters the L1 and L2 once, and the prefetcher still asks for every line. F1's counted 2 MiB read put 0.975 times run 3's requests on the five home nodes (427,991 against 438,961 over the whole command) in 0.648 times the command time (1,391,056 against 2,147,182 ns). So the L3 did not take these reads off the mesh. One DRAM load costs 52.2 ns on run 3 and F1 (52.185 and 52.212 ns) and 52.2 and 52.9 ns on boots C and E. At 9.196 GB/s the 32 MiB stream must overlap about 7.5 loads est. with the L3 off, and at 24.546 GB/s about 20 est. with it on. The core spends 13.78 to 13.93 cycles per line on C and 5.13 to 5.22 on E. The files do not record how many reads are in flight, so they do not show the mechanism.

outlier.what_tests_showed: The build is ruled out: k_read, k_write and k_copy are byte for byte the same in both builds, and boot E against boot C (one build) shows the rise. Boards and run-to-run noise are ruled out: the controls repeat within 0.3 %, the one-core writes from 48 KiB on within 0.3 %, and the read reps spread 1.8 % or less inside each boot. Page placement is ruled out for the DRAM rows and only partly for the OCM rows. A PRFM hint lowers the rate on E (20.196 GB/s with the hint 4 lines ahead against 24.945 plain at 2 MiB; 20.353 against 24.546 at 32 MiB), while on C it adds 4 % or less. With the prefetchers off and the L3 off (boots B and D) one core reads 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB, so the prefetcher supplies almost all the overlap. The sequential 8 MiB chain fell from 6.917 to 2.492 ns per load on E with 0.9997 to 1.0000 L1 prefetch refills per load on both boots (its own entry). Four readers on four DSUs read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s each, the one-core rate, so four clusters do not share one limit; eight readers (two per cluster) read 13.4 GB/s each. Jesse's F1 README states that the home-node counts do not show the L3 taking the counted read off the mesh, and it does not name a cause. Three hypotheses stand, each with a test not yet run: the L3's miss handling keeps more reads in flight per cluster; the prefetcher's requests overlap more with the L3 on; a per-cluster cap on reads in flight. The run 4 page adds a fourth reading, marked hypothesis: the prefetched lines wait in the L3 (about 11 ns from the core, est.) instead of in the SLC across the mesh.

outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31: the data; first written as a limit in run 2's README (membench-jibin-002, 2026-11-02, 'round one's hemisphere write limit is gone'); control run membench-jibin-003 ran 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-03 (script 23:44 UTC to 00:59 UTC)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Run 1: four writers (one per DSU, CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8) wrote 88.8 GB/s at 2 MiB each and 86.8 GB/s at 16 MiB each. Eight writers (CPUs 2 to 9) wrote 88.3 GB/s at 2 MiB and 86.7 GB/s at 16 MiB. One core alone writes 32.0 GB/s at 2 MiB and 32 MiB. So four writers got 21.6 to 22.4 GB/s each and eight writers 10.8 to 11.2 GB/s each, far below one core's rate [membench-jibin-001 bandwidth-perdsu.csv, bandwidth-all8.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows; README 003 'Writes on the two firmware sets']. Run 2, same write kernel and same RTL (0d9e214eb43b): 127.9 GB/s with four writers (+44.1 %) and 155.4 GB/s with eight (+76.1 %) at 2 MiB; 128.0 (+47.5 %) and 151.7 (+74.9 %) at 16 MiB. Run 2's README says every other best row the two rounds shared agrees within 3.6 % (a recompute over the shared bandwidth best rows gives 1.80 % at most, the pair's 48 KiB write). The firmware had changed: SCP 0.34.0 (release) to 0.48.0-nopcie.1 (the box's rebuild with PCIe0 held, debug build), TF-A 0.24.0 to 0.35.0 (both debug) [README 001 line 19, README 002 lines 7, 9, 26, 44 to 47, 92].
outlier.why_wrong: Doubling the writers from four to eight added nothing in run 1 (88.8 to 88.3 GB/s), so one shared limit of about 87 to 89 GB/s sat somewhere in the hemisphere. Its place (DSU, mesh port, home node, memory controller) was unknown. In run 2 the same write rows moved 44 to 76 % while the one-core write stayed at 32.0 GB/s and the read and copy rows of the same commands moved under 0.5 %. A change that large with no change to the write kernel or the RTL contradicted a stable platform, and could come from the firmware or from the code changes between the runs [README 002 line 49; README 003 'Result'].

outlier.what_tests_showed: Control run: on run 1's firmware the four multi-core write rows returned to 88.8, 88.6, 86.8 and 86.7 GB/s, within 0.40 % of run 1 (the eight-writer 2 MiB row moved most, 88.254 to 88.605 GB/s). So the firmware caused the change, not the code or the kernel [README 003 'Result'; bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv of 001 and 003]. Likely cause named in README 003: the new SCP's route overrides from the home nodes to the memory controllers (README 002 counts 15 HN-S-to-SMS route overrides, vertical first, same hop count). The other mesh change, a POCQ class-3 cap for QoS 0 to 7, does not apply to the cores' QoS 14 traffic. The control changed the whole firmware set at once, so the exact component (the overrides, the rest of SCP 0.48.0, TF-A 0.35.0, or the debug build) is not isolated [README 003 line 40]. Placement rows: two writers in one DSU (CPUs 2+3) get 40.9 GB/s on both firmwares (per-DSU limit, not firmware). Two writers on two DSUs (2+4, 2+8) get 64.0 GB/s on both firmwares, 32.0 each. Two DSUs with two writers each (2+3+4+5, 2+3+8+9) get 85.8 and 84.1 GB/s on both. Only the placements that need more than about 87 GB/s over all four DSUs differ: 2+4+6+8 reads 86.6 GB/s on the old firmware and 128.0 GB/s on the new, and the 4- and 8-thread rows likewise [README 003 table; bandwidth-write-cpus*.csv of 002 and 003]. Mesh counts on the control's 2+4+6+8 row: home node 344 (OCM4's home, crosspoint (5,3)) received 2,105,333 requests against 1,275,875 to 1,277,589 at each of the other four nodes, about 829,000 extra. On run 2's firmware all five read 1,276,581 to 1,278,473. Memory-controller requests (5,621,097 against 5,625,931) and misses (5,604,936 against 5,608,583) did not rise, so README 003 reads the extra requests as the same writes received more than once, as retries would be. The counter hns_pocq_retry_all would confirm this and was not run [cmn-counts.csv of 003 and 002; README 003 'Mesh counts on the limited row']. Later runs: run 3 (004) repeated run 2's four multi-core write rows within 0.32 % (127.919, 155.154, 127.981, 152.177 GB/s) and the six placement rows within 0.064 %; the only write row that moved more was the pair's 48 KiB write, -2.29 % (60.457 to 59.070 GB/s), which README 004 attributes to the rebuilt bandwidth binary adding 7.7 to 8.0 ns per pass. Boot F1 (011, the L3 on) repeated the six placement rows within 0.026 % of run 3 (within 0.09 % of run 2), so the L3 does not change a write stream. F1's eight-writer 2 MiB row rose to 165.2 GB/s (+6.45 % over run 3's 155.2), its 16 MiB row to 153.0 (+0.79 %). The core page reads the eight-writer rows (151.7 to 165.2 GB/s across runs 2, 3 and F1) as a shared DRAM write ceiling that four writers at 128.0 GB/s do not reach; that reading is the page's interpretation, not a separate measurement [asimov-c1nano-perf.html tables 4.4, 4.5, section 9; README 004 lines 8, 97, 98].

outlier.title: Two writers in one DSU get 40.9 GB/s, not 64.0; the pair's 160 KiB write rose 23 % on F1
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (001): the pair's 160 KiB write row, 23.5 GB/s per core [results/membench-jibin-001/results/19700101T000000Z/bandwidth-pair.csv row 41; run1-report.html, section 'Shared L2 pair']. Run 2 (002): the writer-placement rows, 2026-11-02 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md line 50].
outlier.what_looked_wrong: CPUs 2 and 3 share one DSU. Writing 16 MiB each, they get 40.922 GB/s together (20.457 to 21.737 GB/s each) [membench-jibin-002 bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv rows 4 to 6]. CPUs 2 and 4, on two DSUs, get 63.984 GB/s (31.982 to 31.993 each) [membench-jibin-002 bandwidth-write-cpus2-4.csv rows 4 to 6]. One core alone writes 31.996 GB/s at 32 MiB [membench-jibin-001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 86]. So two cores of one DSU lose 36 % of their combined one-core rate. The same pair at 160 KiB each wrote 47.029 GB/s in run 1 (23.515 to 24.722 per core) and 47.241 GB/s in run 3 (23.620 to 24.801 per core) [bandwidth-pair.csv row 38 to 41 of 001 and 004]. 47.241 GB/s is 74 % of two one-core writes at 256 KiB (2 x 31.869 GB/s) [membench-jibin-004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 56]. On boot F1 (the L3 on) the pair's 160 KiB write rose to 58.250 GB/s, +23.3 % [membench-jibin-011 bandwidth-pair.csv row 41]. Every write row of 2 MiB and above repeated run 3 within 6.4 %: the largest move is all eight cores at 2 MiB, 155.154 to 165.154 GB/s [bandwidth-all8.csv row 11 of 004 and 011]; the six placement rows read 1.000, for example 2+3 at 40.949 GB/s [membench-jibin-011 bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv row 6].
outlier.why_wrong: Cores 2 and 3 share an L2 (128 KiB), an L3 (256 KiB), a CME and one mesh port [membench-jibin-004 README.md line 32; membench-jibin-011 README.md line 348]. Which shared part limits two writers was unknown. Run 1's hemisphere write limit (86.8 GB/s at 16 MiB per writer) sat on all four DSUs, so a per-DSU limit of 41 GB/s was a new, smaller limit [RUN2-PLAN.md line 108]. For the 160 KiB pair: the two buffers together are 320 KiB, more than the L2 (128 KiB) and more than the L3 (256 KiB). With the L3 off the lines beyond L2 go to the SLC across the mesh. Boot E ran no multi-core row, so the pages give no pointer for why the L3 mode moved this one write row by 23 % [membench-jibin-011 README.md line 145].

outlier.what_tests_showed: The per-DSU write limit does not depend on the firmware: the 2+3 row reads 40.922 GB/s on run 2 (new firmware), 40.939 on control 003 (old firmware) and 40.940 on run 3 [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv row 6 of 002, 003 and 004; membench-jibin-003 README.md line 38]. One CME writes 32 MiB at 61.971 GB/s through CPU 2-3's cluster on run 3, 1.51 times the two cores' 40.940 GB/s [membench-jibin-004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 116]. Jesse's reading (an inference): if the CME's stores leave through the same cluster port, the two-core limit is on the cores' side, not the port's [membench-jibin-004 README.md line 85]. With the L3 on (F1) the same CME write reads 40.445 GB/s by the bracket (40.459 in span), 0.99 times the pair's 40.949 GB/s on the same boot [membench-jibin-011 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 116; bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv row 6]; F2 reads 40.357 [membench-jibin-012 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 116]. So with the L3 on the CME no longer exceeds the pair, and the page keeps the cores'-side reading as a hypothesis [asimov-cme-perf.html, 'Writes beside the cluster's two cores']. The two pages disagree on the pair's shared path: asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 9 says 'For the pair it is the DSU's one mesh port', while asimov-cme-perf.html and Jesse's run 3 README put the limit on the cores' side. Neither page resolves it. The pair's 160 KiB write rose 1.233 times on F1 (58.250 against 47.241 GB/s), its 48 KiB write 1.049 times, while the placement rows and the one-core writes held within 0.3 % [membench-jibin-011 README.md lines 113 and 145; asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.4]. Boot E ran no multi-core row, so no second L3-on observation exists, and the files do not show why [membench-jibin-011 README.md line 145].

outlier.title: The counted 2 MiB read puts 3.35 requests per line and pass on the home nodes, about twice the 40,000-per-node estimate; the dense all-five OCM chain loads the five home nodes unevenly (16 % spread)
outlier.first_seen: run 2 (membench-jibin-002), run on 2026-11-02 (README 002, 'Reading the numbers'); analysed 2026-11-03
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The counted 2 MiB read (bandwidth read kernel, CPU 2, 4 timed passes over 32,768 lines of 64 bytes; run_asimov.sh:151) put 87,386 to 88,013 hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all requests on each of the five home nodes [membench-jibin-002 cmn-counts.csv, rows dram-read-2M-cpu2]. The five nodes sum to 438,695 requests. That is 3.35 requests per line and timed pass (438,695 / (4 x 32,768)). The plan's estimate was about 40,000 requests per node if the buffer spreads evenly [README.md:413; RUN2-PLAN.md:105], so the measured count is about 2.2 times the estimate. Jesse's README states it as 'about twice his estimate of 40,000' [membench-jibin-002 README.md:72]. The dense all-five OCM chain rows (1.25 MiB over five 256 KiB regions, 20,480 lines, '--fresh 3 --flush') put 153,501 / 154,463 / 145,606 / 138,988 / 129,998 requests on nodes 88 / 160 / 216 / 288 / 344 from CPU 2 [membench-jibin-002 cmn-counts.csv, rows ocm-all5-cpu2]. The spread from the highest to the lowest node is 15.8 % ((154,463 - 129,998) / 154,463). The ordering is the same on CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8: node 160 (OCM1) most, then 88 (OCM0), 216 (OCM2), 288 (OCM3), and 344 (OCM4) least. The node-to-region mapping comes from the per-region rows, where each region's own node reads 111,468 to 123,460 against 9,042 to 10,576 on the other four [membench-jibin-002 README.md:70].
outlier.why_wrong: The estimate assumed about one home-node request per line touch. One rep of the bandwidth read command touches every line six times: one fill (fill_buf, bandwidth.c:385), one warm-up pass (bandwidth.c:406), then the 4 timed passes (bandwidth.c:416). 6 x 32,768 = 196,608 touches, which is about 200,000 = 5 x 40,000 (est., derived here; README.md:413 does not show its arithmetic). The measured 438,695 is 13.4 requests per line over the whole command. So each line touch caused about two requests at the home node, not one. The counters span the whole command from before exec to after exit: program load, buffer fill, chain builds, warm-up, flushes and timed passes [README.md:409-410; RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2 'Counters around the whole process']. They cannot separate the timed passes from the rest. The same row counted 213,249 hns_mc_reqs_local_all (requests the home nodes sent on to memory, 6.5 per line) and 364,449 hns_cache_miss_all (SLC misses, 11.1 per line) [membench-jibin-002 cmn-counts.csv]. hns_cache_miss_all counts every qualified lookup that misses, fills and flushes included [membench-jibin-002 README.md:83]. For the all-five chain, the five regions are equal in size (256 KiB each) and each sits in its own home node, so an even count per node was expected. The dense chain command builds three chains over the same lines, walks chain 0 twice untimed, flushes, and times chains 1 and 2 once each [RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2]. The run 3 dense control repeated run 2's all-five counts node for node within -2.3 % to +1.4 % [membench-jibin-004 README.md:118], so the uneven spread is repeatable, not noise.

outlier.title: Home node 344 took 65 % more requests than the others on the old-firmware four-writer row
outlier.first_seen: control run (membench-jibin-003, run 2's code on run 1's firmware SCP 0.34.0 / TF-A 0.24.0), results dated 2026-11-03 [results/membench-jibin-003/README.md, lines 1-7 and 44]
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The control run repeated run 2's writer-placement row with one writer per cluster (CPUs 2+4+6+8, 16 MiB per writer) under the mesh counters. Node 344 (OCM4's home node, crosspoint (5,3)) received 2,105,333 requests. Each of the other four home nodes received 1,275,875 to 1,277,589 requests. That is 828,928 extra requests over the mean of the other four (1,276,405), or 1.65 times as many [results/membench-jibin-003/results/19700101T000000Z/cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8, event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all]. The memory-controller requests (hns_mc_reqs_local_all) read 5,621,097 against 5,625,931 on run 2's firmware. The SLC misses (hns_cache_miss_all) read 5,604,936 against 5,608,583 [cmn-counts.csv of membench-jibin-003 and membench-jibin-002, same label]. On run 2's firmware (SCP 0.48.0 / TF-A 0.35.0) the same row spread evenly: 1,276,581 to 1,278,473 requests per node, a 0.15 % spread [results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8]. Run 1 (membench-jibin-001) had no such row, so the control run is the first place this row ran on the old firmware.
outlier.why_wrong: DRAM writes interleave over the five home nodes. Every other write row in both runs spreads within 0.19 % across the five nodes (recomputed from cmn-counts.csv, labels write-cpus2-3, 2-4, 2-8, 2-3-4-5, 2-3-8-9, both runs). One node taking 65 % more requests with no extra memory-controller requests and no extra SLC misses means the same writes arrived at the home node more than once. Retried requests would do that. Jesse's README states this as the hypothesis and names the counter that would test it [results/membench-jibin-003/README.md, line 45]. This row is one of the rows that hit the old firmware's shared write limit: 86.598 GB/s best on the old firmware against 127.971 GB/s on the new [bandwidth-write-cpus2-4-6-8.csv, rep best, in membench-jibin-003 and membench-jibin-002]. The README gives the old-firmware limit as about 87-89 GB/s [results/membench-jibin-003/README.md, Writes on the two firmware sets].

Cells at the same distance spread 14 to 18 % in both runs. Run 3 sparse bests: 20.14 to 22.97 ns at 1 crosspoint (8 cells, 14.0 % spread), 22.39 to 26.52 ns at 3 (10 cells, 18.4 %), 27.00 to 28.45 ns at 5 (2 cells) [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004, best rows; asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.2, third sub-table]. Run 2 dense bests: 18.46 to 21.36 ns at 1 (15.7 %), 20.49 to 23.44 ns at 3 (14.4 %), 24.48 to 24.68 ns at 5 [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 002; results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:64]. The 20 cells correlate 0.81 between runs 2 and 3, but that includes the distance effect. After removing each run's mean at each distance, the remaining cell differences correlate only 0.22 [codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md:913; recomputed 0.812 and 0.217]. A fit on the step count alone (ns = a + b (|dx| + |dy|)) explains 75 to 76 % of the variance (R² 0.75 run 2, 0.76 run 3) and leaves 0.88 ns rms (run 2) and 1.06 ns rms (run 3); splitting X and Y steps leaves 0.80 and 0.96 ns rms [follow-up-run-plan.md:28; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7; recomputed]. On boot A (005) the same dense chain of ten cells, run once without counters (G2) and once under the crosspoint counters (G6), differed by -0.63 to +3.44 ns (CPU 8 to OCM1: 23.68 against 27.11 ns) [latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6]. The G6 mesh data-flit sums per cell also moved between boots: 1.062 to 1.346 times between boots C and D (up to 35 %), 0.940 to 1.101 C against A, 0.961 to 1.084 D against B [results/membench-jibin-007/README.md:85,109; results/membench-jibin-008/README.md:10; cmn-counts.csv of 005 to 008, recomputed], and 0.360 to 0.731 E against A [results/membench-jibin-010/README.md:155].
outlier.why_wrong: If a load's latency were a base plus a fixed cost per crosspoint step, cells at the same distance would agree within repeat noise. A cell's rank among its distance group would also repeat from run to run. Neither held. Hypothesis H5 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 5): an X step costs more than a Y step. The first fits gave X 1.33 and Y 0.76 ns per step on run 2's dense bests, and X 1.66 and Y 0.92 ns on run 3's sparse bests (R² 0.79 and 0.80) [follow-up-run-plan.md:28; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7]. But the X and Y step counts are coordinate assumptions: no counter had measured the route [follow-up-run-plan.md:122].

outlier.title: Sparse OCM chains read 2 to 4 ns above dense; vary chains faster than sparse (H2, H3, H4)
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (membench-jibin-004), run date 2026-11-03 UTC [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 3]; Jibin's question 2026-11-03 15:52 is from the session transcript only (not in the primary files)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: A sparse chain touches one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads per pass of a 256 KiB region [latency-ocm-region0-cpu2.csv of 004, header: lines=64 sparse=1]. A dense chain touches every line, 4,096 loads per pass. On run 3 the sparse rows read 2.31 ns per load above run 2's dense rows on average over the 20 CPU-by-region cells (range -0.47 to +4.55 ns, higher in 18 of 20 cells) [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004 and 002; README 004 line 9 says 2.3 ns]. On run 4 boot A the sparse rows read 3.73 to 4.33 ns above dense on CPU 2 and 1.79 to 3.56 ns on CPU 8 [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv and -dense-cpu<c>.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 6]. Jibin expected the opposite (transcript only, not in the primary files): dense should hit more, sparse should miss every load, so the gap should be much larger, and dense should have fewer refills than sparse. On boot A the vary chain (a hashed line offset per page) was faster than the sparse chain in 10 of 10 cells, by 1.72 to 6.75 ns by the median of the passes (mean 3.49 ns; by best pass 1.86 to 7.14 ns) [timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 005, CPUs 2 and 8; run-4 page section 6], although it drew prefetches at a similar rate (1.15 to 1.73 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2 against the sparse chain's 1.81 to 2.22) [run-4 page table 3.4]. The dense rows' L1 TLB refills differed by a factor of 27 between regions: 0.005 to 0.136 per load, 21 to 559 per pass of 4,096 loads [l1d_tlb_refill_per_load of latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005; run-4 page table 3.5].
outlier.why_wrong: Both chain shapes read the same region over the same mesh path, so a 2 to 4 ns difference per load needs a cause inside the core. Three hypotheses were written down [run-4 page section 10]: H2, the fixed line offset of the sparse chain is what the prefetcher reacts to; H3, each sparse load takes one L1 TLB miss (one page per load); H4, the 4 KiB page size is what separates the two shapes. The TLB difference between the dense regions came from the per-command mapping alignment: the kernel places each /dev/ocm mapping per process, and on boot A the user-to-physical offset (va - pa) was a multiple of 64 KiB on only 5 of the 110 mappings, of 32 KiB on 8 and of 16 KiB on 23 [README 005 line 27; run-4 page table 3.5 second table: 5 at 64 KiB, 3 at 32 KiB only, 15 at 16 KiB only, 87 at 4 KiB only]. Each command on each boot is its own placement draw [README 007 line 124]. The one dense row whose mapping was 64 KiB aligned (OCM4) refilled the L1 TLB 21 times per pass; the four with 4 KiB-only mappings refilled 42 to 559 times [README 007 line 58; run-4 page table 3.5].

outlier.what_tests_showed: H2 not supported. The vary chain draws prefetches like the sparse chain (1.15 to 1.73 against 1.81 to 2.22 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2) [run-4 page table 3.4 and section 6]. On boot B, prefetchers off, the vary chain is faster than the sparse one by median in only 6 of 10 cells, by -0.91 to +0.09 ns (boot A: 10 of 10, -6.75 to -1.72 ns) [timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-{vary-,}cpu<c>.csv of 006 and 005; run-4 page section 11.5]. So boot A's vary advantage came from the prefetcher. Why its fills helped the vary chain more is a hypothesis without a test. H3 not supported. A sparse load on boot A takes 0.672 to 0.723 L1 TLB refills, 0.000 L2 TLB refills and 0.266 to 1.243 table walks (means over the timed passes) [latency-ocm-region<r>-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005; run-4 page table 3.5]. On boot B the walks read 0.000 per load on every sparse row, and on boot D 0.000 in all 35 passes, while boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) count 0.27 to 1.24, 0.41 to 0.75 and 0.56 to 1.62 walks per sparse load [dtlb_walk_per_load of the TLB-set files of 005 to 010; run-4 page section 13.3]. So the walks were translations for the prefetchers' requests, not the chain's. H4 supported in part. With the 64 KiB translations the L1 TLB refills per pass fell to 11 to 15 on every chain (boots C and D), from 21 to 559 on boot A and 25 to 599 on boot B [run-4 page table 13.1; recomputed from the TLB-set files of 005 to 008]. The sparse-minus-dense gap on CPU 2 (mean of the five regions, best passes) went from 4.01 ns (A) to 2.76 ns (C) with the prefetchers on, and from 1.77 ns (B) to 1.24 ns (D) with them off; it narrowed in 4 of 5 regions on each pair [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu2.csv and -dense-cpu2.csv of 005 to 008; run-4 page section 13.2]. On boot E (L3 on, 4 KiB pages) the gap is 2.77 ns [same files of 010; asimov-c1nano-perf.html, OCM section]. The narrowing is on CPU 2 only: CPU 8's gap widened from 2.468 ns (A) to 2.749 ns (C) by best pass [README 007 line 56]. Over the 69 core OCM rows the hint alone (D against B) gives a geometric mean ratio of 0.985 (62 of 69 rows faster, about 1.5 %), the hint with the prefetchers on (C against A) 0.977 (43 of 69), and the prefetchers with the hint on both (C against D) 0.861 (66 of 69 rows faster on C) [best rows of the 69 core OCM files of 005 to 008; run-4 page table 13.2]. So the prefetchers make these rows about 14 % faster even though they widen the sparse-dense gap, and the hint changes them by about 1.5 %. Jesse's reading: the numbers at this spread do not decide H4 [README 007 line 11]. No sparse or vary TLB-set row had a 64 KiB-aligned mapping on A or B, so A against C and B against D cannot split the fall in TLB refills, or the latency change, between the contiguous bit and the 64 KiB placement [README 007 line 58; README 008 line 60]. The same chain's best differs by up to 23.6 % between two processes of one boot, more than the mean changes [README 007 line 11]. What remains open: on boot D (hint, prefetchers off) the gap is still 0.80 to 1.75 ns per region (mean 1.24 ns), so the page size is part of what separates the two shapes, not all of it [run-4 page section 13.2].

outlier.title: OCM rows with the prefetchers on are noisy: the passes of one row spread up to 68 %, and the same chain differs up to 23.6 % between two processes of one boot
outlier.first_seen: run 2 (002, 2026-11-02): two passes of a per-region row differ by up to 3.444 ns; run 3 (004, 2026-11-03): one row's 7 passes spread 68.1 %; boot A (005, 2026-11-04) against run 3: 12 of 70 shared rows moved more than 3 %
outlier.what_looked_wrong: In run 2 the two passes of a per-region OCM row differ by up to 3.444 ns per load (region 3 from CPU 4: 23.938 and 20.494 ns) [membench-jibin-002 latency-ocm-region3-cpu4.csv; README line 66]. In 19 of the 20 rows the faster pass is the one with fewer L3 read refills per load (in the 20th the two counts differ by 0.001) [002 README line 66; recomputed from the 20 CSVs]. In run 3 the 7 passes of one sparse row spread 5.16 to 14.55 ns per load (22 % to 68 %). The widest is CPU 2 to OCM1: 21.359 to 35.906 ns, 68.1 % [membench-jibin-004 latency-ocm-region1-cpu2.csv; README line 110]. Boot A ran on run 3's platform, and both controls repeated run 3 within 0.5 % (4 KiB chase 2.002 ns, CME round trip 21.004 to 21.005 ns) [005 README line 8]. Yet 12 of the 70 best rows the two share moved by more than 3 %. The largest is CPU 2 to OCM3: 26.391 ns on boot A against 23.719 ns on run 3, +11.27 % [latency-ocm-region3-cpu2.csv of 005 and 004; asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.9]. Of the 12, 8 are core OCM rows, 3 are CME rows and 1 is the 4 MiB DRAM chain (+5.55 %) [recomputed from the best rows of 005 and 004]. On boot C two vary chains with the TLB set moved in opposite directions against boot A: region 0 read 13.734 against 19.906 ns (0.690 times, -31 %), region 2 read 21.531 against 17.047 ns (1.263 times, +26 %) [latency-ocm-region0-vary-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region2-vary-tlb-cpu2.csv of 007 and 005; 007 README line 53]. The faster boot's best pass counted fewer L3 read refills per load each time (region 0: 0.3125 on C against 0.6719 on A; region 2: 0.7969 on C against 0.4688 on A) [same CSVs]. The same chain's best differs between two processes of one boot by up to 23.6 % on the vary chains of boot C (22.9 % on boot A) with the prefetchers on [007 README line 52], and by at most 3.0 % on boot D with them off (region 2's sparse chain: 24.328, 23.703 and 23.609 ns in three processes) [008 README line 38]. One CME row moved too: the 32 KiB repeated chain read 42.156 ns on boot A against 39.721 ns on run 3, +6.13 % [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 004; asimov-cme-run4.html section 3.3].
outlier.why_wrong: A chain walked again over the same lines should take the same time pass after pass. On the dense rows it does: the dense all-five control repeats run 2 within 0.17 ns [004 README line 110]. On the per-region rows it does not. The slow passes carry more L2 refills (correlation +0.84 within rows on run 3) and fewer L3 read refills (-0.31) [004 README line 111]. So the spread tracks what the prefetchers fetch, not the chain's own loads. Each command is also a new process with its own physical page placement [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section on page placement]. A ratio taken from one row between two boots therefore says little by itself.

outlier.what_tests_showed: On boot A a pass's time correlates only weakly with its counts: +0.19 with the prefetch refills (0x81BD), +0.33 with the L2 refills and +0.30 with the L3 read refills [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, pass-to-pass paragraph]. Run 3's sparse rows showed +0.84 with the L2 refills [004 README line 111]. So the count alone does not explain the spread. The largest spread of one row's passes, by boot: A 12.218 ns (latency-ocm-region4-cpu8.csv, 21.813 to 34.031 ns), C 14.422 ns (latency-ocm-region3-tlb-cpu2.csv) and 17.812 ns on a walk row (latency-ocm-region0-walk-cpu2.csv), E 11.172 ns (latency-ocm-region0-vary-cpu8.csv), B 1.437 ns (latency-ocm-region1-cpu2.csv), D 1.640 ns (latency-ocm-region2-cpu8.csv) [recomputed from 005 to 008 and 010; READMEs 006 line 36, 007 line 52, 008 line 38, 010 line 152]. With the prefetchers off (B, D) the spread is about a tenth of what it is with them on. On run 6 the CME OCM passes carry a steady 286 to 292 ns per pass outside the span on F1. The pass-to-pass spread of 3.1 to 8.7 ns per load sits inside the span. On F2 (prefetchers off) the spread falls to 0.2 to 0.7 ns per load (0.2 to 1.3 % of the row, against 5.2 to 22.5 % on F1) [cme-latency-ocm-region*.csv of 011 and 012; 012 README line 141; asimov-cme-perf.html, CME wake-up item]. So the spread is the prefetchers' plus page placement, not a wake-up outside the span. On run 6 F1 the core's sparse rows still spread up to 59.7 % between passes (latency-ocm-region0-cpu6.csv, 19.328 to 30.875 ns) [recomputed from 011]. The number used for OCM is the dense all-five row (20,480 loads, one L3 read refill per load): 26.009 ns on boot A, 24.959 ns on boot C, 26.082 ns on boot E [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 005, 007 and 010; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 1]. Still open: which lines the prefetchers brought in, and why one process places faster than another [007 README line 53].

outlier.title: Run 3's one-core write rows cost 7.7 to 8.0 ns more per pass than run 2's (H6)
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC) against run 2 (002); isolated on run 4 boot A (005, ran 2026-11-04 UTC)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The one-core write rows at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB took 8.0, 8.0, 7.9 and 7.7 ns more per pass in run 3 than in run 2 [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 002, write 'best' rows; ns per pass = bytes_per_thread / (aggregate_GBps x 1e9)]. At 16 KiB run 3 read 30.127 GB/s where run 1, run 2 and the control read 30.578, 30.579 and 30.579 GB/s (-1.48 %) [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 001, 002, 003, 004; 004 README.md, Bandwidth]. 8.0 ns is 16.0 cycles at 2.003 GHz (derived). The offset was the same at every size, so it is a fixed cost per pass, not a rate change. The timed loop (the assembly write kernel) was the same in both runs. The 16 KiB reads got faster at the same time: 58.127 GB/s in run 3 against 57.529 in run 2 (+1.04 %) [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 002, read 'best' rows]. In the 16 KiB two-core pair the faster writer slowed by about 4 ns per pass, not 8 ns [004 README.md, Bandwidth].
outlier.why_wrong: The same assembly kernel on the same platform should repeat within a fraction of a percent, and the other bandwidth rows did (every bandwidth row within 2.3 %) [004 README.md, line 8]. Run 3's bandwidth.c (commit ba834c0) had gained a CME switch in its pass loop. Jesse's pre-queue check of the disassembly estimated that switch at 4 to 15 cycles per pass. The measured 16 cycles sits at the top of that range [004 README.md, Bandwidth]. But run 3 was also a different binary on a different day, so a program cost and a platform drift could not be told apart from the two runs alone. The firmware was not a candidate: run 3 ran on run 2's image copy, firmware (SCP 0.48.0-nopcie.1, TF-A 0.35.0), kernel and OCM module [004 README.md, Platform facts]. The firmware change was between run 1 and run 2, and the control run (003) was for that question [002 README.md, lines 7 and 10].

tests_added.name: G5: run 2's bandwidth program (commit 8ae533c, binary bandwidth_r2) and run 3's (commit ba834c0) run side by side on one boot: the one-core write kernel at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB with run 3's pass counts (256, 128, 64, 32), 3 reps, CPU 2. On boot A the run 3 side was the binary named 'bandwidth', which has run 3's machine code (objdump -d identical) [005 README.md, Build]. On boots B to E the run 3 side was 'bandwidth_r3', ba834c0's bandwidth.c kept verbatim, also run 3's machine code by objdump [006 README.md, Build; 007 README.md, Against boot A]. Files: bandwidth-write-small.csv (run 3's program) and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv (run 2's).

outlier.what_tests_showed: Boot A (005): run 3's program is 11.2, 7.1, 7.4 and 6.7 ns per pass slower than run 2's at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB (30.210 vs 30.847, 31.375 vs 31.517, 31.674 vs 31.750, 31.875 vs 31.901 GB/s) [bandwidth-write-small.csv and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.8]. Both programs read their own run's numbers back within 0.28 % and 0.88 % [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 9]. So the per-pass cost is the program's, not the platform's. H6 supported. A straight line t_pass = fixed + bytes / rate over the four boot A rows gives a fixed cost of 30.4 ns per pass for run 3's program and 21.0 ns for run 2's, both at 32.0 GB/s (est., least squares over four points) [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 12, The arithmetic; verifier recompute 30.4 and 21.0 ns, 31.99 and 31.98 GB/s]. The other boots repeat it at 48 to 256 KiB: B (006) 7.3, 8.3, 8.3 ns; C (007) 7.9, 9.0, 8.3 ns; D (008) 7.3, 8.0, 7.0 ns; E (010) 7.9, 7.4, 7.7 ns (verifier recompute from the same two files on each boot). The 16 KiB row varies by boot: A 11.2, B 3.1, D 11.4 ns slower, but C -0.9 and E -0.8 ns (run 3's program slightly faster) [asimov-c1nano-run4.html sections 11.5 and 13.2]. The run4 page attributes the C and E 16 KiB change to the b79dffa build. Jesse's READMEs say otherwise: on C and E the G5 rows ran bandwidth_r3, which is run 3's machine code by objdump, so the two G5 binaries were the same machine code on all five boots [007 README.md, Against boot A; 006 README.md, Build]. The 'not byte for byte' note in the boot C README is about the default bandwidth binary used by G7 and G8, not bandwidth_r3 [007 README.md, The G8 rows]. Why the 16 KiB row shows no difference on C and E, and only 3.1 ns on B, is Insufficient data in the primary files. A per-pass cycle count from the PMU on the two binaries at 16 KiB would resolve it. On the CRB (an out-of-order V3AE core) the plan notes 89.0 GB/s with run 3's program and 89.3 GB/s with run 2's at 16 KiB, so that core shows no per-pass difference [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 9, G5; a plan note, not a primary results file]. The crb-validation folder holds one program's 16 KiB write at 89.286 GB/s (2026-10-31 build, before run 3's) [crb-validation/20261031T073509Z/bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]. The run 6 pages generalise the finding: the C1-Nano is an in-order core, so work at each pass boundary shows as a fixed per-pass cost [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 7].

outlier.title: One-core L1 read at 58 GB/s, 91 % of the 64 GB/s read path; small writes below the 32 GB/s write path
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (membench-jibin-004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC). Jibin 2026-11-03 asked for a note that the test code's per-pass overhead keeps the small write rows below the write path (edit-jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, comments before 76). Bill's point 7, 2026-11-04 09:28 PST: "The 1 core read from L1 is only 58GB/s. That's WAY too slow." (edit-jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md:229-231). The G8 rows ran on boots C (007) and E (010) on 2026-11-05 UTC.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: One core reads 58.127 GB/s from a 16 KiB buffer that sits in L1 [membench-jibin-004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 7]. The C1-Nano read path is dual 128-bit, 32 B per cycle. At the 2.003 GHz clock that is 64.1 GB/s, so the row is 91 % (90.7 %) of the path. A 16 KiB pass takes 281.9 ns, 564.6 cycles, against 512 ideal cycles (52 cycles over). On the CRB (the Arm reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores at 2.8 GHz) the validation program's single-call read of 32 KiB runs 692 cycles against 683 ideal, 98.7 % of its 48 B per cycle path [crb/data-all.json asm[0] gbps 132.67; follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]. Writes reach the 128-bit write path (32.0 GB/s) only from 2 MiB up: 16 KiB writes 30.127 GB/s, 48 KiB 31.345, 96 KiB 31.664, 256 KiB 31.869, 2 MiB 31.982, 32 MiB 31.996 [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv rows 11, 26, 41, 56, 71, 86].
outlier.why_wrong: A loop over an L1-resident buffer with no refills should run at the load pipes' limit. Suspected cause (plan section 12, hypothesis H8): a fixed cost at every pass boundary (loop exit, return, save and restore of vector registers d8 to d15, the C loop's step, the next call) that an in-order core cannot overlap with the next pass's loads. The cost weighs most on short passes. Run 3 measured only one size inside the L1 (16 KiB), so no fit could separate the per-pass cost from the L1 rate.

Reading rule: fit t_pass = a + bytes / rate through the four best reps; the fit counts only when the largest residual is under 2 % of the smallest pass time; a row is an L1 row when L1 refills are under 0.01 per line (l1_reader.py; follow-up-run-plan.md section 12).

outlier.what_tests_showed:
CRB (V3AE): the looped fit is 4.2 ns per pass + bytes / 134.2 GB/s on CPU 3 and 134.3 GB/s on CPU 60 (residuals 0.5 % and 0.4 %, rule met). The single-call rows read 134.2 to 134.4 GB/s at every size, 1.33 cycles per line = 48 B per cycle. So both forms give the same L1 rate, and the method works. The V3AE's looped per-pass cost is 4.2 ns, 12 cycles at 2.8 GHz.

C1-Nano, boot C: single-call reads 53.103 / 57.898 / 60.249 / 59.812 GB/s at 4 / 8 / 16 / 24 KiB; looped reads 46.180 / 50.234 / 56.586 / 57.962. Boot E: single-call 53.096 / 57.890 / 60.331 / 60.586; looped 40.910 / 50.426 / 56.004 / 57.258. The single-call 16 and 24 KiB rows (59.8 to 60.6 GB/s) are 93 to 95 % of 64.1 GB/s.

The bytes added between the 8 and 16 KiB rows move at 64.8 (C looped), 62.8 (C single-call), 63.0 (E looped) and 63.0 (E single-call) GB/s: the read path's rate on every form and boot.

Write fits pass the 2 % rule on both boots and forms: rate 31.9 (C looped), 32.0 (C single-call), 32.0 (E looped), 32.1 (E single-call) GB/s; fixed cost 23.7 (C) and 25.7 (E) ns per pass looped, 9.1 (C) and 14.0 (E) ns single-call; residuals 1.9 %, 0.0 %, 0.3 %, 0.7 %.

Read fits fail the rule: residuals 5.4 % (C looped), 4.4 % (C single-call), 2.9 % (E looped), 2.1 % (E single-call). The failed four-point fits would give 25.5 / 8.7 ns (C looped / single-call) and 32.0 / 10.5 ns (E), with rates 61.4 to 62.4 GB/s, but the pages do not quote them. The core page's estimate instead takes the 8 KiB pass time minus 8,192 B at the 8-to-16 KiB rate: 11.5 ns est. per pass single-call on boot E (141.5 ns minus 130.1 ns); the same method gives 11.0 ns est. on boot C, and 32.4 ns est. (E) and 36.6 ns est. (C) looped. The run 4 page's table 15b gives each read row's time above the 64 GB/s ideal: 13 to 27 ns per pass single-call, 25 to 45 ns looped.

Conclusion on the pages: the shortfall is the program's per-pass cost on an in-order core, not the L1's rate. The C1-Nano TRM r0p2 (document 107753_0002_06_en) section 1.1 lists an in-order pipeline; the V3AE is out of order and overlaps the boundary.

Open: (1) who owns the per-pass cost that remains in the single-call form, 9 to 14 ns on the write fits and 11.5 ns est. on the read passes; (2) why the C1-Nano's looped read cost (32.4 ns est. on boot E) is about 8 times (est.) the V3AE's 4.2 ns against a clock ratio of 1.4 (2.8 / 2.003); the looped write fits (23.7 to 25.7 ns) are 5.6 to 6.1 times; (3) boot E's 4 KiB looped read reads 40.910 GB/s against boot C's 46.180, with rep spreads of 0.2 % and 0.5 %, while the other 15 G8 rows read 0.972 to 1.013 times C's.
