outlier.title: CRB: single-call L1 read form has slow reps at 16 and 24 KiB (134 to 106 GB/s)
outlier.first_seen: CRB (the Arm reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores, 2.8 GHz) 3-rep sample on CPU 3 (not isolated), 2026-11-04 evening; 21-rep check on CPUs 3 and 60 the same evening (files dated 2026-11-04 17:52 and 17:56). Written up in follow-up-run-plan.md section 12, 'CRB check of the two forms'.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: In a 3-rep CRB sample the single-call read form (--asm-passes, all passes of a rep inside one assembly call) read 134.2 / 134.3 / 120.5 / 106.1 GB/s best at 4 / 8 / 16 / 24 KiB. The rate fell with size. The looped form (one kernel call per pass) read 116.6 / 125.7 / 129.6 / 127.0 GB/s best at the same sizes, so at 16 and 24 KiB the single-call form read below the looped form. With 21 reps the best reps of the single-call form reach 134.2 to 134.4 GB/s at every size (the three-pipe limit, 48 B per cycle at 2.8 GHz). But at 16 KiB only 4 of 21 reps on CPU 3 and 7 of 21 on CPU 60 are fast (within 2 % of the best); the looped form has 13 and 18 of 21 fast reps. At 24 KiB the single-call form has 10 of 21 fast reps on both CPUs, the looped form 14 and 12 of 21. L1 refills are at most 0.0008 per line in every 21-rep rep, fast or slow, and at most 0.0024 per line in the 3-rep sample.
outlier.why_wrong: An L1-resident row should read the same rate in every rep. The form that removes the per-pass call, return and register save should never read slower than the looped form. The refill counters give the incidence of refills, not the time spent on them, so the cause of a slow rep is Insufficient data (codex R26, 2026-11-04). The CRB core is not isolated, so a slow rep on either form may be an interrupt or another core's work. Hypothesis H9 (from the V3AE only): the single-call form shows a slow state of the core more often than the looped form at the two larger sizes. The branch-predictor idea in the original entry is not in the primary files.

CPU 3's slow reps spread evenly from 106.6 to 131.3 GB/s (median 120.8 GB/s). The slowest rep (106.6 GB/s, rep 6) counts 0.0001 L1 refills per line against 0.0002 in the fastest (134.3 GB/s, rep 0), so the refill count does not separate slow from fast. On the C1-Nano boots C and E the slow-state check cleared every single-call row: the best reps at 16 and 24 KiB run 7.4 to 8.2 % fewer cycles per line than the 4 and 8 KiB mean on read (2.12 to 2.14 against 2.31) and 3.3 to 5.8 % fewer on write. The spread check did find slow reps on the C1-Nano single-call read rows: boot C rep 1 at 4 KiB read 47.8 GB/s against a best of 53.1 (spread 9.9 % of best) and the 8, 16 and 24 KiB rows spread 2.8, 2.9 and 3.3 %; boot E rep 1 at 8 KiB read 54.8 GB/s against 57.9 (spread 5.4 %), its other rows 0.2 to 1.7 %. The looped-form read rows spread 0.1 to 1.8 % on both boots. The run 4 page does not report these spreads. The cause of the slow reps on either machine stays open.

outlier.title: Four readers keep 93 % of the one-core rate while four writers keep 100 %; eight readers share a ceiling
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (membench-jibin-004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC per its README); the eight-reader question on run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, ran 2026-11-06 UTC per its README). The dates 2026-11-04 (Jibin's question) and 2026-11-08 (eight-reader question) come from the session transcripts, not from the primary files.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: On run 3 (the L3 off) four readers on CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8 read 34.6 GB/s together at 2 MiB each, 3.72x one core (93 % per core), and 34.0 GB/s at 16 MiB each, 3.70x the one-core 32 MiB row (93 % per core). Four writers on the same CPUs write 127.9 and 128.0 GB/s, 4.00x one core (100 % per core). Eight readers (CPUs 2 to 9) keep 91 % per core at both sizes (67.8 and 66.7 GB/s). Eight writers keep only 61 % at 2 MiB (155.2 GB/s) and 59 % at 16 MiB (152.2 GB/s). On boot F1 (the L3 on) four readers at 16 MiB each read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s per thread, 99.8 to 100.1 % of F1's one-core 32 MiB row (24.6 GB/s). Eight readers at 16 MiB each read 107.6 GB/s together, 13.4 GB/s each, 55 % of the one-core rate; at 2 MiB each 108.7 GB/s together, 13.6 each, 54 %.
outlier.why_wrong: If the read and write paths were independent of each other and of the thread count, reads and writes would scale alike. They do not. The aggregate is total bytes over the slowest thread's time, so one slow thread lowers the whole row. Per thread on run 3 (best rep): the four writers write 31.980 to 31.982 GB/s each, the same as one core alone (31.98 GB/s), so no writer lost anything. The four readers read 8.65 to 9.26 GB/s each against 9.31 GB/s for one core alone: the fastest reader kept 99.4 % and the slowest 93 %. The 2 MiB chase (one dependent load at a time) from CPUs 2 / 4 / 6 / 8 reads 24.1 / 24.6 / 24.7 / 26.1 ns per load, an 8 % spread that matches the 7 % spread in read rate (9.257 over 8.653). With eight readers the per-thread range is 8.47 to 9.04 GB/s, nearly the same as with four, and the aggregate doubles, so on run 3 the spread is a per-core property and not interference. On F1 the eight-reader rows read differently in two sections of the same page: section 9 reads them as one shared chip ceiling of about 109 GB/s (the 2 MiB row, 108.7 GB/s); section 2.3 reads them as a per-cluster cap of about 27 GB/s est. (107.6 GB/s over four clusters), near one reader's rate. The rows on disk cannot tell the two apart. Every row with two cores per cluster also has all eight cores running.

outlier.what_tests_showed: Run 3: the four-reader loss is the slowest thread, and the aggregate is set by the slowest thread. Hypothesis (on the page, not measured): the slowest reader is CPU 8, the core farthest from the home nodes, because its 2 MiB chase is 26.1 ns against 24.1 ns on CPU 2. The program does not record which thread was slowest. Eight writers reach the DRAM write ceiling (155 GB/s on run 3, 165 GB/s on F1). The pair at 160 KiB (two writers in one DSU) shares the DSU's one mesh port: 47.2 GB/s on run 3, 74 % per core. F1: four readers on four clusters lose nothing (99.8 to 100.1 % per thread), so four clusters do not share a limit. Eight readers lose 45 % per core. Whether that is a per-cluster cap or a chip-wide ceiling is open. The pair's 160 KiB read on F1 (33.7 GB/s) sits in L2 and L3 footprints and cannot settle it.

outlier.title: CME L1 chain load 21.4 ns, ten times the core's 2.0 ns, and only 0.37 ns above the register round trip
outlier.first_seen: asimov-bench run 3969 (21.56 ns, quoted in CME-plan.md lines 62 to 63 and the run 3 README line 136); run 3 (membench-jibin-004), ran 2026-11-03 UTC [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 3]
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Through the CME (Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per DSU, with its own 64 KiB 4-way L1 of 1,024 lines) a 4 KiB chain costs 21.376 ns per load [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/cme-latency-dram-small.csv row 16, the best of three reps 21.376, 21.453 and 21.473]. The core's 4 KiB row reads 2.002 ns [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/latency-dram-small.csv row 8], 10.7 times less. The register-only control (cme-roundtrip: DUP then LASTB, no load, 65,536 hops per rep) reads 21.004 to 21.006 ns per hop in all 417 reps across the eight boots from run 3 to F2, at 42.00 to 42.01 CME cycles per hop [cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 012, column cme_cycles_per_load]. Chase minus control is 0.372 ns on run 3 and 0.367 ns on boot E. The Arm LLVM scheduling model lists CLASTB into a general register at 12 cycles in streaming mode [refs/C1Nano-streaming-cme-instructions.s line 104].
outlier.why_wrong: A 21 ns cost for a hit in a 64 KiB L1 fits no cache-level model (the core's L1 hit is 2.0 ns). The run 3 page first said that 21.0 ns is part of the 21.4 ns, that every CME instruction pays it, and that it is a floor. Codex review R1 of the run 3 report rejected that: the chase runs LD1D then LASTB, the control runs DUP then LASTB, and no calibration shows the two dependency chains have the same non-memory cost, so the 0.372 ns difference is valid arithmetic but not a memory latency [codex-review-run3.md lines 24 to 32; the same caveat is R2 of the plan review, CME-plan.md line 473]. The page now calls it 'chain load minus round-trip baseline 0.37 ns, a derived number, not the memory latency' [asimov-cme-perf.html, Short version].

outlier.what_tests_showed: Boot B: 21.021 ns at 4 KiB to 21.263 ns at 64 KiB, best rows, 0.02 to 0.26 ns above the 21.004 ns baseline, with 0.0010 to 0.0156 demand refills per load [results/membench-jibin-006/results/bootB/cme-latency-dram-small.csv rows 13 to 46]. Boot D reads 21.021 to 21.262 ns and boot F2 (L3 on) 21.015 to 21.240 ns on the same rows [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 008 and 012, rows 16 and 46]. So the L1 hit load costs the round trip plus 0.02 to 0.26 ns [asimov-cme-run4.html section on boot B], and most of a load's time is the core-to-CME link both ways. What part of the 21 ns is memory stays Insufficient data: no row separates the link from the CME L1. One run 3 cme-call rep read 82.641 ns per call (39.0 ns per call, 2.50 us per 64-call rep, above the next rep's 43.609 ns), with 168.52 core cycles per call against 90.02 (5,024 extra core cycles per rep by the next rep, 5,033 by the README) and 87.59 CME cycles against 81.05 (419 extra CME cycles) [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv row 8]. The run 3 README reads this as a stall while the CME powers up (inference): in dynamic mode the CME switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us with both cores out of streaming mode (256 idle CME clocks, then a 1,024-tick timed wait, the reset values of its power register, which nothing on this platform writes) [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md lines 89 to 90]. The cme-call best values fall in two groups on every boot: 42.5 to 42.8 ns and 43.4 to 43.9 ns on run 3 and boots A to E, group medians 0.86 to 0.90 ns apart (boot D 42.703 and 43.562; B 42.586 and 43.484; A 42.703 and 43.579; C 42.586 and 43.453) [results/membench-jibin-008/README.md line 86; results/membench-jibin-007/README.md line 84; recomputed from cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 010]. Run 6 moved the clock reads into the span, so its cme-call reads 124.5 to 125.6 ns, again in two groups 1.0 ns apart [cme-latency-*.csv of 011 and 012]. The cause of the two groups is open.

outlier.title: CME chain load climbs from 8 KiB with no step at its 64 KiB L1, and refills reach 17 per load
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (membench-jibin-004), 2026-11-03; Jesse's README item "No clear step at 64 KiB" [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 63]
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Through the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit) the repeated chase reads 21.4 ns per load at 4 KiB, 24.2 at 8 KiB, 31.6 at 16 KiB, 47.6 at 64 KiB, 53.1 at 256 KiB and 70.3 at 32 MiB (best rep per footprint) [cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv of 004, cme-best rows]. Jesse's README put it as +2.9 ns at 8 KiB, +7.4 at 16 KiB, +7.7 at 24 KiB, +6.4 at 48 KiB, then only +1.5 from 48 to 64 KiB and +3.4 from 64 to 96 KiB, the first size past the CME L1 [README of 004, line 63]. The outer-refill event (0x327E, lines from beyond the cluster) reads 1.65 to 3.43 per load at 8 KiB and 14.67 to 16.58 per load at 64 to 128 KiB [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 004, rows size 8192, 65536, 98304, 131072]. A chase does one load per step, so at most one refill per load is expected. Within a footprint the slowest rep had the most outer refills in 7 of the 9 sizes from 4 to 128 KiB [README of 004, line 63].
outlier.why_wrong: The CME L1 is 64 KiB, 4-way, 64-byte lines, so 1,024 lines [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.1, citing TRM 107831 table 6-1]. A chain up to 64 KiB fits, so the load should read flat to 64 KiB and step after. Run 3 counted only inner (0x327D) and outer (0x327E) refills, which cannot tell a demand miss from a prefetch fill. Hypothesis at the time: the CME's hardware prefetcher (128 streams, indexed by instruction address, with its own TLB [asimov-cme-perf.html, CME paragraph, citing TRM 107831]) fetches lines a random chain never uses and evicts the chain's own lines.

outlier.title: CME flushed 8 MiB row (62.6 ns) reads below the walked-once 32 MiB row (70.3 ns), the reverse of the core
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (membench-jibin-004). Jesse's run 3 README raised the refill count on the flushed row (README.md of 004, line 64). The user asked the peer session on 2026-11-03 23:26 whether fresh and flushed rows should read alike (transcript-peer, the scratch copy, line 1331).
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Through the CME (the C1-SME2 streaming unit of the cluster) the flushed 8 MiB chain (every line cleaned and invalidated before each timed pass) reads 62.576 ns per load. The walked-once 8 MiB chain reads 66.246 ns, the 16 MiB 68.709 and the 32 MiB 70.345. So the flushed row is 3.7 ns below the unflushed 8 MiB row, and the latency keeps rising past every cache. The core's rows do the opposite. On the core the flushed 8 MiB row (52.738 ns) is 7.7 ns above its walked-once 8 MiB row (45.077 ns), and it meets the 32 MiB row (52.185 ns). The flushed CME row counts 3.48 to 3.52 outer refills per load, where Jesse's README expected about 1. The CME's walked-once 512 KiB to 1 MiB chains (44.9 to 50.8 ns) also read below the repeated 96 to 384 KiB walks (51.0 to 55.4 ns), a larger footprint reading faster than a smaller one.
outlier.why_wrong: Beyond the SLC (the 3.75 MiB mesh cache) both chain forms should pay the same DRAM time. A flushed chain cannot be faster than an unseen one unless something fills its lines ahead of the load. A footprint that outgrows a cache should not read faster than one that fits it. And a flushed walk should count about one outer refill per load, not 3.5.

outlier.what_tests_showed: Boot A counted the cause of the refills. On the flushed 8 MiB row the CME made 0.99 demand refills and 2.55 to 2.59 prefetch refills per load. On the 32 MiB row it made 1.00 demand and 2.68 prefetch refills per load. The core made 0.0000 prefetch refills per load on its flushed row. So the CME prefetcher runs on a random chain and the core's does not. With the prefetchers off the flushed row reads 71.711 ns (boot B) and 71.714 ns (F2). With them on it reads 62.551 ns (A), 62.053 (E) and 62.080 (F1). So the prefetcher cuts the flushed row by 12.8 to 13.5 % (B against A 12.8 %, F2 against F1 13.4 %). The L3 does not set it: B (L3 off) and F2 (L3 on) agree within 0.003 ns. The repeated 96 to 384 KiB walks were slow because the prefetcher filled 15.1 to 17.1 lines per load there on boot A (14.2 to 15.1 on boot E). The walked-once 512 KiB to 4 MiB rows carried 5.2 to 6.5 prefetch fills per load. With the prefetchers off (F2) the order of the hierarchy returns: 32.8 to 36.0 ns at 96 to 384 KiB (one outer refill per load, served inside the cluster), 37.7 at 512 KiB, 43.0 at 2 MiB, 62.8 at 8 MiB walked once, 71.1 at 32 MiB, 71.7 flushed. The sequential 8 MiB flushed chain reads 21.417 ns with the prefetcher on (A, E) and 71.740 with it off (B), so on an address-order chain the prefetcher hides the whole DRAM time. Which of the prefetched lines the random flushed walk used, the files do not show (README of 012, line 140). On F2 the flushed row still reads 0.65 ns above the 32 MiB walked-once row (71.714 against 71.068); the sources do not explain that small gap. The CME path adds 19.0 ns to a DRAM load over the core's (71.711 against 52.739 on boot B).

outlier.title: OCM through the CME: 9.6 to 18.0 ns above the core, sparse fastest, no order by mesh distance
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (004), 2026-11-03 (UTC) [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 66]; the three chain shapes compared on run 4 boot A (005), 2026-11-04 (UTC) [asimov-cme-run4.html section 3.2 and 6]
outlier.what_looked_wrong: On run 3 the one line per page (sparse) OCM rows read 35.469 to 38.516 ns per load through the CME [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 004, cme-best rows]. CPU 2's own loads of the same chains read 21.359 to 25.781 ns [latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv of 004]. The per-region pass medians did not order by mesh distance: OCM4 (3 crosspoints away) had the lowest median, 38.609 ns, and OCM0 (1 crosspoint) the highest, 42.984 ns [README 004 line 66; medians recomputed from the 7 cme-fresh rows]. By best pass OCM2 (1 crosspoint) was fastest at 35.469 ns and OCM0 (1 crosspoint) slowest at 38.516 ns. The 7 passes of one region spread 6.1 to 10.7 ns, more than the 2.2 to 2.8 ns that two extra crosspoints cost the core [README 004 line 66]. The every-line (dense) all-five row read 44.688 ns through the CME against the core's 25.340 ns [cme-latency-ocm-all5-dense.csv and latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 004]. On boot A the sparse rows read 34.625 to 35.906 ns, the dense rows 38.318 to 42.171 ns (3.2 to 6.3 ns above sparse) and the vary rows 45.391 to 48.813 ns (10.5 to 12.9 ns above sparse) [cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv of 005]. On the core the dense chain is fastest and the sparse slowest, so the CME's order is the reverse [asimov-cme-run4.html section 6]. On boot E the OCM1 row read 28.984 ns while OCM0 and OCM2, at the same distance, read 37.156 and 35.969 ns [cme-latency-ocm-region0..2.csv of 010]. On boot E OCM through the CME costs 9.6 to 18.0 ns more per load than from the core on the one line per page rows [asimov-cme-perf.html section 7].
outlier.why_wrong: Rows at one mesh distance should read alike. The CME path should add a fixed amount over the core's path. The refill-cause counters of boot A show why they did not. On the sparse rows the CME counted only 0.46 to 0.63 demand-read refills per load (pass means) and 0.39 to 0.56 hardware-prefetch refills per load [asimov-cme-run4.html table 3.2; recomputed from the 7 cme-fresh rows of cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 005]. So 37 to 54 % of the sparse loads were L1 hits on lines the CME prefetcher had already fetched (page hypothesis, section 6). The dense rows counted 0.80 to 0.81 demand and 1.40 to 1.47 prefetch refills per load, and the vary rows 0.92 to 0.94 demand refills per load [same files]. The prefetcher's fills hid the demand latency, by a different fraction on each pass and each region. The best pass of a row is therefore the pass where the prefetcher caught the most lines, not the demand latency.

F2 reads 1.001 to 1.028 times boot B, so the L3 does not change OCM through the CME; F2 counts 1.000 outer refills per load, none served by the L3 [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 006 and 012]. With the prefetchers on, F2 reads 1.257 to 1.343 times F1 per region [README 012 line 141]. The 64 KiB contiguous translations change little through the CME: boot D against boot B reads 0.978 to 1.000 on the sparse rows, boot C against boot A 0.962 to 1.069; boot C sparse 33.359 to 37.953 ns, boot D 46.641 to 51.328 ns [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 007 and 008; asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.2]. The page gives the CME's own TLB as the reason [C1-SME2 TRM 107831]. Boot E's OCM1 best pass, 28.984 ns, is the pass cme-fresh5, which counts 0.125 demand refills and 0.906 prefetch refills per load; the other six passes of that row read 36.625 to 42.531 ns with 0.469 to 0.797 demand refills per load [cme-latency-ocm-region1.csv of 010]. So on that one pass the prefetcher fetched about 0.9 of the chain's lines before the demand loads reached them. Why the prefetcher caught so many lines on that pass is not in the files. The pages do not name this counter reading. The OCM read through the CME runs at 0.62 times its warm DRAM-buffer rate on run 3, the reverse of the core; the rows differ in page size and in flushing, so the data do not say which costs the CME [README 004 line 84].

outlier.title: L3 on moves the CME's refills inside the cluster, but the chain is slower at 8 to 32 KiB; the L3-served CME load is 32.8 to 33.9 ns with a hit/snoop split
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot E against boot C (010 against 007), boot E ran 2026-11-05 UTC [README.md of 010, line 3]; run 6 boot F2 L3-event sweep (012), ran 2026-11-06 and 07 UTC [README.md of 012, line 3]
outlier.what_looked_wrong: On boot E (the DSU L3 on) 99.5 % of the CME's L1 refills at 8 KiB come from inside the cluster: 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer refills per load, mean over 3 reps (boot C, the L3 off: 0.59 inner and 3.33 outer) [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007, the 8192 rows]. Yet the chain reads 1.019 times boot C at 8 KiB (24.932 against 24.466 ns per load, best rep) and 1.120 times at 16 KiB (35.065 against 31.303 ns) [same files; README.md of 010, line 109]. On boot F2 (the prefetchers off, the L3 on) the exploratory L3-hit event 0x328E counts only 0.14 to 0.64 hits per load at 96 to 384 KiB at the best rep (0.12 to 0.64 over all reps), while the inner refills are 0.96 to 1.00 per load at the best rep (0.88 to 1.00 over the reps) [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]. The latency falls as the chain grows: 36.0 ns at 96 KiB to 32.8 ns at 256 KiB [same file, best reps]. The L3-served load of 32.8 to 33.9 ns [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012, 192 to 384 KiB] is 6.2 to 7.3 ns above asimov-bench's 26.6 ns for the DSU L3 through the CME [CME-plan.md line 63; asimov-cme-perf.html open items].
outlier.why_wrong: An L3 hit inside the cluster should cost less than a refill from the mesh. Refills moving inside the cluster should lower the chain time, not raise it. With the prefetchers off, every inner refill was expected to be an L3 hit, so the hit count should have been near 1.00 per load, not 0.14 to 0.64.

outlier.title: CME read calls carry about 100 ns of fixed cost per call, write calls none; run 6's in-span clock stamps added about 82 ns per call
outlier.first_seen: run 3 (membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03) two-point fits; Wade's SMSTART/SMSTOP comment 2026-11-05 12:24 PST (jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md line 233); plan section 13 2026-11-05 evening; run 6 boots F1 (011, 2026-11-06) and F2 (012, 2026-11-06 and 07)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Run 3 timed every CME bandwidth pass as one kernel call. A line through the 16 and 48 KiB rows gives the read kernel a fixed cost of 100.6 ns per call at a slope rate of 133.5 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, cme-read 16384 and 49152 best rows: 73.377 and 104.865 GB/s, so 223.3 and 468.7 ns per pass]. The same line through the write rows gives 0.5 ns per call at 63.9 GB/s [same file, cme-write best rows 63.731 and 63.821 GB/s]. Both kernels pay the same register save, SMSTART, SMSTOP and restore, so the two intercepts should not differ by 100 ns. The fixed cost is 45 % of the 16 KiB read pass (100.6 of 223.3 ns). The 1 KiB read call takes 97.1 ns and the 1 KiB write call 39.1 ns [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 004, best rows 10.549 and 26.213 GB/s]; the write call is 23.0 ns est. above its 16.0 ns of stores at 63.9 GB/s. The one-load control cme-call minus the cme-roundtrip chain is only 21.7 ns per call on run 3 (42.703 minus 21.004 ns) [cme-latency-dram-large.csv of 004, rows 7 and 11], which contradicts the 100 ns read intercept. In run 6 the cme-call control tripled: 124.516 to 125.609 ns per call by the best rows (reps up to 125.656), 61.000 to 61.250 ns of it inside the span [cme-latency-*.csv of 011 and 012, 24 files], against 42.516 to 43.609 ns best (reps to 43.922) on boot E [cme-latency-*.csv of 010, 21 files]. The 1 KiB read call read 186.1 ns on F1 and 191.1 ns on F2 (108.0 ns in span on both) against 97.1 ns on run 3 [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read 1024 best rows]. The looped write rows at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB do not lie on a line: largest residual 27.9 ns on F1 and 26.6 ns on F2 [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]. The single-call 96 KiB read reads 1.56 times its looped twin on F1 (68.249 against 43.713 GB/s) and 1.07 times on F2 (42.773 against 39.950) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, 98304 best rows].
outlier.why_wrong: Every call pays the register save, SMSTART, SMSTOP and the restore, so a read call and a write call should carry the same fixed cost. Hypothesis H10 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 13): stores are posted, so the last stores of one call drain while the kernel leaves streaming mode and the next call enters, and the switch hides behind them from 16 KiB up. Hypothesis H11: the read kernel ends with a fold of its 16 accumulators (15 EOR, EORV, FMOV), which waits for every load to return, so most of the read call's cost is the fold and its return dependency. Run 6's cme-call tripled because the run 6 kernels are run 3's plus exactly 15 instructions (2 ISB, 2 MRS of CNTVCT_EL0, 2 ADRP, 3 ADD, 1 SUB, 2 LDR, 3 STR) by Jesse's disassembly [README 011 line 153], and the ISB before the second stamp waits for earlier instructions, so the bracket of every call now holds the stamps' own cost. Bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call, return and the second stamp's eight instructions), not the switch alone [cme_kern.S header lines 11 to 23; README 011 line 155].

outlier.title: CME writes fall from 64 to 52 and 40 GB/s with the L3 on; CME stores stop at half a store per cycle
outlier.first_seen: run 6 boots F1 (membench-jibin-011, 2026-11-06 UTC) and F2 (012, 2026-11-06/07 UTC); the half-rate stores were first seen in run 3 (004, 2026-11-03 UTC)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: With the L3 on, the CME (the cluster's Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit) writes DRAM slower than it did with the L3 off. On boot F1 the CME write reads 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s by the bracket at 16 to 256 KiB and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB; boot F2 (prefetchers off) reads 51.5 to 52.5 and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at the same sizes [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, best rep]. Run 3 (L3 off) wrote 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s at 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. The drop also holds in span (the clock stamps inside the streaming span) from 48 KiB on: 53.5 to 56.3 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB and 40.5 to 42.8 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB on F1; only the 16 KiB row reads higher in span (69.5 GB/s) than run 3's bracket (63.7) [span_GBps column of 011]. The core's own writes did not move: one core writes 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s in run 3 and 30.6 to 32.0 on F1 [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011; README 011 line 109: 1.000 to 1.003 times at 48 KiB to 32 MiB]. The CME's reads did not move either where they can be compared: 36.6 to 37.0 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB on both (36.6 at 32 MiB on both), and 73.8 and 104.6 GB/s in span at 16 and 48 KiB on F1 against run 3's 73.4 and 104.9 by the bracket [README 011 line 204]; at 160 and 256 KiB the F1 reads are 1.114 to 1.117 times run 3's (41.4 and 41.6 against 37.1 and 37.2). Separate from the L3 question: the CME's store rate is below its load rate on every boot. In run 3 at 48 KiB the CME read 104.9 GB/s and wrote 63.8 GB/s, that is 52 and 32 bytes per 2.003 GHz cycle, so half of one 64-byte store per cycle. With the L3 on, the single-call form (every pass of a rep inside one call) reads 109 to 132 GB/s (one 64-byte load per cycle, 54 to 66 bytes per cycle) but writes only 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s (26 bytes per cycle, 0.42 of a store per cycle) [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011; asimov-cme-perf.html table 'The CME L1 on its own']. No source on disk gives the CME store path width.
outlier.why_wrong: A cache that is turned on should not slow a streaming write whose footprint (1 to 32 MiB) cannot fit it (the L3 is 256 KiB). The kernels are run 3's byte for byte by the box's disassembly check [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6], so the change is the platform's, not the code's. Run 6's clock stamps do not explain the drop at 1 to 32 MiB: the outside-span interval is at most 0.5 % of a call there (118.5 to 357.8 ns of calls of 25 to 1,644 us) [README 011, bandwidth rows note], and bracket over span is 0.995 to 1.000 at 1 to 32 MiB (recomputed from 011 and 012). Hypothesis on the CME page: with the L3 on the CME's stores allocate in the L3 and drain through it at the L3's write rate, which is below the CME's store path; with the L3 holding no data the stores went straight to the mesh [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]. No source gives the L3's write rate as a number. The measured CME store rate with the L3 on is 27 bytes per cycle at 48 to 256 KiB in span (53.5 to 54.8 GB/s) and 20 to 21 bytes per cycle at 1 to 32 MiB (40.4 to 42.8 GB/s). Supporting match: one CME writing 32 MiB on F1 (40.4 GB/s) is 0.99 times the 40.9 GB/s that CPUs 2 and 3 write together (16 MiB each) through the same cluster on the same boot [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv of 011; run 3 also 40.9 GB/s, against the CME's 62.0 then]. The page's reading: if the CME's stores leave through the same cluster port, the two-core write limit is on the cores' side, not the port's (hypothesis).

outlier.what_tests_showed: Cause unknown; listed as open on the CME page ('open: why the CME's writes fall with the L3 on') [asimov-cme-perf.html section 10]. F2 rules out the prefetcher (writes 0.927 to 1.000 times F1). The stamp check rules out run 6's clock reads at 1 to 32 MiB (under 0.5 % of a call). The CME bandwidth rows carry no CME counters (bandwidth refuses --perf with --cme) [README 012 line 142], so no refill count sits beside the drop. Side result from F2: the CME prefetcher carries about half of a streaming DRAM read, 17.7 GB/s on F2 against 36.6 GB/s on F1 at 32 MiB (0.48 times) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012 and 011]. Copies fell with the writes: 0.65 to 0.84 times run 3's by the bracket at every size (writes and copies together), 0.65 to 0.89 in span from 48 KiB on [README 011 line 11]. Page defect found during verification: asimov-cme-perf.html's 'CME L1 on its own' row prints an unrendered template, '{BPC6 * max(SINGLE_WR) / 64:.1f} of a store per cycle', where the number 0.42 should appear.

outlier.title: CME wake-up cost per timed span and the OCM pass spread through the CME
outlier.first_seen: run 3 README (membench-jibin-004, CME power section, lines 89-90), 2026-11-03; run 6 in-span data (011, 012), 2026-11-07
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Three views in the run 3 README bound a fixed CME cost per timed span at 0.1 to 0.3 us est. [membench-jibin-004/README.md line 90]. On run 3 the 7 CME passes of one OCM region (64 loads each) spread 6.1 to 10.7 ns per load [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 004, cme-fresh1..7 rows; recomputed 6.11 to 10.73]. On boot E the same 7 passes spread 7.25 to 13.55 ns per load (max minus min), and the pass medians run 3.62 to 12.66 ns above the bests [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 010/bootE]. One run 3 cme-call rep ran 82.641 ns per call against 43.609 and 43.625 in the other two reps: 2,498 ns (2.5 us) longer over its 64 calls, with 5,033 more core cycles (168.52 against 89.88 cycles per call, times 64) and only 419 more CME cycles (87.5938 against 81.0469, times 64) [cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv of 004, cme-call reps 0 to 2].
outlier.why_wrong: The SCP (the system control processor's firmware) set every cluster's CME power controller to dynamic mode at boot [membench-jibin-004/README.md line 35]. By the RTL (read, not measured) the CME in dynamic mode switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us with both cores out of streaming mode, and it cleans and invalidates its L1 on the way off and again on the way back on [README.md line 89]. Every timed span follows a gap outside streaming mode (perf calls, output, often a flush). The programs do not time those gaps, so whether the CME was off at the start of a span is not recorded [README.md line 89]. A fixed cost of 0.1 to 0.3 us est. is up to about 5 ns est. per load on a 64-load OCM pass, 0.3 to 1 ns est. on a 320-load pass, and invisible on longer passes [README.md line 90]. The 2.5 us rep fits a stall while the CME powers up (inference, README.md line 90).

outlier.title: 8 MiB chain in address order through the CME reads 21.4 ns, like a CME L1 hit
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot A (005), measured 2026-11-04 (UTC); the row is new in run 4 (run 3, 004, has no cme-latency-dram-seq.csv). Jesse's README 005 does not mention the row; the first written comparison is README 006 (boot B) and the run-4 CME page.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: An 8 MiB chain in address order, every line flushed first, reads 21.417 ns per load through the CME on boots A, C and E [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010, cme-best rows]. That is within 0.07 ns of the CME's 4 KiB L1-hit row (21.453 ns on A, 21.481 on C, 21.371 on E: 0.036 and 0.064 ns below on A and C, 0.046 ns above on E) [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, 007, 010]. It is 0.41 ns above the 21.005 ns CME round-trip control (no memory load at all) [cme-roundtrip-best rows of the same files]. The row counts 1.00 outer refills per load, so every line still came from outside the cluster. The core's same chain reads 6.917 ns on A and C and 2.492 ns on E [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010].
outlier.why_wrong: Every line of the 8 MiB chain is flushed before the pass, and 8 MiB is larger than the SLC (3.75 MiB). So every line must come from DRAM once per walk. A DRAM-footprint chain at the CME L1-hit time contradicts the footprint unless something fetches each line before the load reaches it.

So the CME prefetcher fetches each line before its load arrives, and each load hits the CME L1. With the prefetcher off the row reads 71.740 ns on B and 71.738 ns on D, with hwprf 0.0000 and rd 1.0000 per load [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 008]. That is 3.35 times boot A's 21.417 ns and is 0.03 ns above the random flushed 8 MiB chain on the same boots (71.711 ns on B, 71.712 on D), the DRAM time through the CME [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008]. The core's chain moved the same way: 6.917 ns with the prefetchers on against 52.762 ns on B and 52.763 on D, 7.63 times [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 008]. The row is the stimulus a hardware prefetcher is built for, so it shows whether the CME prefetch event counts at all; the run-4 CME page uses it for that [asimov-cme-run4.html, Words used here; section 5 chart caption]. Open point on the core side only: the core's chain sits at about an L2 hit (6.9 ns against 6.1 ns for the 128 KiB row), so the core's L1 prefetcher runs ahead by about one L2 hit, while the CME's runs far enough ahead for an L1 hit; the core page marks this a hypothesis [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 5].

outlier.title: Core sequential 8 MiB chain reads 6.9 ns with the L3 off and 2.5 ns with it on, faster than the L2 hit
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot A (membench-jibin-005, run on 2026-11-04 UTC): 6.917 ns per load [results/membench-jibin-005/results/bootA/latency-dram-seq.csv, best row]. Boot E (membench-jibin-010, run on 2026-11-05 UTC): 2.492 ns per load [results/membench-jibin-010/results/bootE/latency-dram-seq.csv, best row]. The 0.49 ns excess over the L1 chain was written up on the core page section 8 on 2026-11-05 (memory asimov-cme-test-state.md). Jibin's question of 2026-11-06 ("you missed the DRAM load time; how did you get 0.49 ns of waiting") is not in the primary files; it comes from the transcript sources only (not verified here).
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The sequential chain is an 8 MiB chain whose members are the 64-byte lines in address order, every line flushed from every cache before each pass [core page glossary; latency-dram-seq.csv header: flush=1 seq=1]. Every load of it is a DRAM read. On boots A and C (prefetchers on, L3 off) it reads 6.917 ns per load, best of two fresh passes [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 and 007]. On boot E (prefetchers on, L3 on) it reads 2.492 ns per load (fresh1 2.501, fresh2 2.492) [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010]. The prefetch counters are the same on all three boots: 1.0000 L1 refills per load, 0.9997 (E), 0.9999 (A) and 1.0000 / 0.9999 (C) L1 refills requested by the hardware prefetcher, 1.0000 L2 refills per load. With the prefetchers off (boots B and D) the same chain reads 52.762 and 52.763 ns per load with 0.0000 prefetch refills [latency-dram-seq.csv of 006 and 008]. For comparison on boot E: the 4 KiB repeated chain (an L1 hit) reads 2.002 ns per load (4.01 cycles), and the 128 KiB repeated chain (an L2 hit) reads 6.023 ns [latency-dram-small.csv of 010]. So on A the DRAM stream costs about an L2 hit, and on E it costs 2.492 ns, which is 4.99 cycles at 2.003 GHz (cycles_per_load column 4.99), one cycle above the L1 hit's 4.01 cycles. The L3 read refill event 0xA2 reads 0.0001 per load on the sequential chain although every line was flushed and came from outside the DSU; on the random flushed chain of the same boot it reads 1.0001 [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010].
outlier.why_wrong: Every load is a DRAM read (the line is flushed first and one L2 refill per load is counted), yet it costs an L2 hit (A, C) or an L1 hit plus one cycle (E). One DRAM read costs 52.659 ns on boot E's random flushed chain [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010], so a 2.492 ns load cannot be waiting for its own line. The L3 is 256 KiB per cluster and cannot hold an 8 MiB stream, so the 2.78 times change from A to E (6.917 / 2.492) with the same prefetch counts per load has no cause in the counters on disk. Jesse's boot E README says the same: "These files do not show why its latency fell" [results/membench-jibin-010/README.md line 113]. The excess over the L1 chain is 0.49 ns, 0.98 cycles, close to one whole cycle. A wait for a late line would not average to a whole cycle [core page section 8].

outlier.what_tests_showed: The DRAM time is overlapped, not missing. With the prefetchers off (boots B and D) the same chain costs the full DRAM time, 52.762 and 52.763 ns per load, the same as the random flushed chain (52.659 ns on E, 52.739 ns on B) [latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008, 010]. So the address order alone buys nothing; the prefetcher does the overlap. On boot E the prefetcher issues a new DRAM read every 2.492 ns while each read takes about 52.7 ns, so it keeps about 21 reads in flight (est., 52.762 / 2.492 = 21.2); on boot A about 7.6 (est., 52.762 / 6.917) [derived from latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 005, 010; core page section 8 draws this as wall-clock lanes]. The stream rate on E is 64 bytes per 2.492 ns, 25.7 GB/s (derived), about the plain one-core DRAM read of the same boot: 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010, best rows]. On boot C the plain read moves 9.294 GB/s (2 MiB) and 9.196 GB/s (32 MiB) [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007], so by the same arithmetic C keeps about 2.8 times fewer reads in flight (est.). The CME's own sequential row is unchanged by the L3: 21.417 ns per load on A, C and E alike, with 1.0000 prefetch refills per load [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]. Hypotheses on the pages, none tested: (1) with the L3 holding data the prefetcher's stream drains into the L3 and the L2 refills complete sooner [run 4 core page 14.2]; (2) the full-L3 mode lets the cluster keep more read requests in flight toward the mesh [core page 2.3]; (3) the extra whole cycle per load is the prefetched line's write into L1 taking the cache for one cycle per line [core page section 8]; (4) either the L1 prefetcher's fills do not allocate in the L3, or 0xA2 counts demand reads only; the TRM text ('level 3 accesses that receive data from outside the L3 cache due to a memory-read operation') does not say which [run 4 core page 3.1]. What the L3 changes in how far ahead the prefetcher runs is Insufficient data [core page section 8].

outlier.title: Boot E's sparse per-region OCM rows got faster with fewer outside refills: the L3 serves part of their loads
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot E (membench-jibin-010), 2026-11-05; repeated on run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011), 2026-11-06
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Boot E is the first boot with the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 in full mode. Its sparse per-region OCM rows (one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads per pass, 7 passes) read faster than on the L3-off boots. From CPU 2 they read 19.078 to 20.391 ns per load (run 3: 21.359 to 25.781 ns; boot A: 22.859 to 27.594 ns). Against boot A, the 10 sparse cells of CPUs 2 and 8 read 0.69 to 1.10 times A's. One cell went the other way: CPU 8 to OCM4 read 23.906 ns on E, +18.7 % over run 3's 20.141 ns and +9.6 % over A's 21.813 ns. The dense all-five control did not move (26.082 ns on E, 26.009 ns on A). The sparse rows counted only 0.33 to 1.00 L3 read refills (event 0xA2, a line fetched from outside the cluster) per load on E, 9 of the 10 cells below 0.8, against 0.70 to 0.96 on A and C. On CPU 2 alone: 0.330 to 0.589 per load on E, 0.739 to 0.772 on A, 0.703 to 0.830 on C. Jesse's boot E README adds that E's OCM passes count up to 0.48 L2 refills per load that neither prefetch event nor 0xA2 accounts for (A: at most 0.0157). The route rows (the dense chase of one region under the mesh counters, CPUs 2 to 8) read 13.972 to 23.190 ns on E, also below the dense all-five row. Note: on the L3-off boots the sparse per-region bests were mostly below the dense all-five row too (run 3 CPU 2: 4 of 5 regions below 25.340 ns), so 'below the dense row' alone was never the anomaly. The anomaly is the drop in time with the drop in outside refills.
outlier.why_wrong: Every OCM load should cross the mesh to the region's home node, so each load should count one outside refill. The L3 is 256 KiB per two-core cluster, the size of one OCM region. The /dev/ocm module maps a region as Normal write-back memory, the cacheable type, so the L3 may hold OCM lines. The sparse chain touches 64 lines per pass, so lines from the pass before can still be in the L3 when the next pass runs. A load that hits the L3 costs about 10.8 ns est. (from boot E's hit set), less than the 26 ns mesh round trip, so a row with part L3 hits reads below the true OCM latency.

outlier.what_tests_showed: The dense all-five chain from CPU 2 reads 26.082 ns on E (A 26.009, C 24.959, run 3 25.340) and counts 1.0010 and 1.0005 outside refills per load in its two passes (mean 1.0008; CPU 8: 1.0009). So none of its loads is an L3 hit and it is the OCM number to quote. F1 repeats it from all four CPUs at 25.445 to 27.702 ns with 1.0007 to 1.0009 refills per load. F1's sparse passes count 0xA2 at 0.425 per load (mean over 140 passes) against run 3's 0.710, with the same L2 refills (2.802 against 2.779). So part of the sparse-row loads were filled inside the cluster on F1, by the L3 on the pages' reading. Which loads hit the L3 is a hypothesis until the hit event is counted on those rows: no OCM row on E or F1 ran under the L3 hit event. The per-region rows on the L3-on boots are below the true OCM latency, and the pages use them only for the order of the regions by mesh distance.

outlier.title: Table-walk rate on the 32 MiB chain differs 129 times between two processes of one boot; 0x8188 never counts
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boots C, D, E (membench-jibin-007, 008, 010), 2026-11-05 UTC; boot D's README (008, The walk rows) is the first file that puts the two rates of one boot side by side
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Boot D ran the same 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages in two processes. The TLB-set row counted 0.0033 and 0.0035 table walks per load (0x34 DTLB_WALK) in its two passes, 0.0034 on average, at 53.266 ns per load best [results/membench-jibin-008/results/bootD/latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2, column dtlb_walk_per_load]. The walk row of the same chain counted 0.4381 and 0.4371 walks per load, 0.4376 on average, at 58.725 ns best [008 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]. That is 129 times more walks (128.7 by the pass means; 132.8 by the best passes, 0.4381 against 0.0033). Boot C read 0.3669 and 0.3655 (TLB-set row, 59.081 ns best) against 0.1849 and 0.1850 (walk row, 56.726 ns best) [007 bootC, same two files]. Boot E read 0.3662 and 0.3655 (57.611 ns) against 0.5113 and 0.5118 (58.705 ns) [010 bootE, same two files]. Event 0x8188 DTLB_WALK_BLOCK read 0.0000 in all 37 pass rows of each boot's six walk files (C, D, E), while 0x818A DTLB_WALK_PAGE equalled 0x34 to four decimals on every 32 MiB stimulus pass. On the five sparse OCM walk rows with the prefetchers on, 0x34 counted up to 2.6094 walks per load on C (region 1, fresh7) and 2.7969 on E (region 3, fresh7), in 33 of 35 and 32 of 35 passes, while 0x8188 read 0.0000 in all 70 passes and 0x818A read 0.0156 per load (one walk in 64 loads) in two passes of C (region 1 fresh5, region 2 fresh7) and 0.0000 in the other 68 [007 and 010 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]. On boot D, prefetchers off, all three events read 0.0000 in all 35 OCM passes [008, same files].
outlier.why_wrong: A walk rate on one chain was expected to belong to the boot (its page size and firmware), not to the process. Boot D's 0.003 walks per load looked like the contiguous hint's effect (boot D mapped the OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations). But the hint changes only the /dev/ocm mappings, and the 32 MiB chain lives on 4 KiB DRAM pages, which the hint does not reach [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 13, line on the 32 MiB stimulus; 008 README, Against boot B]. Boot B, with no hint, read 0.3657 and 0.3661 walks per load on the same row (58.509 ns best) and boot A 0.5204 and 0.5210 (58.810 ns) [006 and 005 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv], so the rate was already spread across boots before the hint. A counter that never reads nonzero (0x8188) cannot be told from a counter that does not count. By the RTL, 0x34 counts a data-side walk when it starts, including walks for TLB requests with the prefetch requester ids TLBID_PF0 to TLBID_PF3, and leaves out the TLB's own prefetch walks [nevis0_tlb_request_slot.sv:1359, :1368; nevis0_tlb_pkg.sv:369-371, as cited in 007 README, The walk rows]. 0x8188 and 0x818A count a walk only when it returns a fault-free translation to the core [nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3374-3376, :3405-3414, same README]. So the OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counted returned no translation to the core. On this RTL a walk that ends in a page entry with the contiguous bit counts in 0x8188, not 0x818A [nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3147, 007 and 008 READMEs], so a nonzero 0x8188 on a boot C or D OCM row would have shown the walker using the hint. It read 0 there, but the 0x34-only walks returned no translation, so these zeros do not test 0x8188.

tests_added.name: Walk counter set (--events walk: cycles, 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2, 0x34 DTLB_WALK, 0x8188 DTLB_WALK_BLOCK, 0x818A DTLB_WALK_PAGE) on six rows from CPU 2: the 32 MiB stimulus and the five sparse per-region OCM chains, commands 40 to 45, each a second process of a chain the TLB-set rows already ran
tests_added.run: run 5b additions, plan section 11 (2026-11-04), implementation commit c3e5c49 on 7921962 and comment-only revision ed6056a; boot D ran ed6056a, boots C and E ran b79dffa (ed6056a plus e024d57 and b79dffa) [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11; codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md lines 1067 and 1081; 007 and 008 READMEs]
tests_added.measures: Designed for goal G-i: which descriptor (block or page) each walk ended in, to show whether the walker used the contiguous entry on boots C and D. The walk rate in a second process was a by-product: the walk row repeats the TLB-set row's chain in another process, so the two rates of one boot became comparable.

outlier.what_tests_showed: The rate is the process's, not the boot's. In all three boots the faster of the two processes is the one that walked less: C 56.726 ns at 0.185 walks per load against 59.081 ns at 0.366; D 53.266 ns at 0.0034 against 58.725 ns at 0.4376; E 57.611 ns at 0.366 against 58.705 ns at 0.512 [the two files per boot named above; 007 README line on the 32 MiB stimulus]. The walk rows' rates are 0.5, 129 and 1.4 times the TLB-set rows' on C, D and E [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13]. Why two processes of one boot differ is Insufficient data: the DRAM chain's physical pages are not logged (the dmesg map lines cover /dev/ocm mappings only [007 README, OCM mappings]); the same chain in several walk-counted processes of one boot would show whether the rate is the process's page placement [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, open items]. 0x818A is validated: on the 4 KiB-page stimulus it equals 0x34 on every pass of C, D and E, as it must when every walk ends in a page entry. 0x8188 stays unvalidated: it read 0 in every pass of every boot, and no row ever had a counted walk that ended in a block or contiguous entry [007, 008, 010 READMEs, The walk rows]. The OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counts are the prefetchers': boots B and D (prefetchers off) count 0 walks per load on the sparse chains, boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) count 0.27 to 1.24, 0.41 to 0.75 and 0.56 to 1.62 per load on the sparse TLB-set rows, and by the RTL 0x34 includes the walks that prefetch-requester TLB requests start [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.3; 007 README, The walk rows]. The files do not show what started each walk or how it ended [007 README]. A demand-only walk event, 0x813C DTLB_WALK_RW, would separate the program's walks from the prefetchers' [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 7]; it was not in any run's counter set. Rule: never quote boot D's 0.003 walks per load as the contiguous hint's effect.

outlier.title: Boot E's 16 and 32 MiB chains read 0.4 to 0.7 ns above every earlier boot; F1's 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB passes sit below every earlier pass
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot E (010), run on 2026-11-05 [README.md of 010 line 299]; run 6 boot F1 (011), run on 2026-11-06 [README.md of 011 line 321]
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The 32 MiB chain reads 52.875 ns per load on boot E. Boots A, B, C, D and run 3 read 52.181, 52.248, 52.238, 52.249 and 52.185 ns on the same row, a spread of 0.068 ns [latency-dram-large.csv row 47 (best) of 010, 005, 006, 007, 008, 004]. So E sits 0.626 to 0.694 ns above every earlier best. The 16 MiB chain reads 51.167 ns on E against 50.692, 50.694, 50.686, 50.682 and 50.785 ns on A, B, C, D and run 3 [latency-dram-large.csv row 43 of the same files]. So E sits 0.382 to 0.485 ns above every earlier best. Both of E's passes at 16 and 32 MiB (51.167, 51.239; 52.875, 52.881) sit above every pass of the four earlier boots [rows 41-42 and 45-46; README.md of 010 line 111]. Two rows at the same latency level did not move: the flushed 8 MiB row reads 52.659 ns on E against 52.657 on C [latency-dram-flushed.csv row 7 of 010 and 007], and the 8 MiB chain reads 45.077 on E against 45.130 on C [latency-dram-large.csv row 39 of 010 and 007]. On F1 the rise did not repeat: the 32 MiB chain reads 52.212 ns and the 16 MiB chain 50.551 ns [latency-dram-large.csv rows 47 and 43 of 011]. Instead both of F1's passes at 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB lie below every earlier pass (run 3 and boots A to E). The gaps to the nearest earlier pass are 0.053 ns at 2 MiB (F1 23.835 and 23.714 against D's 23.888), 0.468 ns at 6 MiB (F1 39.085 and 39.116 against E's 39.584), 0.411 ns at 8 MiB (F1 44.485 and 44.612 against B's 45.023) and 0.119 ns at 16 MiB (F1 50.551 and 50.563 against D's 50.682) [latency-dram-large.csv rows 21-22, 33-34, 37-38, 41-42 of 011, 008, 010, 006; README.md of 011 line 143]. Verifier note from the same CSVs: the 1.5 MiB row also fits this pattern, F1's passes 23.502 and 23.593 ns sit 0.179 ns below the lowest earlier pass (run 3's 23.772) [latency-dram-large.csv rows 17-18 of 011 and 004]; the README of 011 does not list it. The 2 MiB best values are 23.714 ns on F1, 24.096 on run 3 and 24.177 on E [latency-dram-large.csv row 23 of 011, 004, 010].
outlier.why_wrong: Turning the L3 on should not slow a DRAM-sized random chain. The flushed 8 MiB row at the same latency level did not move on E. The counters of the 16 and 32 MiB rows read the same on E and C: 1.0000 L1 and L2 refills per load and 0.9995 to 1.0000 L3 read refills per load [latency-dram-large.csv rows 41-42 and 45-46 of 010 and 007; README.md of 010 line 111]. At 1.5 to 2 MiB the L3 serves almost nothing: 0.962 to 0.965 outside refills per load at 1.5 MiB and 0.979 to 0.982 at 2 MiB on both E and F1 [latency-dram-large.csv rows 17-18 and 21-22 of 010 and 011, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]. So the SLC and DRAM rows were expected unchanged on F1 too, and a drop below every earlier pass had no counter to explain it.

outlier.title: Boot E's 4 KiB looped L1 read reads 40.9 GB/s against boot C's 46.2
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boots C and E (membench-jibin-007 and 010), 2026-11-05 (UTC), both READMEs line 3
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Boots C and E ran the same sixteen G8 rows (one-core L1 read and write at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB, in a looped form and a single-call form). The 4 KiB looped read reads 40.910 GB/s on E and 46.180 GB/s on C. That is 0.886 times C, 11.4 % lower. The five reps of that row spread 0.16 % on E (40.844 to 40.910 GB/s) and 0.53 % on C (45.936 to 46.180 GB/s), so the gap is not rep noise. The row costs 3.13 to 3.14 cycles per line on E against 2.78 to 2.79 on C. The other 15 G8 rows read 0.972 to 1.013 times C's (the largest deviation is the 4 KiB single-call write, 0.972). The 4 KiB single-call read is equal on both boots (53.096 GB/s on E, 53.103 on C). The L1 data refills on the 4 KiB read rows are at most 0.0008 per line on both boots (all G8 rows: at most 0.0199 per line on C, 0.0195 on E).
outlier.why_wrong: E and C ran the same commit (b79dffa) and the same program build (the bandwidth binary is C's once stripped, 6 bytes of an assembler temporary name apart) [README of 010, section 'Against boot C: the L3 alone']. The buffer fits the 32 KiB L1 and the refill counters show it stays there, so the G8 rows on E are a repeat check of C's rows, not an L3 result [README of 010, 'The G8 rows']. A repeat check that differs by 11 % on one row only, with low rep noise, has no explanation in the files: 'these files do not show why' [README of 010, line 170].

outlier.title: Boot F1 against run 3: L1-sized rows moved a few percent and counted latency commands ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longer
outlier.first_seen: run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, boot 2026-11-06 UTC) against run 3 (membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03 UTC); written up in Jesse's F1 README (sections 'Core rows against round three' and 'Mesh counts') and in asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3. The date of the write-up is not in the primary files.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Boot F1 ran run 3's 67 core command lines byte for byte. The rows that fit the 32 KiB L1 did not repeat run 3. The one-core 16 KiB read reads 56.085 GB/s on F1 against 58.127 on run 3 (0.965 times; reps 55.715 to 56.085 against 57.654 to 58.127). The pair's 16 KiB read reads 112.409 against 116.407 GB/s (0.966). The one-core 16 KiB write reads 30.608 against 30.127 GB/s (1.016), back at the 30.578 to 30.579 GB/s of runs 1 and 2. The one-core writes of 48 KiB to 32 MiB repeat within 0.3 % (1.000 to 1.003). The pair's writes at 48 and 160 KiB do not (1.049 and 1.233). Under the mesh counters (cmn-counts.csv, child_elapsed_ns, which spans the whole command) the F1 core latency commands ran longer: the four counted 4 KiB controls 1.310 to 1.423 times run 3's command time, the 20 single-region sparse OCM rows 1.236 to 1.598 times, the four sparse all-five rows 1.167 to 1.208, the dense all-five rows 1.028 to 1.044, the three 2 MiB SLC chains 1.010 to 1.024. The uncounted 4 KiB control ran 1,269,307 ns against 883,269 ns (1.437 times). The counted core bandwidth commands ran 0.648 to 1.027 times run 3's time (the counted 2 MiB read 1,391,056 ns against 2,147,182 ns, 0.648). The timed passes inside the latency commands did not grow: the four counted controls read 2.015 to 2.020 ns per load against 2.012 to 2.019, and the 20 sparse OCM rows read faster (best 17.266 to 22.609 ns per load against 20.141 to 28.453; 0.693 to 0.953 times, all 20 cells below 1).
outlier.why_wrong: A 16 KiB buffer fits the L1, so the L3 (the platform change that F1 was run for) should not touch it. The kernels k_read, k_write and k_copy are byte for byte the same in both builds. So an L1-sized row should repeat, and it did not. For the latency commands, the timed passes repeated or got faster while the whole command ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longer, so something outside the timed passes grew. What differed between the two boots (Jesse's F1 README, 'Core rows against round three'; page section 2.3): the SCP firmware (0.48.0-nopcie.1 on run 3, L3 full mode for cluster 0 only; 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 on F1, L3 full mode for clusters 1 to 4 too), the /dev/ocm module build (F1's adds debug map lines and the clusterpwrstat file; the same 4 KiB mapping), the binaries (commit ba834c0 against 0c190a1: pass and worker differ, with the --asm-passes, --perf and CME paths; chase is the same 34 instructions but its 48 B loop sits inside one 64 B line on F1 and across two on run 3; k_write sits 16 B later in its line), the counter columns on the latency rows (three more prefetch events, no multiplexing, perf_cov 1.0000), the init (F1 ran the box's wrapper, which ran cme_test for about 0.012 s before run_all.sh; both boots ran on CPU 2 under SCHED_FIFO 10 with RT throttling off, so the scheduling is the same), the emulator boards (ga13pd02 boards 6 to 9 against 18 to 21, the same image copy) and the date. The mesh counters give one time per whole command (chain build, flushes and unmap included), so they cannot say which part grew.

Why the 16 KiB reads fell 3.5 % is Insufficient data: the kernels are the same code and the files hold no counters for those rows (Jesse's F1 README: 'These files do not show why'). Which part of each latency command grew is Insufficient data: cmn-counts.csv gives only whole-command time, and the counter cost itself fell (579,353 ns against 658,812 ns). The counted 2 MiB read put 85,518 to 85,777 requests on each home node against run 3's 87,579 to 88,012 (0.975 times) while the command took 0.648 times as long, so the counts do not show the L3 taking that read off the mesh. outlier.title: PMU events that open but count zero: 0x2A on the C1-Nano, prefetch events on the CRB, 0x81C6 before boot E
outlier.first_seen: 2026-10-30 (Jesse: 0x2A opens and reads 0 on the C1-Nano, recorded in common.h and the run 1 README of 2026-10-31); CRB prefetch-event check 2026-11-04 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 8); CRB hit-set check 2026-11-04 (section 10); 0x81C6 zeros on boot B 2026-11-04 (membench-jibin-006)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Event 0x2A (L3D_CACHE_REFILL) opens on the C1-Nano without an error but always reads 0 [common.h perf_open comment; results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 26: '0x2A is not implemented here']. On the CRB (the Neoverse V3AE reference board) the three prefetch events 0x81BC, 0x81BD and 0x0111 read 0.0000 per load on a 4 MiB sequential flushed chain that ran at 2.7 ns per load, against 97.5 ns per load for the random flushed chain, with 0.056 L1D refills and 1.00 L2 refills per load. Some prefetcher clearly acted on that chain, yet the three events counted nothing [follow-up-run-plan.md section 8]. On the CRB the hit set (0x81C5, 0xA0, 0x81C6) also opened and read 0.0000 in all three columns on a 1 MiB repeated row with 1.00 L1 refills and 0 L2 refills per load [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10, 'Verification (2026-11-04)']. On Asimov, 0x81C6 (L3 read hits) read 0.0000 in all 21 rows of latency-dram-small-l3.csv on boot B (006), boot C (007) and boot D (008) [recomputed from the three CSVs]. This kernel opens any raw event number except CHAIN (0x1E), so a successful open proves nothing [results/membench-jibin-008/README.md line 14].
outlier.why_wrong: A zero count cannot be told from 'the event is not implemented' unless a row is built that must produce the activity. On boots B, C and D the L3 held no data (IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 read 0x0, every L2 miss went to the mesh), so a zero 0x81C6 was a true absence of hits and said nothing about the counter [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]. On the CRB the 1 MiB row fit that core's 2 MiB L2, so zero L3 accesses and zero L3 hits were expected there; only 0x81C5 reading 0 beside 1.00 L1 refills showed an event that opens and does not count on that core [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10]. Without a validation rule, a zero prefetch count on Asimov would have been read as 'no prefetching' [follow-up-run-plan.md section 6, line 136].

outlier.title: Harness measurement costs: chip-time estimate, mesh-counter helper cost, sparse-row counts and clock calibration
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (001): 1.237 s of chip time (README of 001, line 9). Run 2 (002): the counted control cost 622,374 ns more than the uncounted one (README of 002, Mesh counts). Before run 3: the CME plan's budget parts summed to 0.99 s, not 0.5 s (codex-review-CME-plan.md line 58). Run 3 (004): 4.1 s est. against 2.918 s measured (README of 004, lines 19 and 130).
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Five harness numbers did not fit. (1) The chip-time estimator gave 4.111 s est. for run 3 [CME-plan.md section 4.4, line 398 and line 642]. It used a launch cost of 14 ms est. per program start taken from run 1 [RUN2-PLAN.md line 360; est_chip_time.py line 32]. Jesse's run 2 README put each command at about 3 to 5 ms est. of chip time [README of 002, line 84]. Run 3 then took 2.918 s [README of 004, line 19]. Before that, the CME plan's first budget claimed 0.5 s est. while its own parts summed to 0.99 s est. [codex-review-CME-plan.md line 58]. (2) In run 2 the counted control row (a 4 KiB chase under the cmncount helper with the mesh counters on) read helper_elapsed_ns 1,163,263 ns. The uncounted control read 540,889 ns. The gap is 622,374 ns [cmn-counts.csv of 002, rows control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2]. (3) Run 3's sparse OCM rows (one line per 4 KiB page) put 0.40 to 0.49 times run 2's dense request counts on the region's home node under the same labels [README of 004, line 118; recomputed from cmn-counts.csv of 002 and 004: 0.400 to 0.493]. (4) The cycles column of a sparse per-region row read 2.07 to 2.26 cycles per ns instead of the clock's 2.00 [README of 004, line 113; recomputed from latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv of 004: 2.068 to 2.259 over 140 passes]. (5) Two review findings on the harness: the counter coverage check (perf_cov, the running time over the enabled time of a counter group) was cumulative, so one multiplexed row would invalidate every later row [CME-plan.md line 494, R4]; and the mesh map in sysinfo.txt listed HN-S #0 to #4 in an order that is not OCM0 to OCM4 [README of 002, Reading the numbers].
outlier.why_wrong: (1) The launch assumption was 2.32 s of the 4.11 s est., 56 % [CME-plan.md section 4.4]. The 14 ms per launch is run 1's whole-run time minus its measured work, spread over its commands, and nothing in a run measures it [CME-plan.md lines 403 and 495; RUN2-PLAN.md line 360]. Jesse's 3 to 5 ms est. comes from run 1's console timing less a model of each command's work, and the console polls at 10 ms [README of 002, line 84]. The 0.99 s sum was 0.10 + 0.25 + 0.05 + 0.03 + 40 x 0.014 s [codex-review-CME-plan.md line 58]. (2) The counted helper makes 38 more sysfs reads than the uncounted one to set its events up (40 against 2), so the 622,374 ns gap is not the counters alone [README of 002, line 74]. (3) The mesh counters cover each whole command: chain build, flushes and warm-up included. A sparse row times 448 loads (7 passes of 64 hops) but flushes 4,096 lines 7 times. If each line operation is one home-node request, the 7 full flushes make 61 to 73 % of a sparse row's excess and the 448 timed loads about 1 % [README of 004, line 118]. (4) Each pass counts 150 to 400 user cycles outside the clock bracket. A 64-hop pass spreads them over only 64 loads, so a sparse row cannot calibrate the clock as the long dense rows do [README of 004, line 113]. (5) PERF_EVENT_IOC_RESET clears the counts but keeps the enabled and running times, so a coverage ratio taken from the raw times was cumulative over the group's life [CME-plan.md line 494, R4]. The mesh map prints crosspoint numbers and each node's logical id within its type, not node ids: HN-S #0 to #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160 and 288, that is OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1 and OCM3 [README of 002, Reading the numbers].

outlier.title: CRB (reference board) lessons that shaped the Asimov method: learned random chains, first-touch cost, write collapse above 64 threads
outlier.first_seen: CRB main sweep 2026-10-30 (crb/results/20261030T193108Z), follow-ups 2026-10-31 to 2026-11-02 (followup2, followup3, root runs). Asimov run 1 ran on 2026-10-31 [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md, line 3], so the main sweep came before run 1 and the follow-ups ran beside Asimov runs 1 to 3.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Four CRB (Arm Phoenix reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores, two CMN meshes) results contradicted the hierarchy. (1) A repeated random chain read 5.4 to 6.8 ns per load at 8, 16 and 32 MiB (6.784, 5.626, 5.424 ns) while the counters showed every load missing the 2 MiB L2 [crb/results/20261030T193108Z/latency.csv, rows 8388608/16777216/33554432 'best']. A single pass over an unseen chain read 26.1 ns at 8 MiB and 30.7 ns at 56 MiB [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/latency-fresh.csv, 'best' rows]. (2) A chain built on one chiplet and walked from the other was first quoted as 2 to 7 ns extra (32 MiB second walk 32.7 to 37.3 ns against 30.2 ns same-chiplet), because the report took the best of two walks. The first walk at 16 MiB cost 85.0 to 88.5 ns per load, the second 31.7 to 33.2 ns, same-chiplet 29.0 to 29.1 ns [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv, fresh1/fresh2 rows]. (3) DRAM write bandwidth fell with more threads: 64 threads 394 GB/s, 96 threads 149 GB/s, 120 threads 141 GB/s [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/asm.csv rows 259, 274, 289]. The placement grid then showed 64 writers on one mesh 394.15 GB/s, 32+32 across the meshes 172.81 GB/s, 16+16 346.49 GB/s; reads with 32+32 still gave 327.91 GB/s [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv and readgrid.csv, 'best' rows]. One writer at 8 MiB was limited to 73.15 GB/s [asm.csv row 102]. (4) The cache that sysfs calls L3 (the 128 MiB SLC, system level cache) missed on 0.81 of loads at 96 MiB and on 0.11 at 64 MiB, far below 128 MiB [crb/results/uncore-20261030T203537Z/cmn-96M-long.csv minus cmn-96M-short.csv, divided by the load difference from chase-long.csv and chase-short.csv].
outlier.why_wrong: (1) A load that misses L2 cannot complete in 5 to 7 ns on this board: the fresh chain shows 26 to 31 ns at the same sizes. The V3AE temporal prefetcher learns any repeated miss sequence and refills L2 just in time [bench/homelat.c:646-648: 'with one fixed order the timed passes fell from 30 ns to 7 ns from the second repeat on']. (2) Best-of-N hides a first-touch cost: the two walks differ by 53 to 56 ns at 16 MiB. (3) More writers should not lower the total. The CRB page reads the fall as a placement effect: the collapse starts once both meshes have about 32 writers or more [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html, 'Writers on both meshes collapse DRAM write bandwidth']. (4) The 64 MiB knee is the per-mesh capacity: each mesh has 64 HN-S home nodes [crb/results/cmn-map.txt, 64 numbered HN-S nodes per map], 1 MiB each (est.), and a buffer is interleaved line by line 50/50 over both meshes [crb-hierarchy-findings.md, root run 2026-11-02].

outlier.what_tests_showed: Fresh chains give 26.1 to 30.7 ns on the CRB from 8 to 56 MiB [latency-fresh.csv]. The cross-chiplet first walk costs 85.0 to 88.5 ns at 16 MiB, about 56 to 59 ns more than a local hit; the CRB page corrected its earlier 2 to 7 ns claim [crb-memory-hierarchy.html, 'A first read of lines cached on the other chiplet costs 85 ns, later reads 32 ns']. The write collapse is a placement effect across the two meshes: 394.15 GB/s with 64 writers on one mesh against 172.81 GB/s with 32 on each [writegrid.csv]; the root run saw no retries or throttling at the home nodes, so the bottleneck is elsewhere [crb-hierarchy-findings.md]. The single-writer limit sits inside the core: part 5 counted zero L1/L2 refills-for-write and write-backs and no crosspoint credit stalls while one writer moved 69.2 to 71.3 GB/s at 8 MiB (62.9 GB/s at 1 GiB), a same-port partner 80.6 to 82.1 GB/s total, two ports 118.9 to 122.1 GB/s, four ports 224.0 to 229.8 GB/s [writepath.csv, 'best' rows per block]. Core-to-slice latency ran 19 to 44 ns by distance [crb-memory-hierarchy.html, from sudo-20261102T054936Z/full/latency.csv]. On Asimov, boot A's fresh random chains from 1.5 MiB to 32 MiB counted 0.000 L2 refills by a hardware prefetcher (event 0x81BD) per load, 0.004 to 0.029 at 512 KiB to 1 MiB, and 0.124 to 0.212 on the repeat rows at 192 to 384 KiB [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, table 3.2]; with the prefetchers off (boot B) the 24 random rows moved only -5.6 % to +5.3 % [same page, section 11.2]. So the C1-Nano does not learn a random chain, unlike the V3AE. The CME does prefetch on a repeated chain: 3.12 to 17.47 prefetch refills per load from 8 to 48 KiB [asimov-cme-run4.html, CME L1 refills chart]. The sparse chain on the CRB ran 145 to 158 ns per hop with 3.8 to 7.3 L2 refills per hop, against 28.9 ns and 1.00 refills for the dense chain, that is 2.8 to 6.3 extra refills per hop [CME-plan.md section 11, lines 596-599]; the plan carried it as a warning about the method, not an Asimov measurement. The raw CSV of that CRB sparse run is not in the cache-perf tree (not in this source).

outlier.title: asimov-bench: CME matrix issue rate read 69 % of the ceiling by counters while the timer said 98 %; st1h at 3 cycles
outlier.first_seen: Three measurements by other teams, all relayed through cme-survey.html (written 2026-11-02, section 9 added 2026-11-02 evening): (a) the timer rows of asimov-bench boots M2 and M3 on 2026-10-12 (engines/cme.py), (b) the counter rows of asimov-bench dpa/stress on Palladium, 2026-10-14 and 15 (Spokane requests 1504 and 1511, FORMAT.md section 6.4), (c) Jacob Geldbach's team on GA13, October 2026, run 4007 (RTL a10181848). Not from any membench-jibin results folder.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Three results did not fit the half-matmul rate of one FMOPA per 2 cycles (ceiling 0.5 issues per CME cycle). (1) The CME counters gave CME_OP_MMDP_ISSUE / CME_CYCLES = 0.3455 on all five workers, which is 69 % of the 0.5 ceiling, while the timer rows gave 1.019 ns per FMOPA = 2.04 cycles, 98 % of the ceiling [cme-survey.html sections 4.2 and 4.3]. (2) Two cores of DSU0 issuing 2 x 4,096 FMOPA together took 8,909 ns, 1.088 ns per FMOPA, against 1.019 ns for one core (4,173 ns for 4,096 FMOPA): the pair got no more total work done than one core, and each instruction was 6.7 % slower [cme-survey.html section 4.2, boot M2]. (3) Back-to-back st1h x2 cost 3.0 cycles per instruction where the RTL reading says 1 [cme-survey.html section 9, Jacob's run 4007].
outlier.why_wrong: Two independent methods on the same unit disagreed by 29 percentage points (98 % by the timer, 69 % by the counters). Arm's own half-matmul test comment says one FMOPA per 2 cycles, and the llvm-mca C1-Nano model gives FMOPA 2.00 cycles per instruction [cme-survey.html sections 2 and 4.1]. For the stores, the llvm-mca C1-Nano model lists ST1B of 2 vectors at 1.00 cycle per instruction and of 4 vectors at 2.00, with 2 cycles of latency; st1h is not in that table [cme-survey.html section 4.1; refs/C1Nano-streaming-cme-instructions.s cited on asimov-cme-perf.html, CME pipeline widths row]. A 3.0-cycle store is three times the model's rate.

outlier.what_tests_showed: Re-balanced loop: 0.4916 to 0.4922 issues per CME cycle, 98 % of the 0.5 ceiling, and CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES = 0.9993 (the CME stayed allocated to the core) [cme-survey.html section 4.3, request 1511]. The bench authors attribute the original 69 % to the in-order front end: about 44 instructions per 8 FMOPA at an IPC of 1.9 [cme-survey.html section 4.3, citing kernels.h cme_fmopa_fit comment]. So the timer and the counters agree once the stream fits the front end. The two-core result (1.088 ns per FMOPA) is explained by the one CME per DSU being time-shared [cme-survey.html section 2]. The st1h 3.0-cycle anomaly stays open: no membench-jibin row uses st1h. The cme-write rows use ST1B of four vectors and gave: run 3 (004, the L3 off) 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s from 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB, which is 32 bytes per cycle or 0.5 of a 64 B store per cycle at 2.003 GHz (derived) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, best of 3 reps; asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1 table]; run 6 boot F1 (011, the L3 on) 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB (26 bytes per cycle) and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB (20 to 21 bytes per cycle); boot F2 (012) 51.5 to 52.5 and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at the same sizes [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012]. The single-call L1 write rows on F1 read 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB, 0.42 of a store per cycle [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011; asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1]. The 0.5 store per cycle of run 3 matches the llvm-mca rate for ST1B of four vectors (2.00 cycles). Why the stores stop at that rate is Insufficient data: no source on disk gives the CME store path width [asimov-cme-perf.html, CME pipeline widths row]. Why the writes fall with the L3 on is a separate open item (hypothesis on the page: the stores allocate in the L3 and drain at its rate) [asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

outlier.title: 3 MiB fresh chain already above the SLC plateau; the 4 MiB row moves between runs; the 8 MiB fresh chain reads 7.6 to 7.7 ns below the flushed one
outlier.first_seen: run 1 (membench-jibin-001, ran 2026-10-31 per its README; report verification dated 2026-11-02 in the session transcript, not verifiable from the primary files). The 8 MiB fresh-vs-flushed question: 2026-11-03 (peer session transcript; run 3 = membench-jibin-004 ran 2026-11-03 per its README). The 4 MiB prefetcher-off move: boot B (006) README, 'Against boot A'.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Fresh chains of 512 KiB to 2 MiB read a flat 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load on run 1 [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :22]. The 3 MiB chain read 25.449 ns, 1.47 ns above the 2 MiB row [:26 vs :22]. The two 2 MiB passes differ by only 0.14 ns (23.980 and 24.119), so the 3 MiB step is about ten times the repeat spread. At 4 MiB the chain read 29.760 ns [:30]. That is 20 % of the way from the 2 MiB SLC row (23.980 ns) to the 32 MiB DRAM row (52.300 ns [:46]), although 4 MiB exceeds the 3.75 MiB SLC. The 4 MiB row is the one latency row that moved between runs 1 and 2 beyond 1.7 % and between run 1 and the control beyond 1.44 % [002 README line 92; 003 README line 51]. Its bests: 29.760 (run 1), 28.704 (run 2), 28.399 (control 003), 28.270 (run 3), 29.838 (boot A), 28.161 (boot B, prefetchers off), 29.216 (boot C), 28.234 (boot D), 28.321 (boot E), 29.379 (F1) ns per load. Boot B's 4 MiB row is 5.6 % faster than boot A's with no prefetch refill on either boot [006 README line 47]. The core's 8 MiB fresh chain reads 45.077 ns per load on run 3 [004 latency-dram-large.csv:39]. The 8 MiB flushed row on the same run reads 52.738 ns [004 latency-dram-flushed.csv:7] and the 32 MiB fresh row 52.185 ns [004 latency-dram-large.csv:47]. The fresh 8 MiB walk is 7.66 ns faster than the flushed one (7.63 ns on run 1: 45.086 vs 52.711). The 6 MiB chain reads 39.753 ns or more on every pass of every boot with the L3 off (16 passes over 001 to 008). CPU 6's 2 MiB SLC chase moved +2.56 % between runs 2 and 3 (24.050 to 24.665 ns; the control run's second pass also read 24.653) while 33 of the 36 repeated latency rows agreed within 0.73 % [004 README line 96].
outlier.why_wrong: An ideal 3.75 MiB cache with the run 1 end points (23.980 ns in the SLC, 52.300 ns in DRAM) predicts 24.0 ns at 3 MiB (the chain fits) and 25.8 ns at 4 MiB (3.75/4 of the loads hit). The measured 25.449 and 29.760 ns are both higher. The transition is spread over 2 to 16 MiB. Under an ideal-LRU model (capacity = size x (1 - (lat - 23.980) / (52.300 - 23.980))), the 3, 4, 6, 8 and 16 MiB points imply 2.84, 3.18, 2.64, 2.04 and 0.88 MiB est. of effective SLC, not one size. 4 MiB sits just over the SLC size, so small changes in how much the SLC holds move its latency [003 README line 51, Jesse's reading]. 8 MiB is more than twice the SLC, so a fresh walk was expected to read DRAM latency like the flushed walk. The 7.7 ns gap means the fresh walk still gets some SLC service that the flush removes (hypothesis: the core counters read 1.00 L3 read refills per load on both rows and cannot show SLC hits). A 5.6 % move at 4 MiB with 0.0000 prefetch refills per load on both boots has no prefetcher cause in the files [006 README line 7 and line 47].

outlier.title: 100 % L1 misses on a 192 KiB chain with a 32 KiB L1 (Jibin's question), and the 32 KiB row as the L1 edge
outlier.first_seen: The 32 KiB repeated row read 2.112 ns in run 1 (001) and 2.108 ns in run 3 (004). Jibin asked the 100 % L1 miss question as page comment 23 on 2026-11-03 11:11 (jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md lines 135-137) and asked for the repeat/fresh/flushed definitions as comment 24 at 12:04 (lines 139-141). The 32 KiB row's move between boots A and B appeared in Jesse's boot B README on 2026-11-05 (results/membench-jibin-006/README.md line 47).
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The run 3 core page listed 1.00 L1 refills per load on the 192 KiB repeated chase (the CSV reads 0.9987 to 0.9989 refills per load, membench-jibin-004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 50-52; the page rounds to 1.00). An L1 refill is a load that missed the L1, so 1.00 means 100 % misses. Jibin asked how a 32 KB L1 can miss on every load and whether the step size is larger than 32 KB (comment 23). The 32 KiB repeated row reads 2.108 ns with 0.0377 to 0.0433 L1 refills per load (membench-jibin-004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28), above the 2.002 to 2.007 ns of the 4 to 16 KiB rows and the 2.013 ns of the 24 KiB row (rows 8, 13, 18, 23), even though 32 KiB is the L1 size. In run 4, with the data prefetchers off, the 32 KiB row read 3.93 % faster (boot A 2.114 ns, boot B 2.031 ns; membench-jibin-005 and -006 latency-dram-small.csv row 28), with L1 refills 0.0398 to 0.0426 per load on A (0.0078 to 0.0087 of them made by the L1 prefetcher, column l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load) and 0.0094 to 0.0112 on B (prefetch refills 0.0000).
outlier.why_wrong: A 32 KiB cache was expected to hold part of any chain, so some loads should hit. The page did not say how the chain is ordered or what the refill counter counts. Answer given by the peer session (transcript-peer.txt lines 1045-1054) and confirmed by the test source: the chain is one random cycle over all lines (latency.c lines 5-6, Sattolo's algorithm yields a single n-cycle). At 192 KiB the chain has 3,072 lines and the L1 holds 512 lines (the CSV headers '# size=196608 lines=3072' and '# size=32768 lines=512'). Each line is revisited only after 3,071 other loads, so every load misses the L1 whatever the step size. The 32 KiB row equals the L1 size: 512 chain lines in a 512-line cache. The peer's reading, a hypothesis and not a measurement: the kernel's own lines and the chain compete for the L1, so 0.04 refills per load is the L1 edge. Why boot B's 32 KiB row is 3.93 % faster than boot A's is not explained in the files. The L1 refill drop from A to B (about 0.030 per load) is larger than the L1 prefetcher's own refills on A (0.008 to 0.009 per load), so the demand misses also dropped when the prefetcher went off; no file explains this. Hypothesis, not measured: prefetched lines evict chain lines at the L1 edge.
