outlier.title: Which crosspoint holds CPU 6's and CPU 8's mesh ports: the per-region OCM pattern alone could not tell them apart
outlier.first_seen: run 2 (membench-jibin-002), README dated 2026-11-02
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Run 2 measured each CPU's load latency from each of the five OCM regions (best of two fresh-chain passes). Sorted by mesh distance, the per-region rows average 19.64 ns per load at 1 crosspoint (8 rows, 18.46 to 21.36), 21.82 ns at 3 (10 rows, 20.49 to 23.44) and 24.58 ns at 5 (2 rows, 24.48 to 24.68) [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:64, recomputed from results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]. That is about 1.1 to 1.4 ns per extra crosspoint. Each CPU's fastest region is one at 1 crosspoint. This places CPU 4's port at (3,2). It does not place CPUs 6 and 8: with the two ports swapped, (5,2) for CPU 6 and (4,3) for CPU 8, each CPU's fastest region is still OCM4 (recomputed here from the same CSVs: under the swap CPU 6's distances would be 5,5,3,3,1 and CPU 8's 3,3,1,1,1, and OCM4 stays the fastest region for both).
outlier.why_wrong: The platform facts put the mesh ports of the clusters of CPUs 6-7 and 8-9 (node ids 280 and 336) at crosspoints (4,3) and (5,2), and the OCM0-4 home nodes (node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344) at (1,3), (2,4), (3,3), (4,4), (5,3) [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:31]. The source of those coordinates is Jesse's reading of the RTL mesh file cmns3_12_1.yml lines 648 to 720: DSU ports at crosspoints 12, 23, 32, 43, 52 and home nodes at 13, 24, 33, 44, 53, written as two-digit (x,y) [HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:19]. Only CPU 2's placement had been checked by measurement (round one's qualification boot). The two candidate assignments for CPUs 6 and 8 give the same fastest region for each CPU. So the fastest-region rule by itself does not say which cluster sits where. Every later distance fit (step counts per cell) depends on this assignment. The per-region rows are also rough: their two passes differ by up to 3.4 ns, and they count 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load, so some lines reach the cluster before their load [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:67]. That spread is the same size as the CPU 8 minus CPU 6 gap used to tell the ports apart.

The all-five rows order the CPUs by their mean distance to the five home nodes: CPU 6 and CPU 2 (mean 1.8 crosspoints) read 25.37 and 25.51 ns, CPU 4 (2.6) 26.11 ns, CPU 8 (3.4) 27.70 ns, 2.19 ns behind CPU 2 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:65; latency-ocm-all5-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]. Under the swapped assignment CPU 8 would be the nearer CPU, so the data put CPUs 6-7 at (4,3) and CPUs 8-9 at (5,2). Run 3 repeats the order by distance: 21.58 ns at 1 crosspoint, 24.25 at 3, 27.73 at 5 (sparse chains), and within each CPU every nearer region's best is below every farther one's [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md:109]. In run 3 CPU 8 minus CPU 6 is +0.48, +4.56, +2.97, +4.03 ns from OCM0 to OCM3 and -1.84 ns from OCM4 (recomputed from results/membench-jibin-004/results/*/latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv). Run 4 boot B (prefetchers off) fits the 20 route cells as 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step with 0.09 ns rms, using these coordinates; boot D repeats it (20.63 + 2.00 per X + 0.98 per Y, 0.13 ns rms); with prefetchers on the residual is 0.90 ns on boot A and 0.80 ns on boot C, and on boot E the fit is not usable (2.05 ns rms) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 4 text 'With the prefetchers off (boot B) the 20 route cells fit...'; all five refits recomputed from latency-ocm-region*-route-cpu*.csv]. Recomputed here: with CPU 6 and CPU 8 swapped, the same boot B and boot D rows fit at 1.61 and 1.62 ns rms with a negative Y slope (-0.18 ns per Y step), so the measured assignment is the only one the step model fits. The G6 counters show the direction with the most outgoing data flits is the X-first direction toward the other end in 20 of 20 cells at the DSU's crosspoint and 20 of 20 at the home node's, on boots A, B, C, D and E; the dominant direction carries at least 75 % of the four directions' flits on boots A to D and at least 61 % on E [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6 text; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section on route counters; recomputed from each boot's cmn-counts.csv]. Recomputed here: under the swapped coordinates only 16 of 20 cells at each end match X-first on boots A and B, so the data-flit directions also reject the swap. These events count the data channel only. They do not identify the read-request route or the response's last link, so the X and Y step counts per cell stay coordinate assumptions.

outlier.title: The kernel's mesh map prints logical ids, not node ids: HN-S #0 to #4 are OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1, OCM3
outlier.first_seen: run 2 (membench-jibin-002) sysinfo.txt, run date 2026-11-02 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:3,78]. Before run 2 the node ids were an open item: RUN2-PLAN.md section 6 (lines 337 to 341) says 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 come from the address map and no perf_event_open with bynodeid had been tried on the image; HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:33 asks the same question.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: The mesh map in sysinfo.txt prints crosspoint numbers (XP #0 to #35) and each node's logical id within its type, not node ids [results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/sysinfo.txt:489-560]. The five HN-S cells read #0 at crosspoint (1,3), #1 at (3,3), #2 at (5,3), #3 at (2,4), #4 at (4,4). The node ids decode to crosspoints as X = bits 8:6 and Y = bits 5:3 [gen_hierarchy.py:51]: 88 is (1,3), 160 is (2,4), 216 is (3,3), 288 is (4,4), 344 is (5,3). So HN-S #0 to #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160 and 288, that is OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1 and OCM3 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:80]. A reader who matches HN-S #n to OCMn places three of the five home nodes wrongly. Jesse's README also states that the kernel's arm-cmn driver places the HN-S filter fields one bit off this RTL's [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:82]; that statement is Jesse's and is not re-checked here. Before run 2, which home node held each OCM region was unverified on the emulator: the node ids came from the address map, and no perf_event_open with bynodeid had been tried [RUN2-PLAN.md:337-341].
outlier.why_wrong: Every per-region latency claim and every mesh-distance claim depends on which home node owns each region (run 2 README, Mesh placement, line 31). A map that looks like a node-id list but is a logical-id list is a trap for any reader. The filter-field offset, if it reached the events used, could have mis-attributed per-node counts. A wrong node id would not count the wrong node silently: the driver rejects it, and the line reads unavailable (Invalid argument) [RUN2-PLAN.md:339-341; results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:81].

outlier.first_seen: run 1 (001): OCM1 read 16.623 GB/s against 9.306 GB/s from a 2 MiB SLC-resident buffer [bandwidth-ocm-region1.csv and bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 001, best rows]; the OCM streaming write of 20.3 to 20.4 GB/s against 32.0 GB/s first in the run 2 README [membench-jibin-002 README line 86]; the CME reversal in the run 3 README (004) line 84, 2026-11-03; raised by Jibin on the run 3 page 2026-11-04 02:01 and 02:12 (peer transcript; not in the primary files)
outlier.what_looked_wrong:
Each home node (HN-S) holds one 1 MiB array in 16 ways. The firmware locks 4 ways of each node as its 256 KiB OCM region, so 3.75 MiB of SLC is left over five nodes [004 README line 34]. That is 768 KiB (12 ways) of SLC per node (derived from the 3.75 MiB; the README does not state 12 ways). On run 3 (004, the L3 off), from CPU 2:
- Read stream from one OCM region: 16.219, 16.619, 16.320, 15.323 and 14.817 GB/s for OCM0 to OCM4 (16.0 over all five) [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 004, best rows]. The two regions three crosspoints away (OCM3, OCM4) read lowest.
- Read stream from a DRAM-address buffer that the SLC holds: 9.311 GB/s at 2 MiB and 10.164 GB/s at 256 KiB [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, best rows].
- The OCM read over the DRAM-address read: 1.57 to 1.72 (the all-five 15.974 over 10.164 and over 9.311; per region the range is 1.46 to 1.79; derived) [004 README line 84 quotes 1.57 to 1.72].
- Write stream to all five OCM regions: 20.326 GB/s; write to DRAM addresses: 31.982 GB/s at 2 MiB and 31.996 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. So the OCM write is 0.64 times the DRAM-address write.
- Chase (one dependent load after another) of one OCM region, run 2 dense rows from CPU 2: 19.770, 18.456, 21.355, 21.535 and 22.001 ns per load (mean 20.62) [latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv of 002, best rows]. Chase of a 2 MiB chain over the same five nodes (SLC-resident): 24.382 ns on run 2 and 24.096 ns on run 3 [latency-dram-large.csv of 002 line 22 and of 004 line 23]. The gap is 3.8 ns within run 2, 3.5 ns against run 3's SLC row.
- Through the CME (the cluster's streaming unit): OCM read 23.178 to 23.352 GB/s per region (23.160 over all five) against the CME's warm DRAM-buffer read of 36.564 to 37.218 GB/s (32 MiB to 256 KiB) [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. That is 0.62 to 0.64 (the all-five over the 256 KiB row: 0.622), the reverse of the core's 1.57 to 1.72 [004 README line 84].
- The CME's five region bests lie within 0.75 % of each other (no distance step); its OCM read reps spread 1.5 % (all five) to 7.9 % (OCM3) against the core's 0.2 % (all five) to 1.3 % (OCM1) (recomputed from the rep rows of the same files).
outlier.why_wrong:
An SLC hit and an OCM read use the same array and the same mesh trip, so they should cost about the same at the node and stream at about the same rate. Instead the OCM read stream is 1.6 to 1.7 times faster than the SLC-served stream, the OCM write is 0.64 times the DRAM-address write, and the two chases differ by 3.5 to 3.8 ns in the OCM's favour.

Things that differ besides the memory:
- Method. The OCM rows are one pass after a flush, over 4 KiB pages. The DRAM-address rows are 4 to 32 warm passes over 2 MiB huge pages [CSV headers of 004: passes=1 flush_before=1 for OCM, passes=4 to 32 flush_before=0 for DRAM; 004 README line 129].
- The node's service path: locked ways against a hashed SLC lookup (hypothesis; no counter separates them).
- The chase comparison is not clean. The per-region OCM rows count 0.77 to 0.94 L3 read refills per load, so some lines arrive before their load and the row understates a single read [002 README line 66]. The all-five OCM chase (1.25 MiB, 1.00 refills per load) reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns ABOVE the 2 MiB SLC chase on every CPU [002 README line 65]. On run 3 the sparse per-region bests from CPU 2 read 21.359 to 25.781 ns, around the SLC row's 24.096 [004 README line 104].

Three hypotheses were recorded (peer transcript; not in the primary files): part of the 2 MiB chain misses the SLC (one miss in ten at 52 ns adds about 3 ns est.); a longer SLC hit path at the node; the /dev/ocm mapping attributes cap the OCM stores. Jesse's reading: the OCM and DRAM rows differ in page size and in flushed-one-pass against warm passes, so the data do not say which of them costs the CME [004 README line 84].

outlier.what_tests_showed:
- Run 3: the CME writes OCM at 19.795 GB/s, like the core's 20.326, while it writes DRAM addresses at 61.971 to 63.865 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. So the OCM write cap is not the core's store path alone.
- Run 6 boot F1 (011, the L3 on): the core's OCM read rose to 20.143, 20.042, 19.883, 20.086 and 20.128 GB/s (all five within 1.3 %; the distance dependence vanished) and the all-five read to 19.822 [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 011]. The SLC-served 256 KiB read rose to 26.297 GB/s, the 2 MiB read to 25.044 and the 32 MiB read to 24.575 [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011], overtaking the OCM read. So the run 3 ratio of 1.6 to 1.7 belongs partly to the read-stream item (read-stream-rise-l3-on): the OCM reads rose 1.21 to 1.36 times, the DRAM-address reads 2.6 to 2.7 times [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 10].
- F1: the core's OCM write stayed at 20.326 GB/s [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011]. The CME's OCM write rose to 30.659 GB/s (1.55 times run 3) [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011], while the CME's DRAM-address writes fell to 40.445 to 52.530 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011].
- F1: the CME's OCM read rose to 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s per region (34.356 over all five), 1.45 to 1.71 times run 3 [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, -all5.csv of 011; asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]. Against the CME's same-size warm 256 KiB DRAM row (41.562) every region still reads lower (0.81 to 0.96); against its 32 MiB row (36.583) only OCM0 (33.6) and the all-five (34.4) read lower [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]. The CME's OCM reps spread up to 19.5 % on F1 [011 README line 206].
- Still Insufficient data: why one core writes OCM at 20.3 GB/s instead of 32.0 on every run (run 2 20.433, run 3 20.326, F1 20.326); why the per-region OCM chase reads 3.5 to 3.8 ns below the SLC chase while the all-five OCM chase reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns above it; and why the CME's OCM read sits below its same-size DRAM read. The page-size and flush-against-warm differences were never separated: the two proposed method-swap rows did not run.

outlier.first_seen: run 3 (004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC), codex review R10a dated 2026-11-03; boot A (005, ran 2026-11-04 UTC); read against boot E (010, ran 2026-11-05 UTC)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Run 3: 19 of the 104 timed CME load rows count zero inner refills (event 0x327D, 'refills from inside the cluster'), while the outer event (0x327E) is above zero in all 104. All 19 zero rows are sparse OCM passes: 6 in cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv (lines 14 to 19, the 1.25 MiB chain), 3 each in cme-latency-ocm-region0.csv (lines 14, 16, 19: passes 2, 4, 7), region1 (lines 16, 17, 19), region2 (lines 14, 16, 18) and 4 in region3 (lines 14, 15, 16, 19) of 004. The run 3 CME page had said both refill events are nonzero wherever the CME loads memory [codex-review-run3.md, section 2 counter validity row]. The same run 3 per-region sparse OCM passes count 1.0000 to 1.0312 outer refills per load (the all5 passes 1.0375 to 1.1031). Boot A: the repeated chase counts 2.413 inner and 12.964 outer refills per load in the best rep at 32 KiB (15.4 in all), 2.811 inner at 48 KiB and 2.079 at 64 KiB [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, lines 34, 38, 43]. As a mean over the three reps the inner share on boot A is 15.8 / 15.2 / 15.8 / 14.8 % at 8 / 16 / 32 / 48 KiB, and on boot C 15.1 / 16.8 / 15.8 / 15.7 / 15.6 % at 8 / 16 / 24 / 32 / 48 KiB [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 007]. On runs 1 to 3 and boots A to D the DSU L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 was in snoop-filter-only mode: boot B's core hit counters read l3d_hit_rd_per_load 0.0000 in all 21 rows of latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 006 [Jesse's boot B README, 'What his rows show']. CPU 3, the cluster's other core, was offline for the whole script on run 3 and on every boot [Jesse's run 3 README line 45; boot A README line 17].
outlier.why_wrong: With the L3 holding no data and the partner core offline, nothing inside the cluster should supply a line. So inner refills were expected near zero on every row. The zero-inner rows on sparse OCM passes fit service from outside the cluster and only needed the page wording fixed. The 2 to 3 inner refills per load on boot A (about 15 % of all refills at 8 to 48 KiB) had no named source in the files. The run 4 CME page section 4 labels the 2.4 inner refills per load at 32 KiB as '(the DSU's L3)', and its section 9.1 says boot A's inner refills 'were read as the other core's caches or nothing (section 4)'. The two sections do not agree.

At 8 KiB boot E counts 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer refills per load, boot C 0.59 and 3.33 [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007; asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]. The page reads boot E's inner refills as L3 hits. On F2 hit plus miss equals inner plus outer in every row, and refill equals outer, by construction (the RTL reading: 0x3290 is the same signal as 0x327E) [Jesse's F2 README, 'The CME L3 events']. 'Miss minus refill' in the best rep is 0.845 per load at 96 KiB and 0.321 at 384 KiB (the hit count 0.141 and 0.637) [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012, lines 50 and 68; asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7]. By the pre-queue check's reading of the RTL these are lines a core's cache supplied: CPU 2 wrote the chain with core stores, so a small chain is still in CPU 2's L2 when the CME walks it. By that reading boot A's inner refills were snoops from CPU 2's caches. The run 4 CME page leaves boot A's source unresolved ('the other core's caches or nothing', section 9.1). No row isolates the snoop cost from the L3 hit. The least-squares split over F2's 15 reps from 96 to 384 KiB, ns per load = a + hits x h + snoops x s + outer x o, recomputed: a 23.4, h 6.7, s 13.9, o 20.4 ns est., rms 0.019 ns; the three count columns sum to about one per row, so the split is collinear and a hypothesis [asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7 caption]. A chain the core never wrote (a hit-only control) is in no run [asimov-cme-perf.html, 'Insufficient data: the L3-event split'].

outlier.title: CME OCM reads put 1.42 to 1.52 times the core's requests on the home node (run 3); with the L3 on, the dense OCM chains through the CME read 7 to 15 % faster, and the CME OCM reads' home-node requests fall to about half
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Run 3 (004): around the CME's OCM read commands the region's home node received 108,075 to 109,528 requests. Around the core's same commands it received 71,687 to 76,534. That is 1.42 to 1.52 times. The dense all-five chase through the CME put 1.33 times the core's requests on the five home nodes together (940,974 against 709,388). The sparse chains through the CME put 0.86 to 1.07 times the core's requests on the home node. Boot E (010, the L3 on) against boot A (005): the dense OCM chains through the CME read 0.85 to 0.93 times boot A (OCM0 35.92 vs 38.67 ns, OCM1 35.25 vs 38.32, OCM2 34.44 vs 38.87, OCM3 35.06 vs 41.22, OCM4 36.97 vs 42.17 ns per load). The all-five dense chain read 43.28 ns on E against 44.77 on A and 44.28 on C. E's dense rows count 1.01 to 1.32 outer refills per load (mean of the two fresh passes) against C's 2.13 to 2.66; the all-five dense row 2.07 on E against 2.46 on A and 2.05 on C. F1 (011): the CME OCM reads reached 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s per region (run 3: 23.178 to 23.352), 1.45 to 1.71 times. Their home-node requests were 50,227 to 50,893 for regions 1 to 4 against 108,075 to 109,528 on run 3 (0.46 to 0.47 times), but 84,080 for region 0 against 108,176 (0.78 times). The all-five read put 0.76 times run 3's requests on the five nodes. The write put 1.05 times while its rate rose from 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s. F1's region reps spread up to 19.5 %. F2 (012, prefetchers off): the reads fell to 0.723 to 0.906 times F1 (27.708 to 33.934 GB/s). Own-node requests were 0.882, 1.521, 1.149, 0.889 and 0.894 times F1 for regions 0 to 4 (74,192; 76,768; 58,464; 44,978; 44,909) and 0.650 to 0.733 times on each other node. Each region read lived 1.046 to 1.085 times as long.
outlier.why_wrong: The same bytes read from the same region should produce about the same number of requests at the owning home node, whichever unit issues them. OCM lives in 4 locked ways of each SLC home node on the mesh. A cluster-local L3 was therefore not expected to change OCM rows through the CME, or to take OCM reads off the mesh. The sparse OCM chain rows through the CME count only 0.00 to 0.03 inner refills per load on run 3, so their lines come from outside the cluster. Region 0 behaves unlike regions 1 to 4 on F1. The write got faster on F1 while its request count rose. The mesh counts cover the whole command (buffer fill, chain build, flushes, controls, timed walks), not the timed loads alone, so they cannot isolate the CME's own traffic.

outlier.what_tests_showed: Hypothesis (Jesse's inference, run 3 README, Mesh counts): the extra run 3 requests are the CME's refills above one per load, its prefetches, seen at the home node. Boot E counts 0.36 to 0.45 prefetch refills per load on the sparse OCM chains through the CME (mean over 7 passes per region) and F1 0.41 to 0.47, which fits run 3's ratios. On E the dense rows' outer refills about halve (1.01 to 1.32 against C's 2.13 to 2.66) while inner refills rise to 0.87 to 1.52 per load (boots A and C: 0.00), so part of the prefetcher's fills come from the L3. The 3-crosspoint regions gain most (OCM3 -6.2 ns, OCM4 -5.2 ns against A). On F1 fewer requests reached the home node, so some level in the cluster served the rest, but which level the counts do not show (011 README, CME rows). With the prefetchers off (F2) the sparse OCM chains through the CME read 1.001 to 1.028 times boot B, so the L3 does not serve demand OCM loads through the CME. With the prefetchers off the OCM reads still ran at 0.723 to 0.906 times F1, above run 3's 23.2 to 23.4 GB/s, and their own-node counts moved both ways (0.88 to 1.52 times F1), so the counts do not say which level served F1's reads. The sessions grouped the OCM read rate's rise with the L3 on with the open read-stream item (read-stream-rise-l3-on). The 8 MiB flushed CME command spread its requests evenly over the five nodes (1,451,065 to 1,461,104 per node on run 3; 1,407,799 to 1,414,866 on F1; 904,587 to 905,781 on F2), as the address hash predicts.

outlier.title: CME wake-up cost per timed span, the OCM pass spread through the CME, and a lone CME call's 280 to 536 ns outside its span
outlier.first_seen: run 3 README (membench-jibin-004, run of 2026-11-03), CME power section, lines 13 and 87-91; run 6 span data (011 boot F1, run of 2026-11-06; 012 boot F2, run of 2026-11-07)
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Three views in Jesse's run 3 README bound a fixed CME cost per timed span at 0.1 to 0.3 us est. [membench-jibin-004/README.md lines 13 and 90]. On boot E the 7 CME passes of one OCM region spread 7.25 to 13.55 ns per load (region 2 to region 1), and the medians sit 3.6 to 12.7 ns above the bests [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 010, cme-fresh1..7 rows; asimov-cme-perf.html section 7 quotes 7.2 to 13.5]. One run 3 cme-call rep ran 82.641 ns per call against 43.609 and 43.625 in the other two reps: 2.5 us longer over 64 calls, with 5,033 extra core cycles (168.52 minus the mean of 90.02 and 89.73 cycles per call, times 64) and only 419 extra CME cycles (87.5938 minus 81.0469, times 64) [membench-jibin-004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv, rows 'ocm,0,cme-call,0..2']. By bracket minus span on F1, back-to-back cme-call calls spend 63.5 to 64.6 ns outside the span (36 reps) and looped bandwidth calls of 1 to 256 KiB 76.0 to 106.2 ns, but a call alone in its bracket spends 285.8 to 292.2 ns on the 42 sparse OCM passes (after a flush and a counter start) and 281.1 to 535.7 ns in the single-call rows: reads 281 to 301 ns and writes 355 to 428 ns after their first rep, and every first rep more (reads 348 to 408, writes 476 to 536) [membench-jibin-011/README.md lines 157-168; recomputed from cme-latency-*.csv, cme-bandwidth-*-asmpasses.csv and the looped cme-bandwidth-*.csv of 011]. About 39 ns of a one-call figure is the bracket's own two clock reads (bracket_overhead_ns=39.0, comment line 3 of every CME latency CSV of 011 and 012).
outlier.why_wrong: The SCP sets every cluster's CME power controller to dynamic mode as each core powers on [membench-jibin-011/README.md line 349]. By the RTL (read, not measured) the CME in dynamic mode switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us with both cores out of streaming mode, cleaning and invalidating its L1 on the way, and switching on invalidates the L1 again [membench-jibin-004/README.md line 89]. Every timed span follows an untimed gap outside streaming mode, so whether the CME was off at the start of a span is unknown [same line]. A 64-load OCM pass would carry up to about 5 ns est. per load of such a cost, a 320-load pass 0.3 to 1 ns est. [004 README lines 13 and 90]. With the clock reads and a back-to-back call taken out, the sparse passes' excess (0.18 to 0.19 us) fits run 3's 0.3 us bound, but the first single-call write reps' excess (0.33 to 0.42 us) does not [011 README line 168]. The files do not separate a wake-up from the rest of a call's entry and exit (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call and return) [011 README lines 155 and 168].

outlier.what_tests_showed: On F1 the best pass of each OCM region spends 286.0 to 289.0 ns outside its span (all 42 sparse passes: 285.8 to 292.2 ns); on F2 the best pass 280.0 to 286.0 ns (all passes 280.0 to 304.0 ns) [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv and -all5.csv of 011 and 012, (ns_per_load minus ns_per_load_span) times loads; 012 README line 141]. The pass-to-pass spread is inside the span: on F1 the 7 passes of a region spread 3.19 to 8.75 ns per load by ns_per_load_span (3.14 to 8.73 by the bracket), on F2 0.16 to 0.36 ns per load in span (0.16 to 0.66 by the bracket, the F2 bracket maximum including one 304 ns outside-span pass of region 4) [same files; asimov-cme-perf.html section 10 quotes the bracket spreads 3.1 to 8.7 and 0.2 to 0.7]. So the spread is the prefetcher's, and it vanishes with the prefetchers off. F2's outside-span times match F1's by row type: cme-call 63.53 to 64.64 vs 63.52 to 64.61 ns (36 reps each); looped 1 to 256 KiB calls 75.8 to 105.6 vs 76.0 to 106.2 ns; single-call reps 280.0 to 523.6 vs 281.1 to 535.7 ns (F2 reads 280.0 to 293.1 after the first rep and 339.9 to 397.4 on the first rep, writes 371.0 to 421.0 and 452.3 to 523.6) [012 README line 144; recomputed from the same CSVs of 012]. So the prefetchers are not the cause of the lone-call excess either. A wake-up inside a span's first loads is bounded, not measured; the first-rep excess of the single-call writes stays unassigned.

outlier.title: Software prefetch 4 and 8 lines ahead at 2 MiB reads slower with the hardware prefetchers on than off (C vs D), and all four hint rows read below the plain loop with the L3 on (E)
outlier.first_seen: run 4 boot C (membench-jibin-007) against boot D (008), Jesse's boot C README section "Against boot D" (lines 107 to 109), 2026-11-05; boot E (010) README line 114, 2026-11-05. The question itself was posed earlier, on the run 4 page after boot B: "Whether the hint adds to the hardware prefetcher's rate is boot C's question" [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4].
outlier.what_looked_wrong: G7 is the one-core read test (bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv): the plain read loop, the loop with a PRFM PLDL1KEEP software prefetch 4, 8 or 16 lines ahead, and a two-stream loop, at 2 MiB and 32 MiB on CPU 2, best of 3 reps. Boot C has the hardware prefetchers on. Boot D has them off. Over the 10 G7 rows C reads 0.795 to 3.869 times D [007 README line 107; recomputed from 007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv best rows]. The plain read of 32 MiB reads 9.196 GB/s on C against 2.377 GB/s on D (3.869 times). But the 2 MiB reads with a software prefetch 4 and 8 lines ahead read 9.651 and 9.862 GB/s on C against 12.145 and 10.890 GB/s on D (0.795 and 0.906 times). Those are the only two G7 rows slower on C [007 README line 109]. On C the hint adds little over the plain loop: 9.651 against 9.294 GB/s at 2 MiB (+3.8 %) and 9.339 against 9.196 GB/s at 32 MiB (+1.6 %). On E (L3 on, prefetchers on) every hint row reads below the plain loop: plain 24.945 / 24.546 GB/s at 2 / 32 MiB, PRFM 4 ahead 20.196 / 20.353 GB/s, PRFM 8 ahead 18.425 / 18.486 GB/s, PRFM 16 ahead 18.446 / 18.285 GB/s, two streams 17.982 / 18.911 GB/s [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv best rows; 010 README line 114: "on E the plain read is the fastest of the five kernels at both sizes"]. The counter l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line (L1 data refills caused by the hardware prefetcher, per 64 B line) reads 0.8524 to 0.9994 in all 30 reps on C, and at most 0.0001 on B and D [007 README line 21; 006, 007, 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv].
outlier.why_wrong: The hardware prefetchers were expected to help a sequential read, or at worst to add nothing. Here the software hint plus the hardware prefetcher reads 9 to 21 % slower than the hint alone at 2 MiB (pf8: 9.862 against 10.890 GB/s, 9.4 % lower; pf4: 9.651 against 12.145 GB/s, 20.5 % lower) [007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. On E the hint 4 lines ahead costs 19.0 % at 2 MiB (20.196 against 24.945 GB/s) and 17.1 % at 32 MiB (20.353 against 24.546 GB/s) [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. The run 4 page had expected the hint to raise the rate: on boot B (prefetchers off) PRFM 4 ahead more than doubled the plain loop (12.146 against 5.031 GB/s at 2 MiB), which supported H7, the hypothesis that the plain loop keeps too few lines in flight [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4 and the hypothesis list]. No counter in the files names the cause of the slowdown. The brief page states this for the plain loop: the refill counters per line are about the same on C and E (L1 0.99 and 0.99, L2 0.96 and 0.97, L1 prefetch 0.99 and 0.99 at 2 MiB), "so they do not show the mechanism" [asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html, item "One core reads 2.7 times more from DRAM with the L3 on"]. C's G7 rows also compare two bandwidth builds: C's bandwidth is rebuilt from b79dffa's bandwidth.c, while B and D ran 7921962's and ed6056a's builds. The read kernels are the same bytes at the same offsets in their 64 B lines; the per-pass loop differs, which Jesse calls negligible for G7's rows (passes of 0.2 to 3.6 ms) [007 README lines 91 and 140].

outlier.what_tests_showed: B and D (prefetchers off) agree on all 10 G7 rows within 0.5 %: D reads 0.995 to 1.001 times B [008 README line 56; recomputed]. So the OCM translation hint (the only other change between B and D) does not touch these DRAM rows. With the prefetcher on (C), the hint rows at 2 MiB are below the prefetcher-off hint rows, and on E they are below the plain loop. What the counters add: on C the hint rows lower l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line from 0.9921 to 0.9934 (plain loop, 2 MiB) to 0.9066 to 0.9072 (pf4), 0.8599 to 0.8625 (pf8) and 0.8524 to 0.8536 (pf16), and raise l3d_refill_rd_per_line from 0.0008 to 0.0012 (plain) to 0.0888 to 0.1437 (hint rows) [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. On E the hint rows lower l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line to 0.4532 to 0.4650 (pf4), 0.2814 to 0.2855 (pf8) and 0.3209 to 0.3427 (pf16) against 0.9927 to 0.9932 for the plain loop, with l3d_refill_rd_per_line at most 0.0032 in every E rep [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv; 010 README line 114]. So with the hint in place, fewer L1 refills are credited to the hardware prefetcher, and the total L1 refills per line stay at about 1.0000. The pages state the result without a cause: "The software hint adds little with the hardware prefetcher on" (run 4 page section 14.3) and "The PRFM variants read below the plain loop on E" (core full page, figure in section 7). Jesse's boot C README lists the two slower rows among "the largest moves" and gives no cause. The brief page marks the L3-on speedup of the plain loop as Insufficient data. No page or README offers a mechanism for the hint rows, and no counter in the files reports requests in flight.

outlier.title: Prefetcher-off boots take 0.28 s more per large CME sweep outside the timed walks; one OCM command lived 8.4 times longer with normal timed passes
outlier.first_seen: Noted in Jesse's README for run 6 boot F2 (membench-jibin-012, file dated 2026-11-07, section 'Where the time went'). The same 0.92 s sweeps already sit in the log.txt of run 4 boots B (006) and D (008), but no README noted them before the 012 README.
outlier.what_looked_wrong: Boot F2 (prefetchers off, L3 on) took 2.839 s of chip time. Jesse's estimator gave 2.389 s. Each of the two 512 KiB to 32 MiB CME chain sweeps took 0.91 s by the log's uptime stamps. The same sweep took 0.63 s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 0.393 s by the estimator. Run 4 shows the same split: boots B and D (prefetchers off) 0.92 s, boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) 0.64, 0.63 and 0.63 s. Yet the timed walks inside each sweep got faster with the prefetchers off: the 22 timed walks add up to 157.1 ms on F2 against 163.9 to 164.0 ms on F1 (boot B 158.0 ms against boot A 164.2 ms). So the extra 0.28 s per sweep is outside the timed walks. Two more oddities: the command cme-ocm-region3-cpu2 lived 62.316 ms on F2 against 7.459 ms on F1 (8.35 times), while its timed passes read 51.734 ns best, in line with the other four regions (47.906 to 52.109 ns). And the flushed 8 MiB CME command lived 1.459 times as long (102.733 against 70.428 ms) while putting only 0.639 to 0.643 times F1's requests on each of the five home nodes; the two timed walks account for about 0.63 million of the 2.54 million fewer requests and 2.5 ms of the 32.3 ms longer life. The rest of the script ran about 0.58 s under the estimate.
outlier.why_wrong: The timed walks got faster with the prefetchers off. So the extra 0.28 s per sweep lies in untimed parts of each command: chain 0's untimed walks, the chain builds, the flushes. The files do not time those parts. The estimator (est_chip_time.py) prices every untimed part with one constant per boot (10 ns est. per chain line built, 7 ns est. per flushed line, 14 ms est. per launch), so it cannot show a prefetcher-dependent untimed cost. A single command living 8.35 times longer with unchanged timed passes has no explanation in the files: its timed passes and its mesh request counts look normal.
outlier.what_tests_showed: Not tested. The 012 README lists where the time went (uptime stamps per command) and marks the cause of the longer untimed parts and of the region 3 command as not shown by these files. No follow-up row or counter for the untimed parts appears in the primary files. Related: F1's counted core latency commands also lived 1.236 to 1.598 times run 3's (membench-jibin-011 README line 149, child_elapsed_ns).

outlier.first_seen: Run 6 boot F2 (membench-jibin-012, ran 2026-11-06 and 07 UTC) against boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, ran 2026-11-06 UTC). The 96 KiB single-call read's 1.56x advantage over its looped twin was first visible on F1 [membench-jibin-011/README.md line 228 to 235, the single-call twins table].
outlier.what_looked_wrong:
Words used here: F1 = run 6 boot F1 (L3 on, prefetchers on); F2 = run 6 boot F2 (L3 on, prefetchers off); bracket rate = aggregate_GBps, the rate over the whole timed call; in-span rate = span_GBps, the rate inside the streaming span; looped form = one call per pass; single-call form = every pass of a rep inside one call (--asm-passes); ldr16 / str16 = the 64 B-per-instruction read / write forms; best = the highest aggregate_GBps over 3 reps.

F2 against F1, best reps:
- CME read at 32 MiB: 17.699 against 36.583 GB/s (0.484). In span 17.702 against 36.591 GB/s (0.484). Reps spread 0.06 % (F2) and 0.03 % (F1) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012 and 011, line 112; reps lines 109 to 111].
- ldr16 (64 B loads) at 32 MiB: 18.036 against 36.611 GB/s (0.493) [same file, line 155].
- CME copy at 32 MiB: 34.192 against 41.235 GB/s (0.829) [same file, line 120].
- CME read at 1 MiB and 2 MiB: 32.812 against 36.640 GB/s (0.896) and 32.758 against 36.921 GB/s (0.887) [lines 82 and 97].
- ldr16 at 2 MiB: 33.811 against 37.123 GB/s (0.911) [line 141].
- CME write at 2 MiB: 39.539 against 42.639 GB/s (0.927) [line 101].
- Looped CME read at 96 KiB: 39.950 against 43.713 GB/s (0.914) [line 37].
- In each of the rows above every F2 rep lies below every F1 rep (recomputed from the rep rows).

The single-call 96 KiB read:
- 42.773 against 68.249 GB/s (0.627). In span 42.855 against 68.461 GB/s (0.626) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 012 and 011, line 21].
- Every F2 rep (37.892 to 42.773 GB/s) lies below every F1 rep (60.136 to 68.249 GB/s) [same file, lines 18 to 20; membench-jibin-012/README.md line 172].
- The other single-call rows read 0.996 to 1.010 times F1's: reads 1.010 (48 KiB), 0.996 (160 KiB), 1.010 (256 KiB); writes 1.003, 1.003, 0.996, 0.998 [same file, lines 7, 14, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56].
- On F1 the single-call 96 KiB read was 1.561 times its looped twin (68.249 against 43.713 GB/s). On F2 it was 1.071 times (42.773 against 39.950 GB/s) [asmpasses line 21 and dram-1core line 37 of 011 and 012].
- On F1 the 48 KiB single-call read reached 127.468 GB/s (F2: 128.768 GB/s, 1.010) [asmpasses line 7].

The 16 KiB rows (a 16 KiB buffer fits the 64 KiB CME L1):
- ldr16 (64 B loads): 56.267 against 46.747 GB/s (1.204, faster). In span 76.674 against 60.007 GB/s (1.278). Reps spread 0.28 % (F2) and 0.34 % (F1). Every F2 rep lies above every F1 rep [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv line 127; reps lines 124 to 126].
- 256 B-load read: 50.409 against 52.171 GB/s (0.966, slower). In span 70.424 against 73.808 GB/s (0.954). Reps spread 0.16 % (F2) and 0.63 % (F1). Every F2 rep lies below every F1 rep [same file, line 7; reps lines 4 to 6].

Writes:
- The 256 B-load write (cme-write) reads 0.927 to 1.000 times F1 across 16 KiB to 32 MiB [lines 11, 26, 41, 56, 71, 86, 101, 116].
- str16 (64 B stores) reads 1.010 at 16 KiB, 0.991 at 2 MiB and 0.992 at 32 MiB [lines 134, 148, 162].
- Single-call writes read 0.996 to 1.003 [asmpasses lines 14, 28, 42, 56].
outlier.why_wrong:
- A 16 KiB buffer fits the CME's 64 KiB L1 data cache [membench-jibin-011/README.md line 349; asimov-cme-perf.html, Words used here, CME]. So turning the prefetcher off should not change a 16 KiB row. Yet the 64 B-load form got 20 % faster and the 256 B-load form 3 % slower.
- 96 KiB exceeds the CME L1. On F1 the single-call form read 1.56 times its looped twin at 96 KiB. On F2 that advantage fell to 1.07 times. So the prefetcher made the single-call form faster past the L1. The other single-call sizes (48, 160, 256 KiB) did not move (0.996 to 1.010).
- The bandwidth rows carry no CME counters. The bandwidth program refuses --perf together with --cme [bandwidth.c line 494: "--perf counts the core cache set; it has no CME set here (latency --cme has one)"; membench-jibin-012/README.md line 142]. So no refill count sits beside any of these moves.
- The nearest pointer with counters is run 4's sequential 8 MiB CME chase (a walk in address order). Boot B (prefetchers off) read 71.740 ns per load against boot A's 21.417 ns (3.35 times slower). Boot A's CME counted 1.0000 hardware-prefetch refill per load; boot B's counted 0 [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006 and 005, cme-fresh1 and cme-best rows].

outlier.what_tests_showed:
- The 32 MiB read halves (0.484) with the prefetchers off, inside the span too (0.484). The 2 MiB read falls to 0.887. The 32 MiB write does not move (40.357 against 40.445 GB/s, 0.998). The CME page reads this as: the CME's prefetcher carries half of a DRAM stream, and the writes do not change [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6, Bandwidth by footprint]. No counter sits beside this reading, because the bandwidth rows carry none. This entry's source entry keeps the halving as a side result under cme-writes-fall-with-l3-on (a cross-reference to another entry, not checked here).
- The single-call 96 KiB read's advantage over the looped form fell from 1.561x (F1) to 1.071x (F2). Jesse's F2 README says: "These rows carry no counters, so these files do not show why" [membench-jibin-012/README.md line 172].
- For the 16 KiB 64 B-load read, Jesse's F2 README says: "These files do not show why the 16 KiB 64 B-load row got faster" [membench-jibin-012/README.md line 142]. The in-span ratio (1.278) is larger than the bracket ratio (1.204), so the gain sits inside the streaming span, not in the call overhead [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv line 127 of 012 and 011].
- No further test for the 96 KiB single-call row or the 16 KiB ldr16 row appears in CME-plan.md or message-to-jesse-round6.md (searched for single-call, 96 KiB, ldr16).

facts.topic: topology: cores and clusters
facts.fact: One Asimov hemisphere has 5 DSU clusters (DynamIQ Shared Units) of 2 Arm C1-Nano cores each, CPUs 0 to 9. DSU 0 (CPUs 0-1) runs the kernel and takes device interrupts; CPUs 2-9 are isolated (isolcpus, nohz_full, irqaffinity=0-1). Each pair {2,3}, {4,5}, {6,7}, {8,9} shares an L2, an L3, a CME and one mesh port (RN-F).
facts.value: 5 DSUs x 2 cores = 10 C1-Nano cores
facts.source: results/membench-jibin-011/README.md 'Platform facts' CPU placement (verified); results/membench-jibin-004/README.md 'Platform facts' (verified); memory asimov-cache-topology-conflict.md (verified); memory asimov-c1-cme-sources.md RTL yaml NUM_CORES 2 (verified)

facts.topic: topology: CME per DSU
facts.fact: Each DSU has one CME (Arm C1-SME2 unit, code name Griffin, r1p3) shared by its two cores; it runs their streaming-mode (SME) instructions. It has its own 64 KiB 4-way L1 data cache (1,024 lines, 16 banks, PIPT, 64 B lines, two 512-bit read paths) and a 24-entry TLB (4 KiB, 16 KiB, 64 KiB or 2 MiB pages). Path: CME L1D, then the DSU L3 memory system, then the mesh; the core's L1 and L2 are not on it. SVL = 512 bits = 64 bytes (cme_test printed svl=64). Half-matmul configuration (FULL_MATMUL FALSE).
facts.value: 1 CME per DSU; CME L1D 64 KiB 4-way; SVL 64 B
facts.source: results/membench-jibin-004/README.md 'Platform facts' CME item (verified); asimov-cme-perf.html section 3.1 lines 68-73 of stripped text (verified); memory asimov-c1-cme-sources.md RTL yaml NUM_CME 1, FULL_MATMUL FALSE, CME_SVL 512 (verified); results/membench-jibin-011/README.md cme_test output svl=64 (verified)

facts.topic: topology: L3 operating modes
facts.fact: Two DSU L3 modes appear in the runs. Snoop-filter-only (IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 = 0x0, ONE_SLICE with SFONLY): the L3 RAM keeps only the snoop filter, no lookup, no allocation, every L2 miss goes to the mesh. Full mode (0x70: bits [7:6]=01 ALL_SLICE, bits [5:4]=11 FULL_ON, cluster operating mode 7): lookup and allocation open in both halves of the L3 RAM. The stock SCP (0.48.0-nopcie.1 and earlier, through scp-v0.51.0) stages full mode for cluster 0 only, so on runs 1-3 and boots A-D the L3 of CPUs 2-9 held no data (L3 read hits 0.0000 per load at 64-512 KiB on boot C's hit set; 0xA0 == 0xA2). The rebuilt SCP 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 (boot E, F1, F2) stages full mode for clusters 1-4 before they power on (uart lines 181-187). The runtime register read (the box's /dev/ocm module file) covers CPU 2's cluster only.
facts.value: SFONLY = 0x0 (runs 1-3, boots A-D); FULL = 0x70 (boots E, F1, F2)
facts.source: results/membench-jibin-011/README.md 'The L3 and the prefetchers' (verified); memory asimov-run2-state.md line 34 (verified); asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2 and 'Words' line 84 (verified); latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 007 and 010 (recomputed: C hits 0.0000; E 0.4651/0.7508/0.9236 at 192/256/384 KiB)

facts.topic: topology: mesh
facts.fact: The interconnect is an Arm CMN S3 mesh, a 6 by 6 grid of crosspoints (XP); distance = |dx| + |dy| crosspoint steps. The kernel's arm_cmn driver maps it (arm_cmn_0, one DTC for the mesh, one DTM per crosspoint; the debugfs map in sysinfo.txt). The DSU's memory interface to the mesh is CHI, 256 bits wide (the CME page cites C1-DSU TRM 107804 chapter 2; the TRM is not on disk). Ten SBSX bridges (toward the memory controllers) sit on the west column x=0 (y=0,1,3,4,5) and the top row y=5 (x=1..5); gen_hierarchy.py asserts exactly 10 SBSX cells.
facts.value: CMN S3, 6x6 crosspoints, CHI 256-bit DSU interface, 10 SBSX
facts.source: results/membench-jibin-004/README.md 'Mesh placement' and 'Mesh PMU' (verified); asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 3 map tooltips (verified: SBSX at (0,0),(0,1),(0,3),(0,4),(0,5),(1,5),(2,5),(3,5),(4,5),(5,5)); gen_hierarchy.py lines 52-85 (verified); asimov-cme-perf.html section 3.1 line 72 (verified)

facts.topic: topology: home nodes and DSU ports
facts.fact: Five home nodes (HN-S) own all addresses; a DRAM address belongs to one by a hash, so a buffer spreads over all five. Node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 at crosspoints (1,3), (2,4), (3,3), (4,4), (5,3) hold OCM regions 0-4 (x = id bits 8-6, y = bits 5-3; recomputed for all five ids). DSU ports: DSU 0 (CPUs 0-1) at (1,2), DSU 1 (CPUs 2-3) at (2,3), DSU 2 (CPUs 4-5) at (3,2), DSU 3 (CPUs 6-7) at (4,3), DSU 4 (CPUs 8-9) at (5,2). From DSU 1's port OCM0-2 are 1 crosspoint away, OCM3-4 are 3. Mean distance of each DSU to the five nodes: DSU 1 1.8, DSU 2 2.6, DSU 3 1.8, DSU 4 3.4 (recomputed). RTL cmns3_12_1.yml: DSU ports at crosspoints 12,23,32,43,52; home nodes 13,24,33,44,53.
facts.source: gen_hierarchy.py lines 52-56 NODES, DSUS (verified); results/membench-jibin-004/README.md 'Mesh placement' (verified); memory asimov-emulator-run-facts.md second reply (verified)

facts.topic: topology: SLC
facts.fact: Each home node has a 1 MiB cache array in 16 ways (System Level Cache). The firmware locks 4 of the 16 ways of each node as OCM, so 12 ways = 768 KiB per node cache DRAM: 5 x 768 KiB = 3.75 MiB of SLC for DRAM lines, 5 MiB in all. Jesse: firmware can lock W = 1, 2, 4, 8, 12 ways (max 768 KiB per region); stock W = 4 (SAM profile cold-boot-ocm-w4). The SLC-to-DRAM step is expected near 3.75 MiB (the pages mark 4 MiB and above 'SLC and DRAM (mixed)').
facts.value: SLC 5 x 1 MiB, 16 ways; 3.75 MiB caches DRAM after the OCM lock
facts.source: results/membench-jibin-004/README.md 'Platform facts' Caches and Firmware (verified); gen_hierarchy.py lines 453-454 and 630 (verified); memory asimov-emulator-run-facts.md (verified)

facts.topic: topology: OCM
facts.fact: OCM (On-Chip Memory) is 5 regions x 256 KiB = 1.25 MiB of addressable SRAM, each region the 4 locked ways of one home node, at 0xE0000000 + n MiB (only the first 256 KiB of each 1 MiB slot is backed). Region n lives in home node n only. Mapped Normal write-back, inner shareable, through /dev/ocm (the box's membench_ocm.ko) in single 4 KiB entries on runs 1-3, boots A, B, E, F1, F2 (cont=0); boots C and D used the 64 KiB contiguous hint (cont=1, cont=64/64). ECC, not initialised at reset: write before read; a never-written line reads zeros on this image.
facts.value: 5 x 256 KiB at 0xE0n00000, one region per home node
facts.source: memory asimov-emulator-run-facts.md (verified); results/membench-jibin-011/README.md 'OCM mappings' and 'Platform facts' (verified); results/membench-jibin-007/README.md and 008/README.md cont=1, cont=64/64 (verified by grep); results/membench-jibin-004/README.md OCM (verified)

facts.topic: topology: DRAM path and memory model
facts.fact: AP DRAM is just under 2 GiB at PA 0xC000000000; Linux MemTotal 1,833,848 kB = 1.75 GiB (1.83 GB decimal), which includes the 256 reserved 2 MiB huge pages. On the emulator it is four embedded Cadence AXI memory models, one per SMS lane (XMS lanes 32-35, the AUX lanes), behind the mesh's SBSX bridges (SN nodes); not LPDDR5X, so no DRAM number is silicon-like. Every delay control on the four models is zero (read latency 0, write-response latency 0, READY delays and burst gaps 0, no bandwidth or refresh scheduler). With controls at zero the model answers 3 lane-clock cycles = 3 ns at the 1 GHz lane clock (checked only in the repo's Xcelium test, not on Palladium). By counting RTL stages (Jesse's inference): SBSX read request to first data beat is 20.0-20.5 ns for SMS ports 0-2 and 19.0-19.5 ns for port 3 (SMS bridge register 0.5 ns each way, 5-6 XMS register slices each way 2.5-3.0 ns, 2 GHz to 1 GHz crossing 7.0-7.5 ns out and 3 ns back, model 3 ns). The rest of the ~29 ns DRAM-minus-SLC gap (52.658 - 23.714 = 28.944 ns on F1, recomputed) is inside the CMN (home-node miss handling, hops to the SN nodes on the west column, CHI-to-AXI conversion), configured nowhere in the tree. Nothing models banks, rows or refresh, so delay does not depend on address order (boot B: address-order 8 MiB chain 52.762 ns, random flushed 8 MiB 52.739 ns).
facts.value: 4 Cadence AXI models, configured delay 0, native 3 ns; ~20 ns fixed RTL pipeline (inference); ~29 ns DRAM leg beyond the SLC round trip
facts.source: results/membench-jibin-011/README.md 'The memory model behind the home node' and 'Huge pages' (verified); sysinfo.txt MemTotal (verified); memory asimov-emulator-run-facts.md (verified); latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006 (recomputed 52.762 / 52.739)

facts.topic: topology: clock
facts.fact: Core clock 2.000 GHz nominal (Jesse: 2,000 MHz) against the 1 GHz generic timer (CNTFRQ 1 GHz: one tick = 1 ns = 2 cycles). The rows agree: 4.01 cycles per 2.002 ns load on the 4 KiB chase (= 2.003 GHz, the conversion the fact sheet uses) and 42.01 cycles per 21.005 ns CME round-trip hop (cme_cycles_per_load 42.0042). CME cycles per core cycle read 0.9989-1.0000 on run 3, so the CME runs on the same clock. Cycle-exact emulator, no DVFS; 1 chip second = 2,776 (run 3), 2,779 (F1), 2,780 (boot E) wall seconds.
facts.value: 2.000 GHz nominal; 2.003 GHz from the 4 KiB row (4.01 cycles / 2.002 ns)

facts.topic: prefetcher: core
facts.fact: The C1-Nano core has a hardware data prefetcher whose fills land in L1 and cause L2 refills. TF-A 0.35.0 leaves it on; TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1 turns it off (boots B, D, F2). PMU events that separate its fills: 0x03 L1D_CACHE_REFILL (every line entering L1), 0x81BC L1D_CACHE_REFILL_HWPRF (lines the prefetcher asked for), 0x17 L2D_CACHE_REFILL, 0x0111 IMP_L2D_CACHE_REFILL_L1DHWPRF (L2 refills for the L1 prefetcher's requests), 0x81BD L2 refills by the hardware prefetchers, 0xA2 L3D_CACHE_REFILL_RD [the page cites Arm C1-Nano Core TRM r0p2 sections 17.1 and 17.2; the TRM is not on disk]. Sequential 8 MiB chain, every line flushed first: boot E (L3 on) 2.492 ns per load with 1.0000 L1 refills, 0.9997 L1 prefetch refills and 0.9997 L2-for-L1-prefetch refills per load; boot B (prefetchers off) 52.762 ns with 0.0000 prefetch refills and 1.0001 L3 read refills per load.
facts.value: core L1 HW prefetcher present; events 0x81BC / 0x0111 / 0x81BD count its fills
facts.source: asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 8 lines 410-414 of stripped text (verified); latency-dram-seq.csv of 010 and 006 (recomputed); results/membench-jibin-011/README.md 'The L3 and the prefetchers' (verified: l2d_refill_hwprf_per_load 0.1120-0.2484 at 192-384 KiB on F1, recomputed from latency-dram-small.csv of 011)

facts.topic: prefetcher: in-flight reads (core)
facts.fact: Estimates from the pages, not counts: with the L3 on (boot E) the sequential 8 MiB chain's 2.49 ns per load against a 52.7 ns DRAM read puts about 21 prefetch reads in flight est. (section 8 figure: reads issued every 2.5 ns, each arriving 52.7 ns later); the 32 MiB stream (24.6 GB/s) overlaps about 20 est. with the L3 on and about 7.5 est. with it off (boot C, 9.2 GB/s, 2.8 times fewer). With the prefetchers off and the L3 off (boots B, D) the 32 MiB read is 2.377 GB/s = 26.9 ns per 64-byte line, about two lines per 52.2 ns DRAM load, almost no overlap. No counter on disk says how many requests the prefetcher keeps open; what the L3 changes in how far ahead it runs is Insufficient data (the page's own words).
facts.value: about 20-21 reads in flight est. (L3 on), about 7.5 est. (L3 off), about 2 (prefetchers off)
facts.source: asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3 'The question in one table' and section 8 (verified); bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 006, 007, 008, 010 (recomputed: 2.377 / 9.196 / 2.377 / 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB)

facts.topic: prefetcher: CME
facts.fact: The CME has its own hardware prefetcher: 128 streams, indexed by instruction address, fills the CME L1D and the DSU L3, works in virtual addresses and keeps its own TLB; its translation requests go back to the core over the CMETLB channel [the CME page cites C1-SME2 TRM 107831 table 6-1, sections 5 and 6.3, chapter 1; not on disk]. CME events: 0x327D inner refills (from inside the cluster), 0x327E outer refills, 0x3280 demand-read refills, 0x32B2 refills requested by the CME prefetcher, 0x3281 write refills (inner + outer = demand + prefetch + write on every row). Effect: the CME chain load climbs from 8 KiB on (boot E: 24.932 ns at 8 KiB, 35.065 at 16 KiB, 45.639 at 64 KiB) with 3.9868-4.0583 prefetch refills per load at 8 KiB and 9.5630-9.9390 at 16 KiB on F1 (0.0000 on boot B); with the prefetchers off (boots B, F2) the chain load stays 21.021-21.263 ns up to 64 KiB and steps to 35.979-37.162 ns at 96 KiB (the CME L1 edge). With prefetchers off the CME DRAM read at 32 MiB halves: 17.699 GB/s (F2) against 36.583 (F1).
facts.value: CME prefetcher: 128 streams, fills CME L1D and DSU L3
facts.source: asimov-cme-perf.html section 3.1 lines 69-70 and Short version (verified); cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010, 011, 006, 012 (recomputed); cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012 (recomputed); results/membench-jibin-011/README.md (verified)

facts.topic: prefetcher: which levels
facts.fact: Levels with a prefetcher in the read sources: the core's L1 data side (fills land in L1 and cause L2 refills; events 0x81BC/0x0111/0x81BD) and the CME's L1D (fills L1D and L3). No read source states whether the DSU L2 or L3 has a prefetcher of its own, nor the core prefetcher's stream count or distance. The C1-Nano SOG text extract has no hardware-prefetcher section (only PRFM instruction rows and the memcpy note 'prefetches one iteration ahead'). Whether prefetches issue before, with or after the demand load is stated nowhere; the only evidence is the sequential chain (lines arrive in L1 'before or while the load waits for them', 2.49 ns per load against the 2.00 ns L1 hit) and the page's own 'Where inside the DSU the L2 prefetch fills come from is Insufficient data'.
facts.value: insufficient data for L2/L3 prefetchers and for stream count, distance and issue timing of the core prefetcher: the C1-Nano TRM prefetch chapter or the IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 field list would give it
facts.source: asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 8 (verified); asimov-cme-perf.html section 3.1 (verified); C1-Nano SOG text extract (grep 'prefetch': line 5641 only; verified)

facts.topic: measured latency: L3
facts.fact: No footprint fits the 256 KiB L3 alone (the 128 KiB L2 is part of the path), so no pure L3-hit row exists. With the L3 on, the repeated chases read 7.821 / 9.527 / 11.004 ns at 192 / 256 / 384 KiB (boot E) and 7.825 / 9.509 / 10.986 (F1); the hit set (latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 010) counts 0.4651 / 0.7508 / 0.9236 L3 read hits per load (47 / 75 / 92 %). With the L3 off (run 3) the same rows read 14.045 / 19.333 / 22.729 ns. The page derives an L3 hit of 10.6 ns (256 KiB row) to 11.0 ns (384 KiB row) est., about 22 cycles est. Through the CME with the prefetchers off and the L3 on (F2), an L3-served chain load reads 32.779-33.910 ns at 192-384 KiB, 11.8-12.9 ns above the 21.0 ns core-to-CME round-trip baseline.

facts.fact: Arm C1-Nano Core Software Optimization Guide 109590_0001_04, section 3.11, Table 3-2 'C1-Nano cache access latencies' (page 66): L1 cache hit 2-4 cycles (2 best case, 4 normal case); L2 cache hit 10-12 cycles (10 best case, 11-12 normal case). facts.topic: Arm doc: C1-Nano core structure
facts.fact: C1-Nano SOG section 1: in-order pipeline with direct and indirect branch prediction; 128-bit SVE and SVE2; configurable vector datapath 2x64 or 2x128 bits (Asimov RTL yaml: VPU_DATAPATH 2x128); dual-core complexes share the L2 cache and VPU. Section 2.33 SME: the CPU issues at most three instructions per cycle to the C1-SME2 unit (four with MOVPRFX fusion); loads and stores two per cycle (the memory-system bandwidth is two wide); SMSTART and SMSTOP single issued. Public LLVM model (llvm-mca test refs/C1Nano-streaming-sme-only-instructions.s): FMOPA and BFMOPA za latency 4, reciprocal throughput 2.00; LD1W za 7 cycles, ST1W za 11; CLASTB to a GPR 12 cycles in streaming mode (4 non-streaming).
facts.value: in-order core, 2x128-bit VPU shared per pair, 3 SME instr/cycle to the CME
facts.source: c1nano-sog.txt lines 195-209 and 5426-5476 (verified); refs/C1Nano-streaming-sme-only-instructions.s lines 64, 85, 104, 229, 234 (verified); memory asimov-c1-cme-sources.md (verified)

facts.topic: Arm doc: CMN S3 mesh and SLC
facts.fact: CMN S3 TRM 107858 r2p3 (as memory crb-arm-docs.md records it from the PDF in the CRB refs folder): mesh of crosspoints, up to 4 device ports per XP (1.4 p17); one home node per address, each HN-S has snoop filter + SLC (p19); SLC definition 2.1.1.3 p54; SLC per node 0 to 4 MiB, 12 or 16 ways (table 1-9 p31); CAL2 = two identical devices on one XP device port (2.1.1.15 p63). Asimov's HN-S nodes use 1 MiB in 16 ways.

facts.topic: Arm doc: CME data path
facts.fact: As the CME page cites them (the TRMs are not on disk): C1-SME2 TRM 107831: the core's MMU translates the address first, so the CME receives a physical address and never asks a translation of its own for a load or store (chapter 5); CMEREQ carries the streaming request, CMETLB the CME prefetcher's translation requests back to the core (chapter 1); one SME2 unit bridge per CME (2.1); L1D 64 KiB 4-way 16-bank PIPT, two 512-bit read paths, prefetcher 128 streams (table 6-1, sections 5, 6.3). C1-DSU TRM 107804 chapter 2: the SCU snoop filter tracks the CME L1D beside the cores' caches; on a simultaneous hit the L3 supplies the line; CHI memory interface 256 bits.
facts.value: CME path: core MMU -> CMEREQ -> CME L1D -> DSU L3 (SCU) -> CHI 256-bit -> mesh
facts.source: asimov-cme-perf.html section 3.1 lines 67-73 of stripped text (verified); memory asimov-c1-cme-sources.md 'Not obtainable by script' (verified)

facts.topic: general textbook: cache latency ranges
facts.fact: Web sources, re-fetched 2026-11-08 where possible. UVM CS2210 memory-hierarchy page (fetched): L1 about 1 ns, ~3 cycles; L2 3-5 ns, ~10-15 cycles; L3/SLC 10-15 ns, ~30-45 cycles; main memory 50-100 ns, 150-300 cycles at 3 GHz. Not re-fetched here (taken from the fact sheet's search summaries): algo.monster 'L1 1-4 cycles, L2 10-20, L3 40-75, memory 100-300 cycles'; Nexthink Kaby Lake i7-7660U at 2.5 GHz: L1 5 cycles = 2 ns, L2 12 = 4.8 ns, L3 42 = 16.8 ns, memory 60-100 ns (arithmetic consistent); Cadence 'Numbers everyone should know' L1 ~4 cycles, L2 ~10, L3 ~40, local DRAM ~60 ns, remote ~100 ns (page returned 403). Asimov's measured 4 / 12 / about 22 est. / 48 (SLC) / 105 (DRAM) cycles fall in these bands; the DRAM at 52.7 ns = 105 cycles is at the fast end because the emulator's memory model has zero configured delay.
facts.source: https://www.uvm.edu/~cbcafier/cs2210/content/07_memory_hierarchy/memory_hierarchy.html (fetched 2026-11-08, verified); https://algo.monster/courses/quant/quant_cpu_cache_hierarchy and https://www.nexthink.com/blog/smarter-cpu-testing-kaby-lake-haswell-memory and https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/breakfast-bytes/posts/numbers-everyone-should-know (not re-fetched; search summaries)

facts.topic: general textbook: small Arm cores (Cortex-A510 / A720)
facts.fact: Chips and Cheese on the Arm Cortex-A510 (fetched 2026-11-08): a 3-wide in-order core (not strictly in-order: it can run past a cache miss for a limited number of instructions), 1.8 GHz maximum; 'L1 accesses complete in four cycles for simple addressing or 5 cycles for complex addressing'; 'L2 latency is somewhere between 9 to 13 cycles'; an L2 TLB hit adds 5 cycles over a dTLB hit (the TRM says 3); 'over 300 ns of memory latency' on that phone. The fact sheet's '3 cycles simple / 4 indexed' passage was not found in this fetch. Not re-fetched: Arm's Cortex-A720 announcement (L2 hit 9 cycles, 10 on A715; L1 32/64 KiB; private L2 128-512 KiB) and Cortex-X3/X4 L2 10 cycles load-to-use.
facts.value: A510: L1D 4-5 cycles, L2 9-13 cycles (fetched); A720: L2 9 cycles (search summary)
facts.source: https://old.chipsandcheese.com/2023/10/01/arms-cortex-a510-two-kids-in-a-trench-coat/ (fetched 2026-11-08, verified); https://fuse.wikichip.org/?p=7529 and https://www.anandtech.com/show/18871/arm-unveils-armv92-mobile-architecture-cortex-x4-a720-and-a520-64bit-exclusive/3 (not re-fetched)

facts.topic: method: what a chase row measures
facts.fact: A pointer chase (chain of dependent loads) gives load-to-use latency; a repeated chase walks a random chain many times (later walks hit whatever cache holds it), a fresh chain is walked once, a flushed chain had every line cleaned and invalidated (DC CIVAC) first. Sparse chains (run 3 on) use one line per 4 KiB page, so a sparse pass never revisits a page (and misses the 16-entry L1 DTLB more often than a dense pass). Refills per load come from PMU events 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2 of the best pass; a fill can be a demand miss or a prefetch. Footprint-to-level mapping: gen_hierarchy.py (run 2 table, L3 off) uses <= 24 KiB L1; 32 KiB L1 and L2; 48-128 KiB L2; 192-256 KiB 'L2, L3 and mesh (mixed)'; 384 KiB-3 MiB 'SLC (mesh cache)'; 4-8 MiB 'SLC and DRAM (mixed)'; >= 16 MiB DRAM. The boot E page (L3 on) labels 192-384 KiB 'L2 and L3 (mixed)' with the hit percentages and 512 KiB 'L3 and SLC (mixed)'.
facts.value: chase = latency; stream = bandwidth; the gap is loads in flight
facts.source: asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 1 'Words used here' and table 4.1 (verified); gen_hierarchy.py lines 293-298 (verified); results/membench-jibin-004/README.md (verified)

facts.topic: (1) which levels have a prefetcher: C1-Nano core
facts.fact: The C1-Nano core has several data-side hardware prefetchers, and the PMU has one L2-refill event per prefetcher: 0x00D9 correlating, 0x00DA spatial, 0x00DB offset, 0x010F stride, 0x0110 TLB descriptor. Which prefetcher fills which level is not stated in the local sources; the per-prefetcher events were not counted in any run (they do not fit in a 6-counter group beside the run 3 events).

facts.topic: (1) which levels have a prefetcher: Cortex-A520 (the predecessor core, public TRM) layout
facts.fact: The public Cortex-A520 TRM, the predecessor core, names: an L1 stride prefetcher (IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1.L1SPFCTL bit 7; L1SPFL2 bit 6: 0 prefetches into L1 and L3, 1 into L1 and L2), L2 spatial, pattern and offset prefetchers (L2GPFCTL bits 21:20, L2PPFCTL 12:11, L2OPFCTL 10:9), an L3 stride and an L3 offset prefetcher (L3SPFCTL 16:15, L3OPFCTL 14:13), an L2 TLB prefetcher (event 0x00DD L2D_CACHE_REFILL_HWPRF_TLBD), per-prefetcher events 0x00DA spatial, 0x00DB offset, 0x00DC pattern, 0x00DE L3 stride, 0x00DF L3 offset, and a translation table prefetcher in the MMU. Section 'Hardware data prefetcher': 'The core includes multiple data prefetchers ... These linefills can be in the L1 data cache, the L2 cache, or the L3 cache, depending on which cache the hardware selects.' The C1-Nano's own TRM (107753) is not on this disk, so whether the C1-Nano keeps this exact layout is not confirmed; the C1-Nano event list (0x00D9 to 0x0110) names a correlating prefetcher that the A520 list does not.
facts.value: A520: L1 stride; L2 spatial, pattern, offset, TLB; L3 stride, offset; MMU table prefetcher
facts.source: Arm Cortex-A520 Core TRM 102517_0001_04_en: text at /tmp/claude-0/-home-jhan-workspace-titan-cache-perf-asimov/ca8b250c-52a6-45d3-bbc5-a704f24ca1dd/scratchpad/a520-trm.txt lines 4041 to 4058 (section 8.5), 15225 to 15320 (IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bits, printed page 194 to 195), 8780 to 8825 (events 0x00DA to 0x00DF), 3238 and 3286 (MMU prefetchers); verified 2026-11-08 against the text; the PDF page numbers 78 to 79 and 135 to 136 were not rechecked

facts.topic: (1) which levels have a prefetcher: CME has its own
facts.fact: The CME (C1-SME2 unit) has its own hardware prefetcher: 128 streams, indexed by instruction address, filling the CME's 64 KiB 4-way L1D and the DSU L3. It works in virtual addresses and keeps its own TLB. A second DSU channel (CMETLB) carries the prefetcher's translation requests back to the core.

facts.topic: (2) timing: the prefetcher trains on a pattern and runs ahead of the demand loads
facts.fact: On the sequential chain with the prefetchers on (boot E, L3 on) every line is still read from DRAM once (1.00 L2 refills per load, lines flushed first), and each load takes 2.492 ns (rep 2; rep 1 2.501). The prefetcher issues reads ahead of the loads, about 21 at a time (est., derived from 52.7 ns per DRAM read divided by 2.49 ns per load). The lines arrive in L1 (0.9997 L1 prefetch refills per load) before or while the load waits. The same chain with the prefetchers off (boot B) takes 52.762 ns per load, one DRAM read per load with no overlap, equal to boot B's own random flushed chain (52.739 ns) and to boot E's random flushed chain (52.659 ns, the 52.66 ns the page's diagram uses).
facts.value: 2.492 ns per load (E, on) against 52.762 ns (B, off); about 21 reads in flight est.
facts.source: /home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf/asimov/asimov-c1nano-perf.html, wall-clock diagram and 'With the prefetchers on the same DRAM reads overlap' paragraph; results/membench-jibin-010/results/bootE/latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv; results/membench-jibin-006/results/bootB/latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv (all recomputed 2026-11-08)

facts.topic: (2) timing: the prefetcher cannot help a dependent random chain
facts.fact: Over the 24 random chase rows from 4 KiB to 32 MiB, boot B (prefetchers off) is within -5.6 % to +5.3 % of boot A (on). A dependent random chase gives a prefetcher nothing to follow: the next address is inside the line being read, so one read must finish before the next starts. The chase latencies are therefore the levels' own on both boots. The 32 MiB row reads 52.181 ns (A) against 52.248 ns (B, +0.13 %); the 8 MiB flushed row 52.739 on both.

facts.topic: (2) timing: the prefetcher's requests cause their own page walks
facts.fact: On boot A the sparse and vary OCM rows count 0.16 to 1.24 walks per load (0x34) and 0.000 L2 TLB refills (sparse chains alone: 0.27 to 1.24); on boot B (prefetchers off) the walks fall to 0.00 and the L1 TLB refills to 0.42 to 0.76 per load. On boot D (hint, prefetchers off) all three walk events read 0 in every one of the 35 passes; on C and E (prefetchers on) 0x34 counts up to 2.61 and 2.80 walks per load, in 33 and 32 of 35 passes. So the walks on the prefetcher-on boots are translations for the prefetcher's requests into other pages, which are not installed in the L2 TLB as demand refills (hypothesis, consistent across four boots).
facts.source: /home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf/asimov/asimov-c1nano-run4.html sections 7 ('Walks without L2 TLB refills'), 11.5 (H3 line) and 13.3 ('The walks are the prefetchers'')

facts.topic: (2) timing: CME prefetcher stream ends and virtual-address behaviour
facts.fact: Prefetch streams end when the pattern breaks, on a DSB, on a WFI or WFE wakeup, or when a data cache maintenance operation commits; the prefetcher is based on virtual addresses and crosses page boundaries while the new page is cacheable and readable. This is the Cortex-A520 TRM's statement for the core's prefetchers (predecessor core), not for the CME; the C1-Nano TRM is not on disk. The sessions' chains flush lines with cache maintenance before the timed walk, which by this rule ends any stream before each pass.
facts.value: stream ends on pattern break, DSB, WFI/WFE wakeup, DC maintenance; virtual-address based

facts.topic: (4) firmware: the registers and bits

mergeNotes: Merge of 17 extractor outputs into 41 distinct outliers, ordered by first appearance (the 'order' field; 'read-stream-rise-l3-on' and the later CME items carry their true chronological order numbers 26 to 31 even where the JSON list position differs). Same phenomena reported by several sources were merged; merged_from lists source key and title. Numbers prefer those that cite a file; where sources disagreed (for example the CME 48 KiB prefetch refills 17.37 vs 17.47, boot A sparse-dense gap by best vs median), both are kept in the numbers or prose. Hypothesis labels used across the sources: H1 prefetch fills on sparse rows, H2 fixed in-page offset, H3 TLB walks per sparse load, H4 64 KiB contiguous hint, H5 X vs Y step cost, H6 per-pass build difference, H7 software prefetch raises one-core read, H8 per-pass cost on the L1 read, H9 CRB slow reps, H10 posted stores, H11 fold cost. Folder map: 001 run 1, 002 run 2, 003 control, 004 run 3, 005-008 boots A-D, 010 boot E, 011/012 boots F1/F2. Items folded into other entries rather than listed separately: boot E OCM1 28.98 ns (in the CME OCM entry), cme-call two-group pattern and the 82.6 ns rep (CME 21 ns entry), CME 32 KiB +6.13 % and per-region 8 % moves on boot A (noise entry), G6 flit counts and OCM mapping alignment draw (mesh-distance and sparse-vs-dense entries), G7 PRFM slower with prefetchers on (9.2 GB/s and read-rise entries), F2 CME DRAM read halving and CME L1 half-rate stores (CME-writes entry), CME L3-event population check (L3-on CME entry), the 256 KiB read slower than OCM and the asimov-bench 15.16 ns L3 gap (L3-held-no-data entry), the per-call write 8 KiB 14 ns step and looped-write non-linearity (per-call cost entry), CPU 6 2 MiB +2.56 % (SLC transition entry). Platform facts the architecture section can reuse (from the sources, verbatim where possible): 5 DSUs x 2 C1-Nano cores (CPUs 0-1 kernel, 2-9 tests), 2.003 GHz core clock (4.01 cycles per 2.002 ns L1 chase), 1 GHz CNTFRQ timer; C1-Nano in order (TRM r0p2 section 1.1), dual 128-bit read path 64 GB/s, single 128-bit write path 32 GB/s; L1 32 KiB I + 32 KiB D per core, L2 128 KiB and L3 256 KiB (one slice, two power portions) per DSU, 64 B lines; L1 data TLB 16 entries, holds a 64 KiB contiguous block as two 32 KiB entries; CMN S3 6x6 mesh, DSU ports at crosspoints (2,3),(3,2),(4,3),(5,2), OCM0-4 home nodes (HN-S ids 88,160,216,288,344) at (1,3),(2,4),(3,3),(4,4),(5,3), distance = |dx|+|dy|, about 2.0 ns per X step and 1.0 ns per Y step (boot B fit); each home node 1 MiB in 16 ways, 4 ways locked as 256 KiB OCM (CMN OCM mode, no memory behind), 768 KiB SLC per node, 3.75 MiB SLC caching DRAM; DRAM behind SBSX bridges to four Cadence AXI memory models with zero delay controls (3 ns native response, about 20 ns RTL pipeline by Jesse's count), no bank/row/refresh model; CME = Arm C1-SME2 (Griffin) r1p3, one per DSU, SVL 512 bits, half matmul, 64 KiB 4-way L1 with 16 banks, own TLB, own 128-stream hardware prefetcher that fills the CME L1 and the DSU L3, path CME L1 -> DSU L3 -> mesh (core L1/L2 not on it); the CME prefetcher runs on random chains, the core's does not. Measured levels on CPU 2 (boot E): L1 2.0 ns, L2 6.0 to 6.1 ns, L3 hit 10.6 to 11.0 ns est., OCM 26.1 ns (dense all-five; 19.6/21.8/24.6 ns at 1/3/5 crosspoints on run 2), SLC 24.2 ns, DRAM 52.7 ns; CME round trip 21.0 ns, CME L3-served load 32.8 to 33.9 ns, CME demand-only OCM 47.9 to 52.1 ns, CME DRAM 71.7 ns. Prefetcher facts: core events 0x81BC (L1 HW prefetch refills), 0x81BD (L2 HW prefetch refills), 0x0111 (L2 refills for the L1 prefetcher), per-prefetcher events 0x00D9 correlating, 0x00DA spatial, 0x00DB offset, 0x010F stride, 0x0110 TLB descriptor (not run); switches IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 ALLPFDIS (core), IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 PF_DISABLE (CME), translation prefetch bits in IMP_CMPXECTLR_EL1; CME events 0x3246 cycles, 0x327D inner, 0x327E outer, 0x3280 demand read, 0x32B2 HW prefetch, 0x3281 write, 0x328E/F/0x3290 L3 hit/miss/refill. In-flight evidence: a sequential DRAM stream keeps about 21 reads in flight est. with the L3 on (2.49 ns per load vs 52.7 ns DRAM) and about 7.6 est. with it off (6.92 ns); with no hardware prefetcher a plain read keeps about two lines per DRAM load (2.38 GB/s); software PRFM 4 lines ahead gives 12.1 / 6.3 GB/s with the hardware prefetcher off. Whether prefetches issue before, with or after the demand load is stated only as 'the prefetcher issues reads ahead of the loads; lines arrive in L1 before or while the load waits' (core page section 8); no source gives the maximum number of in-flight prefetches, and the PMU has no outstanding-miss counter. Two items Jibin chose to leave open by decision: the 0.1 to 0.3 us CME per-span cost and two cores of one DSU in streaming mode at once.

The prefetched lines did not pass through the L3 (0.0001 L3 read refills per load). Whether prefetches issue before, with or after the demand load is not stated on this page beyond "the prefetcher issues reads ahead of the loads" and "the lines arrive in L1 before or while the load waits".

Not on this page (for the peer sources): the run 1 and run 2 first-look outliers, the control run 3 (003) firmware story beyond one line (SCP 0.34.0 gave 87 to 89 GB/s multi-core writes), the CME outliers' explanations (asimov-cme-perf.html), and the SPM phase (postponed, no /dev/asimov-spm).
